David tells her everything is fine, but at night he lies awake replaying the crash-not the moment of impact, but the seconds before, when the truck was still far away and he could have braked earlier, could have seen it coming. He replays the decision, trying to find a way to avoid it altogether.

At home, his wife, Alani, has noticed the changes. She says he is not present. He sits with her during dinner but his mind is elsewhere. He has stopped going to their weekly community gatherings-the small Pacific Islander cultural group they helped found. He used to love the singing, the shared stories. Now he cannot bear the noise, the sudden movements when someone stands up quickly. He flinches. He tells Alani he is just tired, but he knows she is hurt. He feels a distance opening between them that he does not know how to close.

He has nightmares three or four times a week. Sometimes he wakes up screaming, but more often he wakes up in a state of frozen stillness, unable to move, convinced the bed is spinning. He does not tell Alani about those nights. He lies there until his heart slows down, then gets up and goes to his home office, where he opens spreadsheets and stares at them until dawn.

The PCL-5 score of 65 reflects what he carries: the intrusive images that arrive without warning, the guilt over surviving when the truck driver walked away unharmed, the feeling that the world he once trusted is now unpredictable. He has stopped believing in luck, or in planning. Every analysis he does now feels provisional, fragile. He cannot commit to a projection because he knows, with a certainty that has no basis in logic, that something can always come out of nowhere and destroy everything.

He does not use the word trauma. He says he is just having a hard time. But he keeps showing up to our sessions, and sometimes, when he talks about the seconds before the crash, his voice drops to a whisper. He is trying to find a way back to the man he was before the truck drifted into his lane. He is not sure that man exists anymore.

He was eighteen, a first-year student at a university in a city that felt vast and promising. She was a classmate from his UX design course, someone he had helped a few times with Figma layouts. That was all. Within weeks, her messages multiplied - first on the class group, then private DMs, then texts, then calls at 2 a.m. He asked her to stop. She didn't. She began waiting for him outside the design studio, sitting two rows behind him in lectures, appearing at the coffee shop he visited every morning. He changed his routine. She seemed to know it anyway. He moved dorm rooms. She left a note under his new door. The university's security office said they couldn't do much unless she threatened him. She never did. She only watched.

For six months he lived in a state of low, constant dread. His grades slipped. He stopped using the campus app to check his schedule. He wore headphones even when listening to nothing, so he wouldn't have to hear footsteps behind him. The police finally got involved when she followed him onto a bus and sat directly beside him, despite empty seats. A restraining order was issued. She transferred schools. He has not seen her in a year.

Now he is nineteen. He still works as a UX designer, a role he landed through a paid internship that turned full-time. In theory, the job is perfect - he designs interfaces that feel intuitive and safe. But in practice, his office is an open-plan floor, and someone is always walking behind his desk. He cannot focus. He hears her presence in the creak of every chair, every soft cough. He keeps his laptop screen angled away from the aisle. When a colleague approaches from behind, he flinches. Once, he accidentally knocked over his coffee. Now he works from home three days a week, and even there he sits with his back to a wall, his phone face-up and buzzing.

His PCL-5 score is 65. In the sessions, he speaks of the stalking as if it were ongoing. He replays the moments when she appeared - the way she would tilt her head and smile, as though his fear was a private joke. He has nightmares of being followed through endless, identical corridors. He wakes sweating, heart hammering, and checks the locks on his apartment door twice. He avoids the coffee shop near his old university. He deleted all social media accounts. He bought a new phone number, but still feels a phantom vibration in his pocket.

He does not date. The thought of someone taking an interest in him, even kindly, sends a current of cold fear through his chest. He has told his parents back home (they live in Ghana) that everything is fine. He cannot bring himself to explain why he is so tired all the time, why he has stopped answering video calls. His boss has noticed the drop in productivity. The project he is leading - a health app for people with chronic anxiety - is behind schedule. He sits in front of his wireframes, the cursor blinking, and thinks: She is still out there. She knows my name. She knows where I work. He has started taking different routes home, even though he knows it makes no sense. The past tense has not become the past. It is, for him, still unfolding.

He was in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, hired by a geographic magazine to document the last traditional salt caravans. The terrain was brutal-slick mud under a canopy of dripping leaves, the air thick with the smell of wet earth and woodsmoke. He had been walking for three days with a local guide when they were stopped by a group of armed men. The guide tried to explain, but the men's faces were hard, their eyes moving over him like they were inspecting goods. He remembers the click of the safety on an old M16, the cold pressure of a gun barrel against his temple, and then the cloth bag thrown over his head.

For eleven weeks he was held in a bamboo hut, his wrists bound with rough nylon rope that left deep red grooves in his skin. The men spoke a language he did not understand, but he learned to read their moods by the tone of their shouts and the way they slammed the door. He was fed once a day-mushy sweet potato and sometimes a piece of gristly meat. Most of the time he was alone, staring at the mud wall, listening to the rain drumming on the roof. He tried to remember his wife's face, but after a while even her features blurred. He counted the days by the light through a crack in the wall. He lost count.

Now, three years later, he is back home in the coastal town where he and his wife moved decades ago. He is fifty-three years old. He tries to work, but photography has become a different kind of captivity. When he lifts his camera, his hands shake. The viewfinder once gave him a frame of control over the chaos of the world; now it feels like a tiny cell. He takes pictures only of empty landscapes-seascapes, empty streets, buildings with no people. If a person walks into the frame, he waits until they leave. He cannot photograph faces anymore. The eyes remind him of the men who kept him.

His wife has learned to be quiet in the morning. He wakes with a start, heart hammering, convinced he is back in the hut. The ceiling fan sounds like the rotor of an approaching helicopter. The smell of frying fish in the kitchen becomes the smell of cooking sweet potato on a smoky fire. He has to go outside to breathe. He sits on the back step and checks the perimeter of the garden three times before he can calm down.

The PCL-5 score of 62 is a number on paper. In his life, it means he cannot go to the grocery store on Saturdays because the crowded aisles make him feel trapped. It means he has stopped answering his phone because unexpected calls trigger a cold sweat. It means he replays the captivity every night in dreams that leave him gasping, and then he replays it again during the day in fragments-the taste of the cloth bag, the ache in his shoulders, the moment he heard a gunshot and thought it was his last.

His wife asked him last week to take her portrait for a family gift. He picked up the camera, adjusted the lens, and saw her face. He saw the worry lines, the gray in her hair, the love she still holds for him. He lowered the camera. "Not today," he said. He has not touched it since.

He sits in his corner office on the twenty-second floor, the afternoon sun glinting off the harbor. The city spreads out below him-ferries cutting white lines across the blue, cranes swinging over the port. He has been a publisher for thirty-seven years, long enough to have printed the stories of a thousand others, but now he cannot read a single page of his own life. His hands rest on the desk, still as stone, though inside his chest something trembles.

Five years ago, during the annual island festival, he stood with his wife on a newly built grandstand. The wood was still pale, the nails bright. A local band was playing, and the crowd-hundreds of families-clapped in rhythm. The structure groaned once, then twice, then the world split. He remembers the sound: not a crack but a deep, wet snap, like a palm tree giving way in a storm. The platform tilted, and people slid. He grabbed his wife's arm, pulled her toward the edge, and they fell together onto the grass. Behind him, the grandstand folded like a cardboard box. Dust, screams, a child's shoe lying on its side. He helped a woman with a broken leg, then another, then his hands were covered in someone else's blood, and he could not stop shaking.

The disaster was man-made-the builders had used untreated timber, the bolts were undersized, the permits were rushed. Twelve people died. Thirty more were injured. He was one of the lucky ones, the papers said. He even wrote a front-page editorial calling for accountability. But the words came from a place that was already crumbling.

Now he rarely takes the ferry. He drives instead, even though the traffic costs him an hour each day. The ferry dock smells like salt and diesel, and when the horn sounds, his throat closes. He cannot watch people line up at the railing. His wife has learned to book appointments on the mainland only when he is away. She does not complain. At night, he wakes drenched, the dream always the same: he is under the grandstand, pinned, and no one hears him. He does not scream out loud anymore. He lies still, counting her breaths until the shaking stops.

At work, his editorial meetings have become unbearable. He cancels them, sends emails instead. His assistant brings him manuscripts about hurricanes, courtroom dramas, survival stories. He cannot finish them. The latest is a memoir by a woman who escaped a burning building, and he has been editing the same sentence for three weeks: I ran because the fire was behind me. He wants to write in the margin, But what if the fire is inside? Instead, he closes the file.

He has not attended a festival since. Not a parade, not a school play, not even the book launch for his own anniversary edition. He tells people he is busy, but his wife knows. She finds him standing in the dark hallway at 3 a.m., staring at a framed photograph of the island before the fall. He does not turn on the light.

Yesterday, walking home from the station, a delivery truck backfired. He dropped his briefcase, spun around, and crouched behind a mailbox. A teenager on a skateboard laughed. His wife, who had been waiting at the gate, ran to him. She put her hand on his shoulder, and he flinched-not from her, but from the memory of the wood snapping. He whispered, "I'm sorry." She said nothing, just held him until his heart slowed.

In the morning, he will go back to the office. He will stare at the harbor. He will open the manuscript and read the same line again. The work of words is all he knows. But the story he carries has no ending, and he is still inside it.

After several sessions, Mrs. Anowa has begun to share the story of what happened. She speaks in a measured, deliberate tone, the same rhythm she once used to brief ministry officials on complex policy proposals. Now, however, her words carry a weight that settles in the room long after she has finished speaking.

It was a Tuesday afternoon in late November, two years ago. She had just left a meeting at the Ministry of Finance, where she had presented a 50-page analysis on urban housing subsidies-a document she had spent months refining. At eighty, she had no intention of retiring. Her mind was still sharp, her opinions still sought after. She drove her old sedan, the same one her late husband had bought in 1995, along the highway toward her apartment in the eastern suburbs. The rain had started suddenly, a violent West African downpour that turned the asphalt into a mirror of grey sky. She slowed down, gripping the wheel with both hands, her knuckles pale.

The lorry came from her left, running a red light at the intersection. She remembers the sound-a deep, metallic groan mixed with the shattering of glass. Then nothing. She woke up in the hospital three days later, her right leg in traction, four ribs cracked, a deep gash across her forehead. The doctors said she was lucky. The lorry had crushed the driver's side door, but the old sedan's frame had held. She should have died.

Now, two years later, Mrs. Anowa no longer drives. She cannot even sit in the passenger seat of a car without feeling her chest tighten. The first time her daughter tried to take her to the market, she began hyperventilating before they had left the driveway. Her daughter turned back, frustrated and frightened. Mrs. Anowa now takes taxis only when absolutely necessary, and only if she sits in the back seat behind the driver, where she can see both side mirrors. She grips the door handle the entire ride, her eyes fixed on the road ahead, counting the seconds until she can step out onto solid ground.

Her work has suffered. As a policy analyst, she used to thrive on field visits-travelling to rural districts to interview community leaders, assess infrastructure needs, gather data. Now she refuses all assignments that require travel. Her supervisor has been patient, but the team has begun to assign her only desk-based tasks. She spends long hours alone in her office, staring at the same paragraph on a report without reading it. Her mind drifts to the sound of crunching metal, the smell of gasoline and wet earth. She has stopped taking public transport altogether; the honking of buses triggers a cold sweat.

At night, she sleeps in the armchair in her living room, the television on low. The bedroom reminds her of the hospital bed. She dreams of the collision-not the impact, but the moments before it, the headlights of the lorry growing larger, the rain on the windshield. She wakes up gasping, her hands reaching for a steering wheel that isn't there. She no longer calls her daughter, because she doesn't want to worry her. Instead, she sits in the dark, repeating the breathing exercises the physiotherapist taught her for the ribs.

She has not told anyone about the sudden, sharp rages that overtake her when she hears a car horn or sees a truck in her peripheral vision. She has not told anyone that she sometimes wishes she had died in the crash, because then she would not have to live with this constant vigilance, this sense that every intersection is a potential end. She has not told anyone that she misses the woman she used to be-the one who drove confidently through city traffic, who argued with taxi drivers, who traveled to remote villages without a second thought.

Yesterday, during our session, she said quietly, "I used to think policy was about controlling the future. Now I know that nothing is under control. A red light means nothing." She looked down at her hands, the same hands that once typed lengthy reports, now trembling slightly on her lap. She has not touched her policy briefs in three weeks.

She was driving home from her shop late on a Tuesday evening, the back seat full of fabric rolls she'd picked up from the supplier. The intersection was familiar-she'd crossed it a hundred times. The truck came from the left, running a red light at what the police report later described as "excessive speed." She remembers only the sound: a metallic scream, glass shattering, and then silence. When she opened her eyes, her hands were still gripping the steering wheel, but the wheel was crumpled against her chest. The airbag had deployed, leaving a chemical burn across her forearms. Someone was yelling outside. She couldn't move her legs for a few seconds, though they were unhurt. The paramedics cut the door open. She kept asking about the fabric in the back seat.

That was eight months ago. The physical injuries healed-a cracked rib, some deep bruising, a small scar above her left eyebrow that she covers with her headscarf now. But the other part did not heal. She tells me this sitting in my office, her hands folded in her lap, the fingers still steady from years of stitching, but her eyes darting to the window every time a car passes on the street below.

She stopped driving completely. At first, she told herself it was temporary-she would take the bus until the trembling stopped. But the bus felt worse. Every sudden brake, every honk, every time the driver turned left across traffic made her stomach drop, her palms slick with sweat. She started walking instead, even in the winter rain, even when the walk took forty-five minutes each way. She leaves her shop early now, before dark, because night driving triggers the same headlight glare she saw before the impact. Her mother calls her paranoid. Her younger brother offers to drive her, but she refuses-she cannot sit in a passenger seat without clutching the door handle, her foot pressing an imaginary brake.

The tailoring work itself has changed. She used to take pride in her precision-seam allowances exact to the millimeter, hems straight and clean. Now she makes mistakes. She measures twice, cuts once, then doubts herself and measures again. Her boss, the owner of the small alterations shop, has noticed. Last week he told her, gently, that she had sewn a sleeve inside out. She laughed it off, but later, in the bathroom, she stood with her forehead against the cold tile, unable to stop the replay of the crash in her mind. The sound of twisting metal. The smell of gasoline and burnt rubber. She sees it most at night, when she lies down and the day's quiet allows the images to surface. She has not slept through the night since the accident. She wakes at 3:47 AM, the exact time the emergency room clock showed when the nurse asked for her insurance card.

She has stopped meeting her friends for coffee. They used to gather at a café near the old fabric market, but the café is two blocks from the intersection. She cannot go near it. She takes the long way around, even if it means extra time. Her social circle has narrowed to her mother on the phone and a few customers who ask for her by name. She tells herself she is fine. She tells herself it was just a car accident, people survive worse. But her body tells a different story. Her heart races when she hears a truck's air brake. She flinches when a door slams. She has stopped wearing her favorite perfume because the scent reminds her of the floral air freshener dangling from the rearview mirror of the car that hit her.

Last week, a customer brought in a wedding dress that needed beading. The bride's mother stood beside her, animatedly describing the lace overlay. Halfway through, a delivery truck rumbled past the shop window. She froze. The words left her. For a long moment she could not hear the woman-she was back in the driver's seat, watching the headlights grow. She excused herself, went to the back room, and sat on a spool of thread until her hands stopped shaking.

She is here, in my office, because her mother insisted. She does not think she needs help. She thinks she just needs to stop remembering.

Sulochana is sixty-one years old, though her hands look older-cracked and calloused from forty years of bending over rows of okra and brinjal in the coastal farmlands of Gujarat. She tells this story in a low, steady voice, her eyes fixed on a spot on the floor, as if she is watching a scene unfold in a puddle of rainwater.

It happened when she was nineteen, newly married and living with her husband's family in a village near the river. Her husband worked on a tractor for a larger landowner, and she helped with the harvests alongside two other women from the compound. One afternoon, the women sent her back alone to fetch a sickle from the field hut. Inside the hut, a man she knew-a distant cousin of her mother-in-law-was waiting. He grabbed her wrist, pulled her to the dirt floor, and put his hand over her mouth. She remembers the smell of his skin, the sound of her own teeth scraping against his palm, the way the mud pressed cold against her back.

Afterward, she walked home with the sickle. She did not cry. She washed herself at the pump, changed her sari, and served dinner to her husband and in-laws. She told no one. In her mind, she believed she had done something wrong-perhaps she had smiled too much, walked too slowly, worn her dupatta too loosely. For years, she held that belief like a stone in her belly.

Now, here in the therapist's room, Sulochana still does not say the word "rape." She gestures toward her own body and says, "He took something that was not his." Her voice does not waver, but her fingers twist the edge of her chunni until the fabric is damp.

In the decades that followed, she worked. That is the word she uses: "I worked." She rose before dawn, walked to the fields, and bent until her back screamed. The work was a container-a way to fill the hours so there was no room to think. But the thinking found its own way. When she hoes the earth, a certain shape of shadow under a banyan tree will make her freeze, and she will see the dim light of the hut. When a man calls out her name unexpectedly, her breath stops, and she turns very slowly, as if bracing for a blow. The other women have noticed; they say she is "nervous" or "proud." She lets them think that.

She has a husband who is kind in his way-he never raises his voice, brings her tea in the evening. But she has never told him. She cannot. She imagines his face, the way it would collapse into pity or shame, and she feels the old stone grow heavier. At night, when he touches her shoulder, she lies perfectly still, pretending to sleep. She has been pretending for forty-two years.

Her PCL-5 score of seventy-two reflects what she does not say out loud: the nightmares that wake her at three in the morning, drenched in sweat, her heart pounding against her ribs like a trapped bird. She has learned to fall asleep again quickly, before her husband stirs. In the fields, she is hypervigilant-she always positions herself with her back to a tree, facing the path. She avoids the village temple where the cousin sometimes visits for festivals. She has not gone inside a room with a closed door and no windows in thirty years; when she must enter the storage shed for seed bags, she first leaves the door propped open with a stone.

Her body remembers what her mind tries to bury. Her shoulders are permanently hunched, as if bracing for contact. Her stomach clenches at the smell of rain on dry mud. She has lost count of the days she has missed work because a sudden sound-a door slamming, a man's laugh-sent her into a shaking spell that she calls "the fever." Her daughter-in-law, worried, brought her to the clinic.

Sulochana sits now in the quiet room, her hands still. She does not know why she is telling this story. She only knows that the stone inside her has grown too heavy to carry alone, and the fields are not big enough anymore to hold it. She waits for the next session, unsure of what she wants, but certain she cannot keep bending.

She arrives ten minutes early for every session, always taking the same seat-the one with her back to the wall. Her eyes sweep the room once, then fix on the clock above my desk. For the first few minutes, her hands remain folded in her lap, perfectly still, as if she is practicing restraint.

Mrs. Lien is seventy-one, a divorced Southeast Asian woman who still works part-time as a financial analyst. She tells me she likes numbers because they are predictable. "Numbers don't lie, and they don't hurt you," she said in our second session. Her colleagues describe her as meticulous, almost obsessive about checking spreadsheets for errors. She volunteers for the most tedious audits, preferring the quiet of a closed office to the open floor plan she once shared with a team.

The trauma she carries began fifty-three years ago, when she was eighteen and living in a small coastal town. During a period of political upheaval, soldiers came to her home. She was taken from her family and held in a makeshift detention center for eleven months. She rarely speaks of what happened there, but fragments have emerged over our sessions: the damp concrete floor, the constant hunger, the sound of guards' boots echoing down a corridor. She was released after her brother paid a ransom, but her parents had already fled the country. She never saw them again.

In the years that followed, Mrs. Lien married a man she met in a refugee camp, moved to the United States, and built a career in finance. She learned to speak English without an accent, raised two children, and filed for divorce at age fifty-eight after decades of a cold, silent marriage. She tells me she left him not because he was cruel, but because she realized she had never trusted anyone-not even him.

Now, her days are structured around routines that keep her safe. She wakes at five-thirty every morning, drinks one cup of black coffee, and reviews the previous day's stock market data. She avoids leaving her apartment after dark. She has not gone to a movie theater or a crowded grocery store in years. The sound of a motorcycle backfiring on the street can send her heart racing for hours. She keeps her back to the wall in restaurants, and she always chooses a table near the exit.

Her children live in other states, and she speaks to them by phone once a week. She feels a distance she cannot explain-a wall between herself and the world. In our sessions, she sometimes stops mid-sentence, her eyes losing focus. When I ask what she was thinking, she says, "Nothing. Just a memory." She does not elaborate.

At work, she has become increasingly irritable with junior analysts who leave data incomplete. Her supervisor has noticed she seems "on edge" and recommended a medical leave, but she refused. "If I stop working, I'll just sit there," she told me. "I'll think too much."

She dreams of the concrete floor. In the dream, she is still eighteen, still waiting. She wakes with her hands clenched, her jaw tight. She does not cry when she tells me this. She simply folds her hands, perfectly still, and waits for the next question.

She is forty-four years old, a diplomat from a Latin American country who has spent the last twenty years moving between capitals, negotiating treaties, and representing her nation with a calm, polished professionalism. Her apartment is filled with artifacts from posts abroad-a handwoven rug from the Middle East, a small jade Buddha from Southeast Asia-but lately she cannot bring herself to look at them. The memories they carry feel too heavy.

Three years ago, she was stationed in a city that has since become a byword for siege and destruction. She had been there for eighteen months, living in a secured compound with other international staff. The war escalated slowly at first, then in a terrifying rush. She remembers the morning the first shell hit a block away-a sound so loud it seemed to come from inside her own chest. She threw herself to the floor, and for the next six weeks she lived in the basement of the embassy, sleeping on a camp cot, listening to the rumble of mortars and the crack of small-arms fire. The electricity was intermittent, the water unsafe. She lost ten pounds. She stopped changing clothes. The constant, low-grade terror was like a second skin.

On the thirty-fourth day of the siege, a sniper killed a colleague who was walking three steps ahead of her-a young man from her country who had been teaching English to local children. She saw him fall. She saw the blood spread in a dark puddle on the concrete. She did not move. She could not scream. Someone pulled her inside, and she sat in a corner for two hours, shaking, unable to speak.

The evacuation came on a choppy night flight, with no lights, no windows. She does not remember much of the journey. What she remembers is the silence when the plane touched down on home soil-the absence of explosions, of sirens, of her own ragged breathing. She thought she would feel relief. Instead, she felt hollow, as if part of her had been left behind in that basement.

Now, back in the capital, she works in the foreign ministry, coordinating policy for her region. She is good at her job-precise, diplomatic, unflappable. But the office feels wrong. The high ceilings make her anxious; she cannot sit with her back to the door. Every time a phone rings too loudly, she flinches. Her colleagues notice. They say she seems distracted, that she sometimes stares at the wall during meetings. She has stopped attending large conferences, claiming schedule conflicts. The truth is that crowds make her dizzy, her chest tight, her palms slick.

At night, she cannot sleep. She lies awake, replaying the sound of the mortar shell, the sight of her colleague falling. Sometimes she dreams she is back in the basement, but in the dream the walls are closing in. She wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat, and then stays awake until dawn, afraid of what the next dream might bring. She drinks more coffee than she should, and she has started checking the locks on her apartment door three times before bed. She knows this is irrational-her building is safe, her country is not at war-but the compulsion feels necessary, like a prayer.

She has not told anyone at work about the nightmares. She does not want to seem weak. She was trained to handle crisis, to project authority. But the authority has become a mask. Beneath it, she is always scanning for danger, always listening for the sound of a shell, always measuring the distance to the nearest exit.

She canceled her last two vacations, citing workload. In truth, she cannot imagine sitting on a plane again, not knowing where the next explosion might come from. She avoids news coverage of the war she fled; a single image of rubble can send her heart racing for hours. She has stopped seeing friends, stopped going to restaurants. The world outside feels unpredictable, hostile.

She sits in her therapist's office, hands folded neatly in her lap, and describes these things in a measured, clinical tone, as if she were briefieng a superior. But her eyes are wide, watchful. She says she wants to feel normal again. She does not say that she is terrified that normal no longer exists.

She arrives for our session still wearing her work boots, the soles stained with dried mud and copper dust. She apologizes for the smell-says she came straight from a job replacing a water heater in a basement. She sits on the edge of the chair, hands clasped between her knees, eyes scanning the room once before settling on the floor. She tells me she doesn't like basements. Never has.

As a plumber, she spends most of her days in them. She took the job twelve years ago, right after her second child was born, because she needed something steady and she was good with her hands. Her father had taught her how to fix a leaky pipe when she was twelve-one of the rare moments he wasn't angry. She laughs dryly when she says this, then stops. The laugh dies in her throat.

The abuse started long before the pipe lesson. She was five, maybe six, when her mother first locked her in the closet. Her mother was a devout woman, strict, quick to punish. The beatings came with a leather belt, a wooden spoon, sometimes the heel of a shoe. The worst part, she says, was not the pain. It was the waiting. The sound of footsteps on the stairs. The creak of the door. The certain knowledge that she had done something wrong, even if she didn't know what.

She learned to read her mother's moods by the tightness of her jaw, the way she set down a cup. She learned to walk quietly, to make herself small, to never ask for anything. She still walks quietly. Her husband teases her about it, says she creeps up on him. She doesn't tell him it's survival.

At work, she is known as dependable, meticulous, a little distant. She prefers jobs where she works alone. When a customer stands too close while she's under the sink, her shoulders lock up. Her heart starts pounding. She has to count the threads on a pipe fitting-one, two, three, four-to stop herself from crawling out and running. She keeps her tools organized in the same order every day. If something is misplaced, she feels a sharp spike of panic, like she's forgotten a rule and punishment is coming.

She has been married for twenty-two years. Her husband is gentle, patient. He doesn't raise his voice. But sometimes, when he speaks to her from another room, she flinches. She hates herself for it. She has two children in college now. When they were small, she never spanked them. She would walk away instead, stand in the bathroom with the water running until her hands stopped shaking.

Nighttime is the hardest. She lies awake, replaying scenes she has never told anyone. The feel of the closet door clicking shut. The sting across her thighs. The silence after the beating, when her mother would pray aloud, asking God to forgive her for having such a difficult child. She still believes, somewhere deep, that she was a bad child. That she is still a difficult person to love.

She doesn't cry in session. She holds herself very still. She tells me she came because her husband said she seemed "not really here" some days, and because she found herself screaming at a broken pipe last week, crying and hitting it with a wrench until her knuckles bled. She didn't feel the pain until later. She just felt the rage, old and hot, rising from a place she thought she had sealed shut.

When the hour ends, she stands, zips her jacket, and says she has another job in the afternoon-a clogged drain in a crawl space. She will have to lie on her stomach in the dark for hours. She will do it because she knows how. Because the dark, at least, is familiar.

She sits in the chair with her hands folded in her lap, her posture straight, almost rigid. The calluses on her palms are deep, the nails short and clean-a working woman's hands. She speaks in a low, steady voice, but her eyes flicker to the window whenever a car passes on the street below, as if bracing for something unseen.

The story begins in a small farmhouse in the foothills of the Alps, where she was the youngest of five children. Her father was a forester too-a man respected in the village for his knowledge of timber and trails, but at home he was a different creature. The beatings started when she was five, often for small infractions: a muddy footprint on the kitchen floor, a dropped spoon, a silence he mistook for defiance. He used a leather strap, sometimes a birch switch he cut himself from the woods he loved. She learned to read the shift in his breathing, the way his jaw tightened before the blows came. By the time she was eight, she had stopped crying during the beatings; she had learned to go somewhere else in her mind, to the cool dark of the forest floor where the moss held the shape of her body like a secret.

Her mother never intervened. When she left the house in the mornings to gather kindling, her mother would say, "Don't anger him today." That was the only protection offered.

She married at twenty-one, partly to escape. Her husband was a quiet mechanic, patient and steady. She told herself she could leave the past behind. But the hypervigilance never left her. She would wake before dawn to check the locks, even in their small safe village. She flinched when he reached for her in the dark. She never spoke of her childhood; she believed that words gave the memories weight. The marriage lasted eleven years. He eventually said he felt like he was living with a ghost-her body was there, but she was always scanning for a danger he could not see.

After the divorce, she moved back to the region of her childhood but bought a cottage on the opposite side of the valley, far from the farmhouse. She took a job with the forestry service, and it was there she found the only constant in her life. The work demanded solitude and strength: marking trees for selective harvest, monitoring for bark beetle infestation, clearing trails after winter storms. She preferred the high altitude stands of larch and stone pine, places where the air thinned and the silence stretched for miles. It was the only place she felt safe.

But the safety is fragile, and it is fraying now at seventy-three. Her body is slowing down-her knees ache after a long day, and she can no longer carry a chainsaw for hours. Retirement looms, and with it the threat of stillness.

Three weeks ago, during an early morning patrol, a sudden gust of wind snapped a dead branch from a spruce above her. The crack was sharp, unmistakable. She dropped to the ground, covered her head, and stayed there, trembling, for nearly ten minutes. It was as if the sound had opened a trapdoor under her feet and she had fallen through decades, back to the farmhouse kitchen, back to the whistle of the switch cutting air.

Since that morning, she has stopped working. She tells herself it is because of the rain, because of a cold she caught, but she knows the truth. She cannot walk into the woods. The smell of pine needles-once a comfort-now carries the sour metallic tang of her father's sweat. She dreams of him standing at the edge of her bed, hand raised. She wakes gasping, her nightgown soaked. She has started checking the locks again, three, four times before bed. She avoids the window that faces the mountain ridge, because the sight of the tree line makes her stomach clench.

She came to therapy because her general practitioner suggested it, after she admitted she had not left her cottage in eight days. She says the loneliness is not new-she has always been alone. But lately the loneliness has teeth. She describes a constant dull roar in her ears, a tightness across her shoulders that never releases. She cannot watch television shows with raised voices or sudden arguments; she mutes them or leaves the room.

In the session, she speaks of her father's hands. Not how they looked, but how they smelled-of tobacco and pine resin. She says she has carried that smell inside her for sixty-eight years. Then she goes quiet, stares at her hands, and does not cry. She never cries. That was the first rule she learned: stay still, stay silent, and wait for it to end.

Tane is a forty-two-year-old electrician who lives with his partner, Leilani, in a coastal town in Aotearoa. He was assaulted eight months ago, outside a petrol station on a Friday night. He had stopped to fill up after a late job wiring a new build, and three men jumped him from behind. He doesn't remember much of the beating-just the crack of his own ribs and the taste of blood. Someone stole his wallet and his phone, and left him unconscious on the concrete.

For the first few weeks afterward, Tane told himself he was fine. He took a week off work, then went back because the foreman needed him on a commercial site. But he couldn't stop scanning the carpark. Every time a car door slammed behind him, his shoulders would shoot up to his ears. His hands would shake on the wire strippers. Once, when a coworker touched his shoulder to ask for a tool, Tane swung around with his fist raised. He apologised, said he was just tired, but his heart kept pounding for an hour.

The nightmares started around the same time. He doesn't dream about the assault directly-mostly he sees faces floating toward him out of darkness, hears footsteps that don't stop. He wakes up drenched in sweat, convinced someone is in the room. Leilani has learned not to reach for him in the dark. She told him last week that she feels like she's sleeping next to a stranger. Tane knows she's right. He used to be easygoing, the kind of bloke who would laugh over a barbecue. Now he watches the door of every pub they pass. He stopped going to his uncle's fishing trip because the boat jetty had too many blind corners.

At work, his concentration has frayed. He double-checks circuits three times, then doubts himself. On a ladder last Tuesday, he heard a sudden bang from a nearby dumpster and nearly lost his balance. He held onto the beam so hard his fingers cramped. The foreman asked if he was okay, and Tane just nodded. He doesn't talk about it. He can't. The words get stuck in his throat like a physical blockage. When Leilani asks how his day was, he says, "Fine," and turns on the television to drown out the silence.

The most exhausting part is the hypervigilance. Tane checks the locks before he can fall asleep. He has started parking his van so that he can see the entrance of any building he enters. If a stranger walks too close behind him in a hardware aisle, he steps aside to let them pass-and then he feels shame, rage, a hot flush of something that makes him want to hit something. He hasn't hit anyone. But he has snapped at Leilani for leaving a window open, for making a sudden noise in the kitchen. Afterwards, he sits on the edge of the bathtub and stares at his hands.

He used to fix things. That was his pride: he could trace a faulty wire back to its source and make the lights come on again. Now he feels like a broken switch-live current, but no connection. The world used to feel solid. Now every shadow holds a threat, every unexpected sound is a prelude to pain. He carries the assault in his body: a tightness across his chest, a constant low-level tremor in his legs. He has started drinking two beers every night just to take the edge off, and sometimes three. Leilani hasn't said anything yet, but he sees her watching.

He doesn't know how to tell her that he feels like he is still lying on that concrete, waiting for someone to notice him.

He shows up for his shift a half-hour early now, even though the locker room is still empty and the fluorescent lights buzz alone. He needs that extra time to walk every hallway first, to check the stairwell doors, to scan the parking lot from the third-floor window. He knows it doesn't make sense-the mugging happened three blocks from the hospital, not inside it-but his chest doesn't care what his mind knows.

It was a Tuesday night, eleven months ago. He had just finished a double shift in the ICU, too tired to wait for the bus, so he started walking toward the train. The streets were quiet, wet from earlier rain. He remembers the smell of fried noodles from a cart, the way his scrubs clung to his back. A man stepped out from behind a dumpster, asked for his wallet. He handed it over. Then another man appeared, and there was a knife, and then he was on the ground, and the knife was at his throat, and he heard himself say, "Please, I have a wife." They took his phone, his watch, his badge. Left him bleeding from a small cut on his jaw.

He went to work the next day. He didn't tell anyone. Not his supervisor, not his wife. He thought if he just kept moving, it would dissolve. But it didn't.

Now, when a patient's monitor beeps too fast, his hands shake. When a visitor stands too close to him at the nurses' station, his peripheral vision narrows. Last week, an elderly man with dementia grabbed his arm during a wound dressing, and he jerked away so violently he knocked a tray of supplies to the floor. He apologized, said he was startled. The patient didn't remember, but he does.

He avoids the stairwells. He takes the elevator even if it means waiting five minutes. He has not walked to the train station since that night. His wife drives him to work now, or he takes a rideshare. She asked once why he stopped riding the bus, and he said he was saving time. She knows he is lying. She has asked him to talk to someone, but he says, "I'm fine, I'm a nurse, I've seen worse." And he has. He has held dying patients, cleaned wounds that would make most people faint. But this is different. This is the feeling of his own pulse backing up into his throat every time he hears footsteps behind him, even in his own home, even when it's just his wife coming into the kitchen.

At night, he wakes up in a cold sweat, sometimes not even sure what he dreamed-just a flash of concrete, a glint of metal, the sound of his own voice begging. He lies still beside his wife, counting her breaths, forcing himself to stay in the room. But he doesn't sleep again.

At work, he is quieter now. The other nurses notice. He used to joke with the families, used to stay late to chat with the night crew. Now he keeps his head down, follows his rounds, and leaves the moment his shift ends. He cannot stand the feeling of being watched. He has started wearing his watch on his right wrist instead of his left, because the watch that was taken was on his left, and seeing that empty space still makes his stomach seize.

He knows something is wrong. He scored a 68 on that questionnaire the clinic gave him-he looked it up online. But knowing the number doesn't bring back the feeling of being safe. It only gives him a name for the thing that has taken up residence behind his sternum. He arrives early, leaves quickly, sleeps poorly, and trusts no one. He is a good nurse. But he is not the same man.

She is twenty-one years old, but when she speaks, her voice carries a weight that belongs to someone much older. She came to therapy because her partner said she was "disappearing" - that sometimes she would be sitting right next to him on the couch, but her eyes would go somewhere else, somewhere dark, and she wouldn't hear his voice until he touched her arm. She agreed to come, she told me, because she is tired of being afraid of her own bedroom.

She grew up on a small island in Oceania, surrounded by ocean and family. She wanted to help people, so she trained as a nurse. When she turned nineteen, she joined a peacekeeping mission in a conflict zone, deployed with a medical unit. She was proud. She believed in the work.

The traumatic event happened on a Tuesday. She remembers the heat first - thick, wet, pressing against her skin. Her team had been called to a village after reports of an ambush. She was the one who triaged the wounded. There was a young girl, maybe seven or eight, with shrapnel wounds across her chest and face. The girl was conscious, and she kept reaching for her mother, who was already dead a few meters away. The patient's name was Talia. She never forgot that name.

She worked on Talia for nearly an hour. The surgical field was inadequate; the lighting flickered from a generator. She held pressure, she packed wounds, she tried to keep her talking. At one point, Talia looked up and said, "It hurts," and then she stopped breathing. No dramatic explosion. No heroic last words. Just silence and the sound of flies. The body grew still, and she remembers feeling her own pulse in her teeth.

She was rotated out two weeks later. She did not tell anyone what happened. She told herself she was fine. She came home and resumed nursing at a busy urban hospital, working the emergency department. At first, she thought the shift was good - she could stay busy, stay focused. But now, every time a pediatric trauma case comes in, she smells the generator. She hears the flies. She has to excuse herself to the staff bathroom and press her forehead against the cool tile until her heart slows down.

Her partner is kind, patient. But she cannot be intimate with him anymore. Not because she doesn't love him, but because the sound of his breathing at night reminds her of someone trying to stay quiet before an attack. She sleeps in the living room most nights, curled on the couch with the television on low, because the dark is a threat. She avoids war movies, news about conflict zones, even the word "deployment." She stopped answering calls from her old unit. She deleted the photo of Talia from her phone, but she still sees her face when she closes her eyes.

At work last week, a child came in with a laceration from a fall. The mother was crying. She found herself unable to approach the bedside. Her hands started trembling, and she felt a hot wave of nausea. She told the charge nurse she had a stomach bug and went home early. She spent the rest of the day lying on the bathroom floor at home, listening to her own breath, convinced that something terrible was about to happen.

She does not want to talk about the military. She does not want to remember the deployment. But the deployment remembers her. It shows up in the way she scans every room for exits, in the way she flinches when a car backfires, in the way she has stopped making plans for the future because she is not sure she will be alive to see them.

She has not slept more than four hours in a row in eight months. She has not cried since it happened. She wants to feel something, but all she feels is the cold, flat hum of vigilance. She told me, "I am still nursing. I am still here. But I am not in my body anymore. I am somewhere else, and I don't know how to come back."

She arrives for her sessions still wearing her clinic scrubs, the blue fabric soft from repeated washings. Her hands are strong-the hands of someone who has spent decades guiding bodies through rehabilitation-but she keeps them folded in her lap, fingers interlaced, as if bracing for a blow. She is fifty-nine years old, divorced, and lives alone in a small apartment near the hospital where she works. She chose physical therapy, she says, because she wanted to help people heal. But she didn't know then that healing would become the very thing she can't seem to reach for herself.

The story she tells begins in a sunny kitchen in a small town in Mexico, when she was eight years old. Her grandmother-her abuela-was the one who raised her after her mother left for the United States. The grandmother was devout, strict, and tired. When the girl spilled milk, or spoke too loudly, or laughed in a way that seemed disrespectful, her grandmother would take her by the arm and lead her to the back room. The belt came first, then the wooden spoon, then the closed fist. The grandmother never apologized; she always said, "Esto es por tu bien"-this is for your own good.

Years later, in her sessions, she describes the pattern with clinical detachment, as if she is presenting a case. She remembers the precise sting of leather on her thighs, the way she learned to stand perfectly still so as not to make it worse. She remembers the shame of wetting herself during a beating, and her grandmother's disgust. She never told anyone. Her mother was too far away, and her mother's new husband didn't want her. So she learned to be invisible, to anticipate every mood, to please at any cost.

Now, as a physical therapist, she is surrounded by bodies in pain. She touches patients every day-arms, legs, backs, necks-but each touch is carefully calibrated. She has developed a habit of explaining every movement before she makes it, warning her patients before she places her hands on their shoulders. "I'm going to palpate your subscapularis now," she says, her voice even. Some patients find her thorough; others find her cold. But she cannot help it. When a patient flinches, even slightly, her own body locks up. Her jaw tightens, her breath shortens, and she has to step back, pretending to adjust a treatment table.

She has been divorced for fifteen years. Her ex-husband was a kind man, she says, but she never felt safe with him. When he raised his voice-even in excitement, even in laughter-she would go silent, disappear into herself. He asked her once why she always apologized for things that weren't her fault. She couldn't answer. The marriage ended because she never let him in. She still has no close friends. Her colleagues describe her as reliable but distant. She eats lunch alone in the staff break room, scrolling through her phone, jumping at every unexpected sound-a dropped clipboard, a slammed door, a patient's sudden cry of pain.

At night, she sleeps in a small bed pushed against the wall. She keeps the bedroom door open, a habit born from a childhood when a closed door meant punishment was coming. She lies on her back, arms at her sides, and listens. Footsteps in the hallway. The creak of the building's settling. She is always waiting. She doesn't remember nightmares, exactly-just a low hum of dread that follows her into dreams and out of them. In the morning, she checks the lock on her apartment door three times before leaving for work.

She told her story for the first time in session last month, in a flat, compressed voice. She had never said it out loud before, not to a partner, not to a friend. She cried for the first time in years-a tight, choked sob, as if the tears had to be forced through a narrow passage. Afterward, she apologized. "I'm sorry," she said. "I don't know why I did that."

She still hasn't told her mother. She still hasn't told anyone at work. She comes to therapy because a colleague suggested it after she froze during a pelvic floor treatment, unable to touch a patient who reminded her of her grandmother. She wants to stop freezing. She wants to stop apologizing. She wants, she said once, to feel like she belongs in her own body.

María sits at her desk in the small editorial office she rents two blocks from her apartment in Medellín, her hands hovering over the keyboard. The cursor blinks on an empty document, a manuscript she has been avoiding for three weeks. She tells herself it's just a difficult chapter-a memoir of exile that needs trimming. But her chest tightens anyway. She reaches for the glass of water, notices her hand trembling, and sets it down.

She remembers the morning in 1999 when she still lived in Bogotá, the sound of the first mortar round hitting the plaza. She was walking to her job at a small publishing house, her leather satchel filled with page proofs. The blast knocked her off her feet, threw her against a wall. For a moment, everything was silent, a ringing in her ears. Then the screaming began. She lay there, unable to move, thinking of her then-husband, who had left for work an hour earlier. She never learned if he had made it to his office. They divorced two years later, not because of the bomb, but because neither of them could speak about what had happened. The silence became a wall.

Now, twenty-five years later, she lives alone in a quieter city, editing manuscripts from home. She chose this profession because it allowed her to control her environment-no open-plan offices, no unexpected loud noises. But each new project arrives with its own threat. The memoirs are the hardest. She cannot read a description of a checkpoint, a sudden bang, a crowd scattering, without the world tilting. She has learned to scan the first few pages for keywords. "Explosion." "Gunfire." "Morgue." She skips those paragraphs, marks them for later, returns to them only when she can force herself to breathe slowly, hands flat on the desk.

Her sleep is a battlefield. She wakes at 3:00 a.m., heart racing, convinced she heard a helicopter. The ceiling fan clicks, and her mind turns it into a distant siren. She has stopped drinking coffee after 2:00 p.m. and bought blackout curtains, but the memories come anyway: the smell of dust and cordite, the weight of a stranger's body pressing her into the ground, her own voice saying the Act of Contrition over and over.

Her daughter, who lives in Miami, calls every Sunday. María listens, but her answers are short. She cannot explain why she flinched when the delivery truck backfired last week, why she stopped going to the mercado since the new security guard started yelling at a vendor. She tells her daughter she is fine. The PCL-5 she filled out at her primary care doctor's request scored a 39-she only knows because the nurse left the paper on the counter. She never discussed it with anyone.

Last Tuesday, an author sent a new manuscript-a collection of dispatches from wartime Sarajevo. María opened the file, read the first line: "The shelling began just after dawn." She closed her laptop, walked to the kitchen, and stood at the sink for twenty minutes, running her hands under cold water. She thought about calling a friend, but who would understand? She is an editor. She edits words. Words are safe.

She returns to the keyboard now, adjusts her glasses. The cursor still blinks. Outside, a motorcycle backfires. She jerks, knocks the water glass over. It spills across the desk, across the printed pages she had finally laid out. She watches the ink blur, and for a moment she is back on the street, blood seeping through her skirt, unable to scream. Then she blinks, grabs a towel, wipes the desk down. She does not call anyone. She just opens another document, one about gardening, and begins to edit.

He remembers the light first. Grey morning light slanting through the kitchen window, the smell of tea brewing, and then the sound of his mother's voice, sharp and thin. He is seven years old, standing in the doorway of the small house near the sugarcane fields. His father is home from the fields early, still carrying the machete. The noise comes next-a chair scraping, a plate breaking, his mother backing against the wall. He stands frozen, watching his father's hand rise and fall. He does not scream. He does not run. He just stands there, eyes wide, as the grey light turns into something heavy and permanent. His mother's eyes meet his for a moment, and she whispers, "Go outside, Kwame." He goes. He stands in the yard, trembling, listening to the sounds he cannot unhear.

Now he is forty-five. He still lives near the fields, but in a different country, a different province. He works for a large fruit farm, tending rows of apple trees from dawn until the heat breaks. The work is steady, solitary. He likes the quiet, the repetition of pruning and picking, the way the trees do not ask anything of him. But the quiet is never really quiet. In the early mornings, when the mist hangs low between the rows, his chest tightens without reason. He catches himself holding his breath, listening. For what? He cannot say. The clang of a metal bucket might send a jolt through his spine, and he stops, hand over his heart, until the rhythm settles.

He does not talk about his childhood. When his partner, a woman he has been with for six years, asks about his family, he shakes his head and says, "Long time ago. Nothing good to remember." She has learned not to press. At night, he sleeps on his side of the bed, rigid, waiting. The nightmares come two or three times a week: the same kitchen, the same grey light, the same sound of something breaking. He wakes with his fists clenched, drenched in sweat, unable to fall back asleep. He gets up before dawn, makes tea, and stares at the wall until it is time to go to the fields.

During the day, he works hard-harder than the younger men. He checks the branches for signs of disease, pulls weeds by hand, never allows himself a pause. If he stops, the images return: his mother's face, his father's hands. He has learned to fill the silence with labor. His supervisor once joked that he is the most productive man on the crew. Kwame forced a smile, but inside he felt nothing. Praise feels hollow, like a stone dropped into a deep well. He does not feel proud. He feels tired.

His relationship suffers in small, quiet ways. His partner wants to hold his hand, to talk about the future. He pulls away. Not because he does not care-he does, deeply-but because closeness feels dangerous. Intimacy means vulnerability, and vulnerability means the past can get in. When she touches his shoulder unexpectedly, he flinches. He apologizes, but the apology is thin. He cannot explain why a sudden touch makes him want to run. He cannot explain that he is always on alert, listening for a sound that never comes.

The world feels thin to him, like a skin stretched over a wound. The apple trees are beautiful in spring, but he does not see their pink blossoms-he sees branches that could become weapons. He hears a loud truck backfire in the distance and his heart slams. He avoids group meals, crowded places, any setting where he cannot watch the door. He sits alone under a tree at lunch, eating his bread in silence, scanning the horizon.

He has not told anyone the full story. Not his partner, not the doctor he saw once for his high blood pressure. The memories live in his body-in the knots of his shoulders, in the way he startles at a raised voice, in the sleepless hours before dawn. He goes to work. He comes home. He sits in the dark. Some days, he wonders if this is just how life is. Some days, he wonders if he will ever feel safe.

She remembers the exact moment her life split into before and after. It was a Tuesday night, near the end of her shift at the dive bar where she works. Her phone buzzed with a text from her younger brother, Todd: "Got jumped. Bad. At the bus stop. Cops took me to Mercy." She read the words standing behind the bar, a half-empty bottle of Jack in one hand, and for a few seconds the world went quiet. She left her apron on the stool, told the cook she had a family emergency, and drove to the hospital with her hands shaking so badly she had to pull over twice.

Todd was alive. That's what the doctors kept saying, like it was supposed to be a comfort. But when she finally saw him in the ICU, his face so swollen he was almost unrecognizable, his left arm in a cast, tubes running from his chest, she felt something crack open inside her. He had been walking home from his night class when three men cornered him for his phone. They beat him with a metal pipe. The police later said it was a random robbery. To her, it felt like the world had suddenly become a place where this could happen to anyone she loved.

In the weeks that followed, she stayed at the hospital every night after work, sleeping in a plastic chair, her hand wrapped around his uninjured fingers. She refused to leave him alone. When he finally came home, she moved in with him temporarily, cooking his meals, checking his bandages, scanning his face for any sign of pain. But even after he started to heal physically, something in her refused to settle.

Now, eight months later, she is back in her own apartment and back behind the bar. But everything has changed. She works the same shift-Thursday through Monday, four p.m. to close-but the job no longer feels like a familiar rhythm. It feels like a minefield. Every time she hears a raised voice from the back of the room, her hand freezes over the tap. When a customer slams a glass on the counter to get her attention, her heart starts hammering so hard she can't hear the order. She has started avoiding the section of the bar nearest the door, because she can't stand having the exit out of her sight.

She used to be good at chatting with regulars. Now she finds herself scanning their faces for potential threat. A man in a hoodie. A group of young guys laughing too loud. She catches herself holding her breath until they leave. Her boyfriend, Mark, who she's been with for three years, says she seems "jumpy all the time." She snapped at him last week when he walked up behind her in the kitchen. She didn't mean to-it was just his footsteps, too quiet, and for a split second she was back in the hospital hallway, waiting for bad news.

She hasn't told anyone the worst part. The images that come at night. She'll be half-asleep and see Todd's face, but not the way he looks now-younger, eleven years old, riding his bike in their old neighborhood. And then she sees the pipe coming down. She jerks awake, drenched in sweat, and cannot go back to sleep. She has started drinking after her shift-not just a shift drink, but three or four, sometimes more, because the alcohol is the only thing that quiets the replay. She knows it's not smart, but it works for a few hours.

She still calls Todd every day, but the conversations have become short. She can't stop asking him if he's safe, if he locked his door, if he's sure he's okay. She hears the exhaustion in his voice, but she can't help it. She needs to know. She needs to be sure. And she never is.

Amira is seventy-one years old, a nanny for the same family for nearly fifteen years. She is small and wiry, with silver-streaked hair pinned neatly beneath a scarf, and hands that are never still-folding laundry, smoothing a blanket, straightening a picture frame. She speaks softly, often apologizing for "wasting time" with her story.

The event that shattered her happened fourteen months ago, in late spring. She was pushing three-year-old Leo in his stroller along a busy avenue, heading toward the playground. She remembers the light was bright, the air smelled of pretzels from a cart. A man in a red jacket was shouting ahead of them-maybe at someone in a car, maybe at no one. She didn't think much of it; she had seen angry people on the street before. She turned the stroller to cross at the corner. Then she heard a sound like a metal pipe hitting pavement, except louder, deeper. She looked back. The man in the red jacket was on the ground, and another man was running. There was blood spreading, dark and fast, from the man's chest. Amira froze. The stroller's wheel caught on a crack, tipping slightly, and Leo started to cry. That cry broke her trance. She grabbed the stroller and ran, not toward the playground, but back to the house, her legs shaking, her breath shallow. Inside, she locked the door, pulled Leo out, and held him so tight he squirmed. She did not call anyone. She did not tell the parents when they came home. She told herself it was nothing, just a street thing, over quickly.

But it was not over. That night, she could not sleep. Every time she closed her eyes, she saw the red jacket, the dark stain, the man's face-blank, like a mask. She heard the sound again, a percussive thud that made her jerk upright. Her husband, Hassan, asked if she was sick. She said she was tired.

The next day, she could not walk past the corner. She took a different route to the playground, a longer one, but even then her heart raced. She began scanning every face, every hand, every open car window. She flinched when a delivery truck backfired. Leo looked at her with wide eyes and said, "Amira scared?" She smiled and said no, but her hands were shaking.

Over the following months, the world became a dangerous place. She stopped taking Leo to the park altogether. She told the mother the playground was too crowded. Instead, she played with him in the backyard, her back to the fence, always watching the gate. She began checking the locks three, four times a day. She woke at 3 a.m. with her heart pounding, soaked in sweat, the image of the bleeding man vivid as a photograph. Sometimes she saw it while making Leo's lunch-the red jacket superimposed on the kitchen tile. She would blink hard until it faded.

She stopped watching the news. She stopped answering phone calls from her sister. She felt a constant tightness in her chest, a low hum of dread. She told Hassan she didn't want to go out for dinner anymore, or to the mosque. He asked what was wrong, and she said nothing, just old age. But she knew it wasn't old age. She felt guilty-she should have done something, called an ambulance, screamed for help. Instead she had run, leaving a man to die on the pavement. She did not know if he had died. She never checked. She couldn't.

Now, in sessions, she sits on the edge of the chair, her purse in her lap. She speaks in fragments, then stops, apologizes. She says she is afraid to go back to that street. Afraid for Leo, afraid for herself. She has started to wonder if she should quit her job, but the family is kind and she loves the boy. She feels hollow, tired, and old beyond her years. She wants to feel safe again, but she cannot remember what safe felt like.

Sessions with this woman began slowly. She is sixty-seven, a widow, a database administrator who works remotely from her small apartment in a coastal city. She is Oceania-born on an island nation, her accent still carrying the lilt of her childhood. She lives alone now, her husband dead for eleven years. She does not speak of him in the early sessions except to say, "He was a good provider." It takes three meetings before the story unfolds.

The abuse began forty years ago, not long after their wedding. He was a fisherman, strong and quiet. The first time he hit her, she had forgotten to buy his brand of cigarettes. He backhanded her across the mouth. She thought it was an accident. Then it happened again when she was late bringing him dinner. Then again when she spoke to a man at the market. Over the years, the beatings became a rhythm: a week of peace, then a night of rage. She learned to read his moods the way a mariner reads clouds. She stayed because of their children, because of shame, because she believed his apologies. He died of a heart attack in his boat. She did not cry.

Now her life is organized around safety. She works from home, maintaining databases for a small logistics company. Her apartment is her fortress: three locks on the door, a security camera facing the hallway, the blinds always drawn. She spends hours at her computer, entering data in neat columns, running queries, building reports. The work requires intense concentration, which she welcomes. It keeps the memories at bay. But they break through anyway. Sometimes a sudden sound-a truck backfiring, a door slamming-makes her flinch so violently she spills her tea. She has to get up and walk in circles until her heart slows.

At night, she dreams of his hands. In the dream, she is trying to run but her legs are sand. She wakes gasping, sheets tangled. She has not slept through the night in years. She avoids going out alone after dark. She avoids the market where they used to shop together. She has not visited the beach since his funeral, even though she once loved the ocean. Her children call, but she keeps conversations short. She tells herself she is fine. When her daughter asks about her childhood, she changes the subject.

Her body remembers what her mind tries to forget. She has constant tension in her shoulders, a knot behind her left ear from where he grabbed her hair. She finds herself scanning rooms for exits, even in her own kitchen. She has not had a romantic partner since his death. The thought of being touched makes her stomach turn.

She came to therapy because her daughter noticed she had stopped leaving the apartment except for groceries. The daughter said, "Mom, you're a ghost." That word stung. She is here now, in the chair across from me, hands clasped tight. She tells me about the databases she manages, how she likes that everything has a place, that errors are flagged and corrected. She wishes life had such a system. She looks out the window. "I thought if he died, I would be free," she says. "But he's still inside my head." She presses her palm to her chest, where the fear lives, and waits for the next question.

He is a 55-year-old painter, a man whose hands once moved with quiet purpose across canvas-broad strokes of ochre and umber, the careful blending of sky into sea. He has a workshop behind his house, where the smell of turpentine and linseed oil used to mix with the sound of his son's laughter. That was before.

The trauma happened eighteen months ago. His son, a twenty-three-year-old mechanic, was killed in a hit-and-run while walking home from a friend's house. The phone call came at 11:47 p.m.-a policeman's voice, flat and official. He remembers the hallway tiles, the way his knees hit the floor, the phone still in his hand. He did not cry then. He stood up, walked to the bedroom, and told his wife. Her scream is still embedded in the walls.

In the weeks that followed, he could not enter his studio. The sight of a half-finished painting-a portrait of his son that was meant to be a birthday gift-made his chest tighten until he could not breathe. He told his wife he would finish it later. He never did. Eventually he covered it with a white sheet, but even that does not help. Sometimes he walks past the studio door and feels a jolt, as if the room itself is dangerous.

He stopped painting entirely for six months. When he finally forced himself back-because the bills needed paying, because his wife looked at him with worry-his hands were different. They tremble now, especially when he tries to paint faces. He works only on abstract landscapes, and even then he avoids the color blue. Blue was his son's favorite. The last time he accidentally mixed a cerulean tone, he had to leave the room, sweating, heart pounding, convinced he could hear his son's voice calling his name from the next room.

He cannot drive past the intersection where the accident happened. On days when his route forces him near it, he takes a long detour, arriving at job sites late and short-tempered. His wife has stopped asking him to go to the grocery store because he will return empty-handed, claiming they didn't have what she wanted. She knows the truth: the store is on the same block as the bus stop where his son used to wait.

Sleep is a battlefield. He wakes three or four times a night, gasping from dreams that he cannot fully recall but that leave him with a metallic taste in his mouth and the sensation of cold glass against his cheek. He often sleeps in the guest room now, because his wife's breathing sounds too much like his son's did when he was a child with asthma. The guilt of that thought-that he cannot stand the sound of the woman he loves-makes him pull the blanket over his head.

He drinks. Not heavily, but regularly. Two beers after dinner, sometimes three on weekends. The alcohol dulls the edge of the intrusive images: his son's face in the casket, the police officer's badge catching the light, the moment he had to identify the body. He did not look for long. But he saw enough. That image plays in a loop, especially when he tries to be still.

He has not cried since that first night. He told me during our third session: "Tears are for children. My son is gone. What good do tears do now?" His jaw is always tight. He clenches his fists when he talks about the driver who was never caught. He has thought about finding him. He has thought about revenge. That frightens him more than the nightmares.

His wife tells him he is not the same man she married. He knows she is right. The man who used to whistle while scraping his palette, the man who teased his son about his greasy fingernails-that man is buried somewhere beneath the debris of that November night. He still goes to work, still paints walls and ceilings for clients, but the joy is gone. It is just motion now, muscle memory, a body going through the rituals of a life that no longer feels like his own.

She sits in the corner of her animal clinic, the afternoon sun slicing through the slatted blinds. A client's Labrador whines from the exam room, but she cannot bring herself to open the door. Her hands tremble as she reaches for a cup of cold coffee. The smell of antiseptic and wet fur mixes with something else-a phantom scent of smoke and damp earth that never quite leaves her.

It started four years ago, during the dry season. She lived in a small coastal town, the kind where everyone knew her as the woman who could calm a panicked horse with a whisper. Her husband, a fisherman, was at sea when the first shells fell. She remembers the sound-not a boom, but a tearing, like the sky itself was being ripped open. She was in her clinic, her hands inside a stray dog's abdomen, when the floor lurched. The dog's owner, an elderly woman, screamed and ran. She stayed. She finished the surgery by flashlight, her fingers working by memory while the building groaned.

That night, she packed a bag with bandages and suture kits. She became the village's makeshift medic for animals and humans alike. For three weeks, she moved through a world of shattered walls and wounded bodies. A child brought her a goat with a shrapnel wound in its flank. A soldier asked her to hold his hand while he died. She did not cry. She could not. She just kept stitching, kept cleaning wounds, kept telling herself that this was what she was trained to do-fix things, mend flesh, bring comfort.

Now, in her quiet clinic thousands of miles away-a safe country, a new life-she cannot stop hearing the goat's bleating. It comes at night, or when she is alone in the exam room. She sees the child's face, the soldier's eyes. The memories are not pictures; they are physical. Her chest tightens. Her skin crawls. She has learned to check the exits of every room she enters, a habit that made her husband laugh at first, then worry.

Her work is both anchor and trigger. She can still perform a surgery with steady hands, but the smell of blood-even a small cut on a cat's paw-makes her stomach turn. She has started to avoid certain procedures: anything involving a foreign object, anything that requires her to work in silence. She plays music now, loud and cheerful, to drown out the quiet that reminds her of the nights she spent alone with the wounded.

Her marriage has become a careful dance. Her husband wants to hold her, but she flinches when he touches her from behind. She sleeps in a separate room because his snoring-a sound that once comforted her-now sounds like the rumble of distant artillery. She tells him she is fine. She tells herself the same thing. But last week, she canceled a routine surgery on a golden retriever because the dog's owner reminded her of the old woman who ran from the clinic. She could not explain why. She just said she was sick.

The PCL-5 score of 78 came from a screening she took online, late one night when she could not sleep. She did not show it to anyone. Instead, she sits here, in this sunlit room, her hands still trembling, waiting for the Labrador's owner to leave so she can go home and check all the locks again. She knows she is not in a war zone anymore. But her body does not know that. Her body remembers everything.

Rana is a 51-year-old hotel manager at a large downtown property. She has held this position for nearly twelve years, overseeing a staff of over eighty housekeepers, front desk agents, and maintenance workers. She is married to Tariq, a civil engineer, and they have two grown children living abroad. Rana describes herself as someone who "used to be calm under pressure" and proud of her ability to handle crisis situations. That changed two years ago, on a Tuesday in late August.

The hotel's pool maintenance crew had been using a concentrated chlorine-based algaecide in an enclosed pump room. A faulty valve released a plume of toxic gas into the adjacent storage corridor where Rana was inspecting linens. She remembers the smell first-sharp, biting, like bleach mixed with burning metal. Her eyes immediately stung, and her chest tightened. She stumbled out, gasping, coughing so hard she vomited. Three housekeepers were also affected. The fire department arrived, the building was evacuated, and she was treated at the emergency room for acute chemical inhalation. Physically, she recovered within a week. But the chemical smell never really left her.
