When a colleague once praised his work on oral traditions from the coast, he excused himself and spent the next hour in the restroom, staring at the floor. He has not replied to invitations from his brother in Accra for three years. He feels a heavy guilt, convinced that if he had been a stronger swimmer, if he had not insisted on that beach, she would be alive. His students notice he sometimes pauses mid-sentence, his eyes unfocused, and then resumes as if nothing happened.

He canceled all travel plans indefinitely. The last time he flew was to attend his daughter's memorial, and the plane's descent over the ocean triggered a full-blown panic attack. Since then, he takes trains or stays put. His office walls are bare except for a single photograph of Amara as a child, turned facing the wall. When a well-meaning student gave him a seashell as a gift, he thanked her stiffly and later threw it away in the department dumpster. There are days when his mind returns to the beach without warning-while he is lecturing on Yoruba proverbs or reading a student's essay on identity. He continues grading, but his hands tremble. He repeats to himself that it was an accident, but the words feel hollow. At night, he sometimes dials Amara's old phone number just to hear the disconnected tone, then hangs up without leaving a message. He tells no one about this ritual.

During the second year of the civil war, Amina was in the central market of her hometown, buying vegetables for dinner. The explosion came without warning-a blast wave that lifted her off her feet and threw her against a concrete pillar. She remembers the sound less as noise and more as a physical force that pressed through her chest. When the ringing in her ears faded, she heard screaming. Blood streaked her arms from a deep gash on her elbow, but she does not remember feeling pain. Instead, she remembers the stillness of a child's sandal lying a few feet away, separated from its owner.

Amina made her way home through broken glass, weaving through bodies and rubble. Her husband found her an hour later, sitting in the kitchen, still clutching the empty shopping bag. She did not speak about what she saw. That night, she lay awake, her body taut, listening for sounds that were not there.

In the months that followed, Amina buried herself in her work. She managed large infrastructure projects for a construction firm in her new country, where she and her husband had resettled. She needed to keep busy-every minute accounted for, every risk mapped out in spreadsheets and contingency plans. She became known as a micromanager, double-checking every contractor's timeline, demanding weekly progress reports and daily status updates. Her team complained that she never let go of control. But Amina felt that if she relaxed for even a second, something catastrophic would slip through.

She avoids the city center now. The weekly grocery run she once enjoyed has become a tactical operation: she goes only at off-peak hours, takes the perimeter aisles, keeps her back to the wall. Her husband does the shopping for big events-holidays, family dinners-because Amina cannot handle the noise of a crowded market. The smell of raw meat, the clatter of voices, the sudden shout of a vendor-they drop her straight back into that Tuesday afternoon, the air thick with dust and screams.

At night, her sleep is shallow. She wakes with a jolt, heart racing, convinced she has heard an explosion. Her husband's gentle hand on her shoulder sometimes helps, sometimes makes it worse-she does not want to be touched when she is coming out of the dream. She has stopped attending public celebrations. Her sister-in-law criticized her at a family gathering last month. "You're hiding," she said. Amina nodded. It was true.

Her attention at work has frayed at the edges. She spends hours re-reading emails, searching for hidden threats in a contractor's wording, second-guessing her own calculations. A minor delay sends a spike of dread through her. She cannot let go of the feeling that a disaster is just around the corner-not in some abstract, "something might go wrong" way, but in the visceral certainty that the floor will disappear beneath her feet.

Her husband has tried to talk with her, to pull her back into intimacy. But Amina feels as though a pane of glass sits between her and the rest of the world. She sees others laughing, planning vacations, arguing about small things-and she cannot connect. The old pleasure she took in hosting dinners, in walking through a construction site and visualizing the finished building, has become muted, like a sound turned down very low.

She came to therapy because her boss gave her an ultimatum after she missed three deadlines in two months. She sits on the edge of the chair, hands clasped, eyes scanning the room. She does not want to talk about the explosion. But she also does not want to keep living inside a body that will not stop bracing for a blow that already landed.

Joseph is a 65-year-old African man who works as a stock clerk at a large discount retail store. He arrived in the United States thirty years ago, and he still speaks with a soft, lilting accent that reminds his wife of the village where they grew up. Married for forty-two years, he has three grown children and four grandchildren. On the surface, his life appears settled-a small house with a garden, a steady job, a weekly card game with old friends. But since the flood, nothing is settled inside him.

The flood came two years ago, during a rainy season that was supposed to be mild. Joseph was at work when the storm surge hit his neighborhood. By the time he got home, the water was waist-deep in his street. He waded through the murky brown current, calling his wife's name over the roar of the rain. She was safe-she had climbed onto the roof with the neighbor. But the neighbor, an elderly woman named Mama Esther, had slipped. Joseph saw her body float past him, her gray head bobbing against a broken fence. He grabbed her arm, but the current was too strong. She drifted away. He searched for hours until rescue workers pulled him away. They never found Mama Esther.

Now, every time it rains-even a light drizzle-Joseph's chest tightens. He cancels plans, calls in sick, and sits in the darkest corner of his living room with the television off. His wife knows to leave him alone. "It's just a little water," she says gently, and he snaps, "You don't know." He apologizes later, but the shame lingers. He cannot explain why a passing shower makes him feel like he is drowning.

At work, Joseph has become quiet and jumpy. He used to chat with customers about their gardening projects, recommend the best bags of soil. Now he avoids the garden section altogether. When a child drops a soda bottle on the tile floor, the crack of plastic hitting concrete makes him drop what he is holding. His coworkers have noticed. "You okay, Joe?" they ask. He forces a smile and says he is just tired. He volunteers for the night restocking shifts, when the store is empty and the aisles are silent. He prefers the quiet. But even then, the hum of the fluorescent lights reminds him of the drone of rescue helicopters, and he finds himself standing frozen in the back room, staring at boxes of paper towels, unable to remember what he came for.

He sleeps poorly. He wakes at 3:00 a.m. with his heart hammering, convinced that water is creeping under the bedroom door. He checks the floorboards with a flashlight, then stands at the window, watching the street for rising water. His wife has learned to sleep on the couch when the nightmares are bad. Joseph does not tell her about the images that flash behind his eyelids: Mama Esther's open eyes, the taste of muddy water, the sound of his own screams that he cannot stop.

He has stopped going to the weekly card game. The friends talk about their grandchildren, about vacations, about the weather. The weather. Someone mentions a forecast, and Joseph feels heat rise up his neck. He excuses himself to the bathroom and does not come back. He tells himself he will go next week, but he never does.

His wife brought home a small plant for the kitchen window. Joseph threw it in the trash. "It reminds me of the mud," he said, and then he could not look at her. He knows he is changing, becoming someone cold and brittle. He wants to be himself again, but the self he remembers feels like a stranger. At sixty-five, he expected to feel tired. He did not expect to feel hunted.

Mrs. D., a 71-year-old forensic analyst, still works three days a week at the regional crime lab, though she has not processed a single piece of evidence from a violent crime in the past eight months. She used to love the puzzle of it-the way a single hair, a grain of soil, a smudge of blood could tell a story. Now the story she sees is only her own.

It happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late October. She had stayed late at the lab to finish a complex ballistics report, and the parking garage was nearly empty. As she reached her car, a man came up behind her. He pressed something hard into her back-she still doesn't know if it was a gun or a knife-and forced her into the passenger seat. He drove her to an abandoned warehouse on the edge of town. She remembers the cold of the concrete floor, the smell of rust and diesel. He told her not to look at him, but she saw his boots: black work boots with a distinctive scuff mark on the right toe. He tied her hands with a phone cord he had in his pocket. He took her wallet, her phone, her wedding ring. Then he left. She managed to free herself after an hour and walked to a gas station three miles away.

The police caught him six weeks later. She identified his boots in a lineup. That part felt like justice. But the rest of it-the part that lives inside her-has never been sentenced.

In the months after the assault, Mrs. D. stopped sleeping. She would lie next to her husband, Frank, staring at the ceiling, her heart pounding at every creak of the house. She began to avoid the parking garage at work. She takes the bus now, even though it adds forty minutes to her commute and Frank has offered to drive her every day. She cannot explain why the bus feels safer-it does not. The seats are too close, the sudden stops make her flinch, and any man in work boots triggers a cold sweat. But at least the bus has other people. The garage is empty, and emptiness now feels like a trap.

Her work has become a minefield. She used to examine crime scene photographs with clinical detachment. Now, when she sees a picture of a ligature mark, she feels the phone cord around her own wrists. When a detective describes a victim's fear, she feels her own throat tighten. She has begun requesting only property crimes and fraud cases-anything without a person in it. Her supervisor has noticed. Mrs. D. told him she was "slowing down" with age, but she knows it is not age. It is the way her mind replays the warehouse scene in perfect, unwanted clarity: the echo of his footsteps, the scrape of the cord, the weight of her ring being pulled off.

She has also become what her daughter calls "a security fanatic." She checks the locks on every door three times before bed. She refuses to answer the phone if the number is unknown. She keeps a small can of pepper spray in her purse, in her coat pocket, and on the nightstand. Frank has tried to be patient, but last week he said, "Honey, he's in prison. He can't hurt you." She looked at him and said, "I know." But the part of her that knows does not reach the part of her that feels.

Last month, at the grocery store, a stranger tapped her on the shoulder to ask for the salt. She spun around so fast she knocked a jar of pasta sauce off the shelf. It shattered on the floor. She started shaking and could not stop. The store manager brought her a chair and a glass of water. She told him she was fine, but she was not fine. She left the cart full of groceries and walked home.

She has not told Frank about the nightmares-the ones where she is back in the warehouse, but this time he does not leave. She wakes gasping, the sheets twisted around her legs like the phone cord. Some mornings she lies in bed until Frank leaves for work, too exhausted to face the day, too ashamed to explain why.

Yesterday, during a routine staff meeting, a young analyst presented a case involving a home invasion. Mrs. D. sat at the back of the room, her hands clammy, her vision tunneling. She heard the word "restrained" and felt her throat close. She excused herself to the bathroom and vomited. She stood at the sink, looking at her own face in the mirror-the same face she saw in the rearview mirror that night, trying not to cry because he had told her not to make a sound. She is a forensic analyst, a woman who has built a career on examining the details of violence from a safe distance. But the distance is gone now. The violence is inside her, and it has taken up permanent residence.

She still smells the gun oil. It lingers at the back of her throat some mornings, thick and metallic, even though the robbery was eighteen months ago. She works alone at her bench, a magnifying loupe pressed to her eye, setting tiny prongs around a sapphire. The concentration used to feel like a meditation. Now every shadow that passes the front window makes her freeze, tweezer hand suspended mid-air, heart hammering so hard she can see the pulse in her own peripheral vision.

The man came in just after three o'clock on a Tuesday. She remembers the exact time because she had been thinking about closing early-her back ached from hunching over a ring repair. He was wearing a gray hoodie, which wasn't unusual for the neighborhood. He asked to see a gold chain in the display case. She turned her back to unlock the cabinet, and when she turned around, he had vaulted over the counter. He pressed the muzzle of a revolver against her temple. She can still feel the cold circle of metal, the way it pushed her head sideways, the whisper of his breath as he told her to open the safe. She did. She gave him everything. He told her to lie face-down on the floor and count to one hundred. She counted. She remembers the dust bunnies under the counter, the smell of her own sweat and the rubber mat's stale coffee. She reached ninety-eight before she heard the door chime, signaling he was gone.

Now she cannot walk past that jewelry store. She leases the space still-she has to, the inventory is bonded-but she hired a young woman to manage the front. She works in a back room she had built with a reinforced door and no windows. She tells herself it's efficient; she can focus on the detailed work without interruptions. But she knows it's a cage of her own making. She never leaves the bench for lunch. She brings a thermos of soup and eats over a cloth, crumbs caught in the velvet. She jumps at the buzz of the intercom, and sometimes she has to ask the manager to come unlock the door to let her use the restroom, because she can't bring herself to walk through the showroom alone.

Her sleep is fractured. She dreams of counting-coins, gemstones, seconds-but she never reaches one hundred. She wakes at 3:17 most mornings, a specific time she does not understand. She lies still in the dark, listening for footsteps. Her apartment is small, on the third floor, and she has installed three deadbolts and a chain. She checks them twice before bed, and sometimes again after a nightmare. Her neighbor once knocked on her door to borrow sugar, and she dropped to her knees behind the sofa, heart in her throat. She didn't answer. She stayed there until the knocking stopped, then checked the locks again.

Her hands, once steady enough to set a one-point diamond with a single breath, now tremor when she hears raised voices. A customer argued with the manager last week over a refund, and she had to put down her pliers for twenty minutes to stop her fingers from shaking. She cannot watch movies with guns. She changed her ringtone from the standard ringer to a soft classical piece, because the default phone chime sounds too much like the door chime of the store.

She has stopped seeing her old friends from the local gem and mineral society. They invite her to potlucks and trunk shows. She makes excuses. The idea of standing in a crowded room, people behind her, people she cannot see-it makes her nauseous. She does not date. She tells herself she is too old, too set in her ways, but truthfully, she cannot imagine trusting a man enough to let him stand close. She avoids the subway. She takes cabs, sitting in the back, watching the side mirrors.

Yesterday she found herself staring at a crack in her bathroom tile. She realized she had been staring at it for forty minutes, not thinking, not feeling, just-blank. Empty. Like the inside of the safe after he emptied it. She splashed water on her face and told herself to get a grip. But she did not move for another ten minutes. She just stood there, listening to the hum of the fluorescent light, wondering if she would ever feel like the person she was before the door chimed.

She wakes at three in the morning, her breath already short. For a moment, she doesn't know why-then the image flashes: her brother's car crumpled against the highway barrier, the blue lights painting his face. She has seen worse in her work, bodies pulled from rubble, families weeping in refugee camps. She has held a camera steady while children cried. But this is different. This was Sam.

The call came during a city council hearing she was covering for the evening edition. She stepped into the hallway to answer, and the voice on the other end-her mother's, hollowed out-said, "Sam had an accident. He's gone." She did not cry. She went back inside, wrote the rest of her notes, filed the story, and drove home. That was eighteen months ago.

Since that night, her apartment has become a fortress she cannot leave. Not for groceries, not for assignments. She told her editor she needed to work from home, pitched long-form pieces that required only phone interviews and archive digging. The lilt of her voice remains professional, steady-she can still charm a source, still coax a quote. But the moment she hangs up, the tremor returns. Her hands shake as she reaches for the half-empty glass of water that has sat beside her laptop for three days.

She used to love the chase: the press pass around her neck, the crush of bodies at the scene, the adrenaline of a breaking story. Now the news alerts on her phone feel like threats. She is terrified that the next notification will be another name she knows, another person whose face she will never see again. She has uninstalled every social media app, then reinstalled them in the middle of the night to check if anyone has died, a ritual that leaves her hollow.

Sam was younger by four years. She drove him to school, saved him from bullies, taught him how to parallel park. After her divorce-messy, bitter, finalized two years before the accident-he was the one who came over with takeout every Tuesday. He left a pair of sneakers by her door that she cannot bring herself to throw away. She also cannot walk past them without her stomach clenching.

Her mother calls every Friday. The conversations are short. "Are you eating?" "Yes." "Are you sleeping?" "Yes." The lies come easily. The truth is she eats standing over the sink, cold noodles from a container, because sitting at the table means facing the empty chair across from her. She sleeps in two-hour stretches, always startled awake by the sensation of a phone vibrating in her pocket. She checks her voicemail three times a day, hoping to hear Sam's voice-and dreading it. Last week she opened her notes app and found a draft she had written: What to say at the funeral. She does not remember writing it.

At her desk, she pulls up a story about a bridge collapse in another country. She scrolls through the comments, reading the names of the dead. She is looking for something: guilty relief that none of the names are familiar, then a hot wave of shame for feeling relieved, then a cold numbness. She closes the laptop, opens it again, and stares at the blank document waiting for her next lead. The cursor blinks. She remembers Sam's laugh, the way he tilted his head when he was about to tease her, the dent in the passenger seat of her car that she never fixed. She presses the heels of her hands into her eyes until she sees stars.

The journalist in her still knows how to find the story. But the woman in the chair cannot find the door.

María comes from a close-knit family in a small city in the southwest. When she was nine years old, her younger brother, Mateo, was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She remembers the exact moment her mother came home from the pediatrician's office, sat on the edge of the sofa, and told them in a voice that was too steady, too controlled. Mateo was five. María spent the next three years watching her parents transform into people who spoke in hushed tones about neutrophils, platelets, and port-a-caths. She learned to read the fear in their eyes before they said a word. She learned to be quiet, to be helpful, to not add to their worry. She was the good girl who never complained, who made her own sandwiches, who did her homework without being asked. Inside, she was terrified. Every time Mateo's fever spiked, she thought he was dying. Every time her mother cried in the kitchen, she imagined a funeral.

The treatment worked. Mateo is now a healthy, rambunctious seventeen-year-old who plays soccer and barely remembers those years. María remembers everything.

Now María is twenty-two, single, and works as an accountant at a mid-sized firm in the city. She is precise, efficient, and never misses a deadline. Her supervisor calls her "the calculator" because she rarely speaks in meetings but always catches the error in a spreadsheet no one else saw. She likes the work because it demands focus. When she is buried in numbers, she doesn't have to think about the other things.

But the numbers don't always protect her. A few months ago, a coworker was talking about her son's ear infection and María felt her chest tighten. She excused herself, walked to the bathroom, and stood with her hands gripping the sink until the urge to cry passed. She hasn't talked to anyone at work about Mateo. She hasn't talked about it at all, really, not since the day the doctors said he was in remission. She told herself it was over. She told herself she was fine.

She isn't fine. She avoids hospitals, which is difficult because her office is two blocks from one. She takes a longer route to work so she doesn't have to walk past the entrance. She cannot watch movies or TV shows where a child is sick. Even the word "cancer" in a commercial makes her heart race. She has not visited her parents' house in three months because her mother keeps a framed photo of Mateo in the hospital, and María cannot look at it without feeling like she is back in that waiting room, the smell of antiseptic and the sound of beeping machines.

At night, she has trouble sleeping. She lies awake replaying the moment a nurse came out to tell her parents the results of a test, the way her mother's hand shook. Sometimes she dreams that Mateo is still sick, that she is a child again, helpless. She wakes up drenched in sweat, her heart pounding, and it takes her a long time to convince herself that he is fine, that it is over, that she is in her own apartment and not in that room. She drinks too much coffee to get through the day, and then she cannot sleep and the cycle repeats.

She has stopped answering calls from her mother. She knows her mother just wants to chat, to ask about her job, to invite her for Sunday dinner. But every time she sees her mother's name on the phone, she feels a wave of dread. She loves her family, but being around them pulls her back into the trauma. She feels guilty for avoiding them, but she does it anyway.

At work, she is respected but distant. She eats lunch alone at her desk. She has no close friends. She dated a man briefly last year, but when he asked about her childhood, she shut down. He thought she was cold. She couldn't explain that the question felt like a hand reaching into her chest.

She doesn't think of herself as traumatized. She thinks of herself as someone who got through a hard time and now has a hard time talking about it. She does not connect her hypervigilance, her avoidance, her chronic feeling of dread to the years she spent watching her brother fight for his life. She just thinks she is tired.

She is tired. And she is still that nine-year-old girl, waiting for the next piece of bad news, even though there is none coming.

He was forty-three when they came for him. A Thursday afternoon, the kind of humid, slow-moving day that made time feel like it might stop. He was walking home from a job site - a beachfront villa he was helping a client renovate, choosing wood finishes that would hold up against salt and sun. He remembers the heat, the smell of frangipani mixing with exhaust from a passing truck. Then the truck stopped. The men inside wore uniforms he didn't recognize, but their faces were familiar enough: hard, tired, bored. They pulled him in before he could react. The door slammed. That was the last sunlight he saw for four hundred and thirteen days.

He tells this story in fragments, over several sessions. He arranges the details the way he once arranged furniture - slowly, deliberately, leaving space. The cell was roughly the size of a walk-in closet, which he finds bitterly ironic now. He spent most of his career thinking about how to make small spaces feel open, how to use mirrors and light to trick the eye. The cell had neither. It had a concrete floor, a bucket, and a single bulb that burned day and night. He lost track of time faster than he expected. He counted breaths, then bricks in the wall, then the number of times the guard changed - at least that gave him a rhythm. But the noise kept him raw: the scrape of boots, the rattle of a chain, the distant sounds of others being questioned, crying, or going silent.

They wanted information he didn't have. Or maybe they just wanted to break him. He was released in a prisoner swap, thin and hollow-eyed, but alive. He never learned why he was taken. The official explanation was a mistake, a case of mistaken identity. He still doesn't believe it.

When he came home, his wife was waiting. She held him for a long time without speaking. For a while, he tried to go back to work. But the first client meeting was in a windowless conference room, and he couldn't breathe. He excused himself, walked outside, and stood in the parking lot until his hands stopped shaking. He started avoiding small rooms altogether. He took only jobs that involved open-plan living, floor-to-ceiling windows, wraparound verandas. He became known for his light-filled spaces. Clients praised his sensitivity to natural light and flow. They didn't know he was designing against the memory of a concrete box.

His wife died eight years ago. Cancer. He was with her at the end, in a hospital room that was small and white and smelled of antiseptic. He stayed for three days without leaving, even though the walls seemed to contract every time the door closed. He didn't tell anyone that it was the hardest thing he had ever done - not because of the grief, but because the room was so much like the cell. He thought he was past that. He wasn't.

Now he lives alone in a house he designed himself, open in every direction, with sliding glass doors that let the breeze through. He wakes at three or four in the morning, every morning, because that was when the guard used to make his rounds. He lies still, listening. His heart pounds. He knows he is safe. He tells himself this. It doesn't matter. The fear lives in his body now, a kind of second skeleton. He checks the locks twice before bed. He arranges his furniture so no chair faces away from the door. He never takes on clients who want basements or windowless studies, even if the money is good. He doesn't explain why. He just says it's not his style.

He still works. It's the only time he feels close to something like peace - when he's choosing fabrics, matching colors, imagining a room that could hold a family's whole life without suffocating them. Sometimes a client asks for wall-to-wall carpeting, and his stomach turns. He remembers the feel of damp concrete on his cheek. He says he prefers hardwood, offers a discount, and the client usually agrees. He never tells them why.

He has stopped attending social gatherings. Friends from before - from that other life - call occasionally. He lets the phone ring. He prefers the company of his work: swatches, blueprints, the clean line of a wall he can open to the sky. He is seventy-two years old, and he has spent nearly thirty years trying to make spaces that feel like freedom. But at night, in the dark, the cell returns. He doesn't sleep. He waits for the sound of boots.

For the first few sessions, Tom spoke about his work as if it belonged to someone else. He is a social worker at a community mental health center, fifty-three years old, married for twenty-seven years to a woman named Diane. He came to therapy because his supervisor expressed concern-not about his clinical skills, but about his sudden inability to be in the same room as certain clients. Specifically, male clients who remind him, in some way he cannot name, of a night five years ago that he has never told anyone about.

The night happened at a conference out of state. Tom had attended a workshop on trauma-informed care, and afterward went to the hotel bar with a colleague he had known for years. They drank, they talked shop, and then the colleague offered to walk him back to his room. Tom remembers the hallway carpet, the hum of the ice machine, the way the key card slipped from his hand. He remembers the colleague's hand on his shoulder, then on his chest, then on his belt. He remembers saying no-or thinks he did-but the colleague did not stop. Tom froze. He lay still on the bed while it happened, eyes fixed on a crack in the ceiling drywall, counting the seconds until it was over. He never spoke of it again. The colleague left the agency six months later. Tom told himself it was a mistake, a misunderstanding, a lapse in judgment. He told himself he was not the kind of man who gets assaulted.

Now, in the present, Tom wakes at 3:47 a.m. almost every night-he knows the time because he has memorized the digital glow of his alarm clock. His heart pounds. He feels a pressure on his chest that he mistakes for a heart attack at least twice a month. He does not tell Diane. Instead, he lies still, just as he did on that hotel bed, and waits for the feeling to pass.

At work, he has become irritable with clients who are slow to open up. He finds himself scanning the waiting room before sessions, avoiding certain faces. Last month, a new client-a man in his forties with a soft voice and a similar build to the colleague-sat down across from Tom and said, "I just need someone to believe me." Tom excused himself, went to the bathroom, and stood with his hands gripping the sink for ten minutes. He told his supervisor he had a stomach bug.

He avoids intimacy with Diane. When she reaches for him in bed, he feels a surge of nausea, a bolt of something like lightning behind his ribs. He makes excuses-tired, headache, late paperwork. She has started asking if something is wrong. He says everything is fine.

Tom no longer watches movies with scenes of violence or unwanted touch. He switched from news podcasts to instrumental music. He drives the long way home to avoid the street where the conference hotel still stands. On the surface, he functions: he meets deadlines, attends staff meetings, remembers his clients' medication lists. But inside, he is always counting. Ceiling cracks. Seconds. Heartbeats. The number of people he can trust: zero. The number of times he has told the story: zero.

He does not understand why his body reacts this way. He is a social worker. He knows the literature. He has validated a hundred clients who said, "I don't know why I can't just get over it." But when he looks in the mirror, he does not see a survivor. He sees a man who did not fight back, who did not report, who has spent five years pretending a thing did not happen-and who now flinches when a colleague touches his shoulder in the break room.

As a firefighter, he had seen his share of burning buildings and mangled cars, but nothing prepared him for the sounds of a city without a roof. When his unit volunteered for a six-month relief deployment to a war-torn region, he went because he believed he could help. He believed in the skill-set he had honed for a decade: controlled breathing, situational awareness, the ability to move toward danger while others moved away. He thought it would translate.

It did not.

In the first week, his convoy hit a crater where a road used to be. He remembers the dust settling in his mouth, the taste of grit and gasoline. He helped carry a man whose leg had been torn open by shrapnel. The man's wife followed them, screaming a language he could not understand but whose meaning he knew perfectly. He put pressure on the wound. The man looked at him with an expression he still cannot name-relief, terror, or accusation. The man died before the helicopter arrived.

He does not talk about the children. He told me once, in a flat voice, that there was a playground that had been hit. He stopped talking about that part of the deployment three sessions ago. I do not push. Instead I notice how his hands tighten on his knees when he says, "I did my job."

When he came home, his wife said he seemed different. He did not feel different; he felt gone. The first time he returned to the fire station, the alarm bell sent him under the kitchen table before he could think. His crew laughed it off as a joke. He laughed too, because laughing was easier than explaining that for three seconds he was back in that convoy, hearing the thud of an explosion that had not happened yet. He started sleeping in the living room because his wife's breathing at night sounded like someone counting down.

His PCL-5 score of 40 reflects what he has known for months: he is not fine. He re-experiences the worst moments during quiet moments at the station-a sudden whiff of diesel, the crackle of a radio, the way a certain colour of dust settles on the engine bay floor. He avoids news coverage of the conflict. He avoids pictures of sand. He avoids the international section of the grocery store because the packaging reminds him of a market he drove past every day. He stopped volunteering for the big calls. His captain noticed. He told the captain he had a bad back.

Marriage has become a series of near-misses. He does not want to fight, so he agrees to everything. His wife says he is not present. She is right. He is somewhere else, standing in a dust cloud, trying to remember what it felt like to believe that the world was a place where children played in playgrounds.

He came to therapy because his wife said he scared her when he woke up screaming. She said he looked at her like she was a stranger. He does not remember those moments. But he remembers the dust, the taste of it, and the man's eyes. He remembers thinking, I am supposed to be the one who helps. Now he is not sure what he is supposed to be.

He still goes to work. He still puts on the gear. But inside the helmet, the noise of the city sounds like the noise of a city that is about to disappear.

She first noticed him at the parent-teacher conference in early March. A tall man in his mid-thirties, he introduced himself as the older brother of a student in her sixth-grade class. He asked detailed questions about his sister's progress, which she answered politely, but something about his lingering gaze unsettled her. She brushed it off-parents could be intense. But over the next few weeks, she started seeing him everywhere. Outside the school gate after dismissal. In the parking lot, sitting in his car. Then came the emails. First one, then two a day, always professional on the surface but with a strange, possessive tone: "I thought about what you said today. You really understand my sister." She stopped opening them after the fifth.

By April, he was waiting near her classroom door when she stayed late to grade essays. She began leaving with another teacher, making excuses. Then one afternoon she found a note on her windshield: "You looked tired today. I'll take care of you." Her hands shook as she drove home. She told her boyfriend, who wanted to call the police immediately, but she hesitated-he hadn't done anything illegal, she said. She felt foolish, as if she was overreacting. But she couldn't shake the image of his face at the window.

The breaking point came in late April. She arrived at school at 7 a.m. to find the lock on her classroom door broken. Inside, her desk drawer was open, the student rosters scattered. Nothing was taken, but on her whiteboard, written in small letters near the bottom: "Missed you." She froze in the doorway, her heart slamming against her ribs. She called security, then the police. They reviewed footage but never found him on camera in the hallway-he knew the blind spots. A restraining order was filed, but he'd already vanished.

Now, eight months later, she still teaches at the same school. She changed classrooms, but every morning she checks the locks three times before sitting down. She scans the parking lot for his car, though she's never seen it again. The fear hasn't faded; it's just shifted shape. She can't tolerate being alone in her classroom after 4 p.m.-if she stays late, she leaves the door open and texts her boyfriend the exact time she plans to leave. He picks her up most days now, though she didn't ask him to. She feels grateful but also smothered, resentful that her life has shrunk to this checklist of safety behaviors.

Her teaching has changed. She used to love the energy of parent-teacher nights, but now she dreads them. She sits facing the door in the school library, her hands clasped under the table to hide their trembling. One of her students' fathers has a similar build, and whenever he walks into a meeting, her vision blurs and she hears the whiteboard marker scrape, the memory flooding back. She excuses herself to the restroom, splashes cold water on her face, and tells herself to breathe. But the panic doesn't stop-it just waits for the next trigger.

At home, she avoids her phone. Every notification makes her jump. She deleted her social media accounts but still checks the email junk folder obsessively, as if hoping to see a message from him so at least the waiting would end. She hasn't had a full night's sleep since April. Her boyfriend says she's on edge, snapping at him for small things-leaving the back door unlocked, walking too quietly into the room. She knows she's pushing him away, but the part of her that wants closeness is buried under the weight of constant vigilance. She can't shake the feeling that he's still out there, waiting for her to let her guard down.

Naveen is a 29-year-old shopowner whose family has run a small grocery store in a suburban strip mall for two decades. He took over the shop three years ago, and it's where he spends most of his waking hours. Now, though, he finds himself scanning the aisles even when there are no customers, his shoulders tight, his eyes fixed on the entrance. He tells me he used to enjoy the quiet routine of stocking shelves and chatting with regulars. These days, certain voices or sudden footsteps make his stomach drop before he can stop it.

He came to therapy several weeks ago at the urging of his girlfriend, Priya. He was reluctant. He still struggles to explain what happened, because the story feels improbable to him: a young man, physically strong, letting himself be hurt by the woman he loved. The abuse began about a year into their relationship, during a minor disagreement. She slapped him. He was stunned-too shocked to react-and then apologized for upsetting her. Over the next several months, the slaps turned into closed fists, and the apologies from her became accusations that he had provoked her. He started walking on eggshells, second-guessing every word. He never fought back. "I thought if I just took it, she'd see I was trying to make it work," he says.

The worst incident happened eight months ago, on a Friday night. They were at her apartment. She accused him of flirting with a female customer at his shop. He denied it, and she began hitting him across the face and chest. He tried to leave, but she blocked the door. He ended up on the floor, curled into a ball, as she kicked his ribs. He still has a faint scar on his forearm from where a glass vase shattered and cut him. After that night, he broke up with her, blocked her number, and hasn't seen her since. But the silence inside his shop has become a different kind of noise.

Naveen now struggles with a constant sense of dread. When a customer's voice rises even slightly-asking for a refund, complaining about a price-his heart pounds so hard he can't hear their words for a few seconds. He has stopped going to the bank on the same street where she used to park her car. He goes to a different ATM three blocks away, even though it takes longer. At night, he dreams of being pinned against a wall, unable to move, and wakes up with his fists clenched. He has begun drinking two or three beers after closing to numb the restlessness, but the images of her face stay.

His relationship with Priya is suffering. He loves her, but when she reaches for him in bed, he freezes. He worries she will see the scar on his forearm and ask questions he can't answer. He has started snapping at her for small things-leaving a light on, speaking too loudly on the phone-and then feels a shame so heavy it keeps him from apologizing. In session, he often looks at the floor, rubbing his hands together. "I'm supposed to be the one who's in control," he says. "I own a business. I'm the one people count on. How do I tell anyone I let a woman beat me up?" He laughs dryly, but his eyes are wet.

He has not told his parents, aunts, or cousins. In his community, a man who is abused is seen as weak, and a man who complains about his partner is seen as ungrateful. So Naveen keeps the story locked inside the shop, where he can arrange the cans of chickpeas and bags of rice into neat, predictable rows. It is the only thing he can still control.

She was twenty-two years old, a radioman with a logistics unit in her home country's army. The convoy was ambushed on a rural road at dusk. Mortars, then small arms fire. Her job was to call in support, but the radio went dead. She remembers the smell of diesel and wet earth, the sound of a man screaming in a language she could not quite place over the chaos. She pressed herself flat against the floor of the armored vehicle, counting her own breaths. When the shooting stopped, three soldiers from her company were dead. She was not physically hurt. For weeks afterward she told herself she was fine, that she had done her job, that the dead were just unlucky.

That was twenty-seven years ago. Now she is forty-nine, divorced, living alone in a one-bedroom apartment in a suburban city. She works IT support for a mid-size insurance company, taking calls from employees who cannot log in or whose printers have jammed. Her voice is calm and patient on the phone. She talks clients through rebooting their machines, step by step, never raising her voice. But when a call ends abruptly or a colleague pops into her cubicle without warning, her heart slams against her ribs. She needs a few seconds to steady her hands before she can type again.

She moved to the United States fifteen years ago, after marrying an American engineer she met online. The marriage lasted six years. She never told him the details of what happened in the convoy, only that she had served. He would ask why she flinched when he touched her shoulder from behind. She would say she was just jumpy. He grew frustrated. She grew quiet. The divorce was amicable on paper, but it left her with a deep sense of failure she cannot name.

At work, she keeps a small bottle of lavender oil in her desk drawer and dabs it on her wrists when the day feels too loud. She avoids the break room during lunch because the chatter and clatter of silverware remind her of the metal fragments rattling inside a medevac helicopter. She eats at her desk, alone. She has two close friends, both from a veterans' support group she attended for a year. They text sometimes but rarely meet in person. She finds crowds exhausting. She stopped going to the grocery store on Saturdays.

She still has nightmares, though fewer than before. In the dream, she is back in the vehicle, and the radio crackles with static. She cannot make out the words. She wakes with her jaw clenched and a thin layer of sweat on her neck. On those mornings she takes a long shower, then drives to work fifteen minutes early to avoid traffic. She prefers the empty parking lot.

She has not spoken about the ambush in years. When a well-meaning coworker once asked about her military service, she said she did clerical work and changed the subject. She does not wear any insignia or veteran identifiers. On Independence Day, she stays inside with the windows closed and noise-canceling headphones on.

She is functional. Her clients rarely complain. Her supervisor appreciates her reliability. But she carries the ambush with her every day, not as a memory she tries to suppress, but as a low hum beneath everything else. She avoids loud noises, sudden movements, crowded hallways. She checks exits in restaurants automatically. She has not dated since the divorce. Some evenings she sits in her living room with the lights off, scrolling through her phone, waiting for the day to end.

She does not think of herself as a victim or a hero. She thinks of herself as someone who got through it and got on with life. But the getting on has required a kind of vigilance she rarely notices until a car backfires in the parking lot, and she finds herself under her desk, heart pounding, before she even knows she has moved.

He arrives to sessions precisely on time, often a few minutes early, sitting in the same chair by the window. He is tall, with a quiet intensity, his hands rarely still-tapping his knee, adjusting his watch, straightening the edge of his notebook. He is a tax inspector, and he speaks about his work with a dry precision that mirrors his demeanor: numbers, deadlines, irregularities. It took three sessions before he mentioned the accident at all.

The event happened eighteen months ago, on a clear Tuesday morning. He was driving to a client's office, an audit that had been rescheduled twice. The other driver ran a red light at an intersection he had passed a hundred times. He remembers the sound-a deep, metallic crush-and the way the steering wheel slammed into his chest. He was trapped for nearly twenty minutes before the fire department cut him free. No one died. He had three fractured ribs, a punctured lung, and a deep gash on his forehead. He was in the hospital for ten days.

At first, he tells me, he thought he was fine. He went back to work after six weeks, eager to reclaim his routine. But routine no longer fit. The first time he sat behind the wheel again, his hands shook so badly he had to pull over. His supervisor allowed him to work remotely, reviewing documents from home. He welcomed the excuse-it meant he could avoid the highway, the intersections, the sound of brakes. But avoidance bled into other parts of his life. He stopped meeting friends for coffee. He stopped going to the grocery store. He stopped driving altogether, relying on delivery services and a neighbor for errands.

He does not describe these changes with distress. He describes them as logical reactions to an unsafe world. When I ask about the divorce, which happened six months before the accident, he shrugs. "That was a different collapse." But I notice he speaks about his ex-wife in the present tense, as though she is still a looming presence. He was the one who ended it, he says, because he could not give her what she needed. He does not say what that was.

In our sessions, he often returns to the intersection. He can still feel the impact in his ribs, even though they healed. He wakes up at 3:17 a.m. almost every night-he knows the time because he checks his phone, then cannot fall back asleep. During the day, he is easily startled: a car horn outside his apartment sends his heart racing; a sudden knock on his office door makes him flinch. He has stopped riding in taxis or ride-shares because the feel of acceleration makes him nauseous.

His work has become a refuge, but also a cage. He audits small businesses now, never traveling to their sites. He scrutinizes receipts, bank statements, payroll records-anything that can be contained in a spreadsheet. He tells me he feels safest when he is alone in his apartment with his laptop and a cup of black tea. He has lost eight pounds in the last three months because he forgets to eat.

He does not believe he has PTSD. "I just have a bad memory and a careful lifestyle," he says. But he also admits that he no longer trusts his body, no longer trusts other drivers, no longer trusts that the world is predictable. When I ask if he has considered driving again, he shakes his head slowly. "There is no reason to," he says. "Everything I need is here." He gestures around my office, but his gaze is fixed somewhere else-on the intersection, on the sound, on the moment before the metal began to scream.

He tells the story like a report at first-flat, professional, as if he's giving a briefing to a new supervisor. But his hands give him away. They rest on his knees, gripping the fabric of his uniform trousers, then releasing, then gripping again. Raj is forty-one, a park ranger in a large forest reserve in southern India, and for fourteen years he knew every trail, every waterhole, every sound the jungle made after dark. That knowledge is what saved him, and that knowledge is what haunts him now.

It happened during the dry season, four years ago. He was on a routine patrol in a section of the reserve that bordered a logging road, an area he had warned his team about for months. He remembers the heat, the smell of dust and dry leaves, the way the cicadas went quiet just before the truck appeared. Three men, one with a rifle. They grabbed him from behind, pinned his arms, and shoved a burlap sack over his head. He still feels the coarse fabric scraping his lips when he tries to describe it, and he stops, swallows, then continues.

They kept him for eleven days in a makeshift camp deep in the forest. His own forest. He could hear the calls of langurs and peacocks, familiar sounds turned strange. They questioned him about patrol schedules, ranger checkpoints, the location of camera traps. He gave them nothing, but that didn't seem to matter. They tied him to a tree at night, wrists raw from the rope. They fed him once a day-cold rice, sometimes with a piece of dried fish. He learned to count the hours by the movement of shadows on the ground where he sat, his back against the bark, his ankles bound. He learned to tell when a man was about to strike by the way his shadow leaned forward, the line of his arm rising. That knowledge sits in his body now, a muscle memory he cannot turn off.

After eleven days, a patrol found the camp during a sweep. There was a brief exchange of fire. Raj was left behind as the men fled. He remembers the sound of boots on dry leaves, running away, and then silence. He stayed sitting against the tree even after the rangers called his name. He could not move his legs. He thought they were still tied.

In the months that followed, he returned to work. The park service gave him a desk job-paperwork, permit reviews, scheduling. He accepted it without complaint. He told himself he was fine. But the forest began to feel different. He could no longer walk a trail without his heart accelerating at every snapped twig. He stopped eating fish because the texture reminded him of the cold rice. He began to scan the treeline constantly, even when he was in his own backyard. His partner, Anjali, noticed he no longer wanted to sit outside at night. He made excuses-mosquitoes, the cold-but really it was the darkness. The darkness had become a thing that could hold him.

He started carrying a knife in his pocket, even to the grocery store. He checks the locks on their apartment door three times before bed. The sound of a car door slamming on the street makes him freeze mid-sentence, and he does not always remember what he was saying.

At work, he is meticulous, almost rigid. He reviews patrol logs with a fine-tooth comb, looking for gaps, for patterns. His colleagues think he is dedicated; they do not know he is trying to map every possible space where a man could be taken. He avoids the section of the reserve where the incident occurred. He tells himself it is not relevant to his current duties. But when another ranger mentions that area in a meeting, Raj feels a cold wash of sweat on his back and a pressure in his chest that makes him want to stand up and leave the room. He stays, because he is a professional. He stays, and he grips the table until his knuckles are white.

He dreams of the tree. Not the men, not the ropes-just the tree. Its bark pressing into his spine. The smell of dry earth. He wakes up with his legs tangled in the sheets, heart pounding, convinced he cannot move. Anjali reaches for him, and he pushes her away without meaning to. He apologizes later. She tells him it's okay. He doesn't believe her.

He told me all of this in a quiet, measured voice, his eyes fixed on a point somewhere above my left shoulder. When he finished, he let his hands go still on his knees. He said, "I used to know that forest better than my own skin. Now I walk through it like a stranger. And I don't know how to find my way back."

He sits across from me, hands folded tightly in his lap, the knuckles pale. His posture is precise, almost rigid-the same way he describes arranging columns of figures in his tax consultancy office. He tells me he has been having trouble sleeping, but that's not why he came. His wife made the appointment. She told him he's "not the same person" she married. When he says this, his jaw tightens, and he looks past me, toward the window, as if searching for an exit.

He was twenty-nine when he volunteered as a relief worker with an international NGO. It was a three-month deployment to a war-torn region in the Middle East. He had just passed his CPA exam, felt restless, wanted to do something meaningful before settling into a career. He describes the first weeks as a blur of dust, heat, and the constant low thrum of generators. He worked in a field hospital, handling logistics-supplies, transport, paperwork. Numbers, he says, were his refuge.

Then came the airstrike. He was in the storage tent, counting boxes of IV bags. The ground shook. The lights went out. He heard screams, then a child's voice calling for her mother. He ran outside. The main clinic was gone. He helped carry the wounded for hours. He remembers a girl, maybe seven, her leg crushed. He held her hand while a doctor amputated. She stopped crying at some point. He doesn't remember the rest of that night, only the wet warmth of her small fingers in his.

When he returned home, he tried to go back to his old life. But the numbers didn't feel safe anymore. Now, when he reviews a client's tax return, he sometimes sees the girl's face in the columns of figures. He blinks, and she's gone. He tells himself it's just stress, fatigue. He starts staying late at the office, working weekends. His wife asks why. He says he's busy. The truth is, he can't bear the quiet of home. The silence reminds him of the stillness after the airstrike, when the only sound was his own breathing.

He avoids restaurants that serve Middle Eastern food. The smell of cumin or cardamom makes his stomach clench. He flinches when a car backfires on the street. He drives the long way to avoid a construction site where a jackhammer sounds like a mortar. His wife tries to hold his hand; he pulls away without thinking. He feels guilty about that, but he can't explain why his skin crawls.

He has nightmares most nights-the girl's face, the dust, the darkness. Sometimes he wakes up already on his feet, heart pounding, searching for an exit in his own bedroom. He hasn't told anyone this. Not his wife, not his doctor. He came to therapy only because she threatened to leave. He says he's fine-his work is fine, his clients are fine. But his hands are still in his lap, and he hasn't let go of his grip the entire hour.

When I ask what he hopes to get from coming here, he is quiet for a long time. Then he says, very softly, "I just want to stop seeing her." He doesn't mean his wife. He means the girl. He means the piece of himself he left in that tent.

Carlos sits in his parole officer cubicle, the same one he's had for nineteen years. Fluorescent lights hum overhead. On the wall hangs a faded certificate of appreciation from the state. He doesn't look at it anymore. He stares instead at the clipboard on his desk, at a parolee's name he has to call next-a young man, twenty-three, same age as his own son. Carlos's hand trembles slightly when he reaches for the phone. He steadies it with his other hand. This is new, the trembling. It started six months ago.

Six months ago, on a Thursday evening in late October, Carlos was driving home from a mandatory training. The training was about de-escalation techniques-ironic, he thinks now. A taillight on his sedan was out. He didn't notice. The patrol car behind him flashed its lights. He pulled over calmly, as he had done a hundred times. He kept his hands on the steering wheel, waited. He knew the protocol. He was one of them, after all.

The officer who approached was young, white, with a crew cut and mirrored sunglasses even though the sun was setting. Carlos said, "Good evening, Officer. I'm a parole officer with the county." He had his badge on his belt, visible. The officer didn't look at the badge. He told Carlos to step out of the vehicle. Carlos complied. Then the officer said, "You match a description. Put your hands behind your back." Carlos tried to explain. The officer grabbed his wrist, twisted it. Carlos felt a sharp pain, then his face hit the asphalt. A knee pressed into his spine. He heard shouting, a second pair of boots. He was handcuffed, his own radio-the one he used to check on parolees-digging into his hip. He stayed very still, because he knew what could happen. He had seen cases. He had processed the paperwork for men who did not stay still.

They held him for forty minutes before a sergeant arrived and recognized him. Apologies followed. A small settlement offer arrived in the mail two weeks later. Carlos did not cash the check. He kept it in his nightstand drawer, under a copy of his birth certificate.

Now, at work, Carlos feels the phantom pressure of that knee when he leans forward to type. He flinches if a colleague claps him on the shoulder. His supervisor, a white woman in her sixties, noticed and asked if he was sleeping. He said yes. He is not sleeping. He wakes at 3:47 a.m. every night, heart pounding, the smell of asphalt in his nostrils. He lies beside his wife, Elena, listening to her breathe, and he thinks about the officer's mirrored sunglasses. He cannot make himself angry. That would be simpler. Instead, he feels ashamed-ashamed that he is afraid of his own uniform, ashamed that he carries the paperwork for men who were treated worse than he was, ashamed that he cannot stop the tremor.

His work has changed. In the past, he visited parolees in their homes, sat at their kitchen tables, drank their coffee. Now he makes them come to his office. He keeps his office door open. He places his chair so he can see the hallway. One of his parolees, a middle-aged man convicted of non-violent drug offenses, asked him the other day, "You okay, Mr. Olivares? You seem jumpy." Carlos said he was fine. He changed the subject to the man's upcoming drug test.

At home, Elena has started sleeping in the guest room. She said it's because he tosses. She said it's because he snaps at her for nothing. Last week, when their son came home from college for the weekend, Carlos saw him walk silently past the bathroom door and felt a surge of protective fear so strong that his chest seized. He imagined his son pulled over, his son's face on the asphalt. He said nothing. He went to the garage and sat in his car for half an hour.

Carlos has not told anyone about the event. Not Elena, not his coworkers. He does not want to be seen as a victim. He is a parole officer. He enforces the rules. He believed in the system. He still does, he tells himself. But when he drives through his city and sees a patrol car in his rearview mirror, his foot lifts off the accelerator. His hands grip the wheel exactly as they did that October evening. And he waits.

Patient Vignette: Liam, Age 21

Liam sits at the edge of the chair, his palms resting flat on his thighs as if he's trying to keep himself from floating away. He arrived fifteen minutes early for the session, apologizing twice for being "a bother." His voice is soft, almost a murmur, and his eyes rarely lift from a fixed point on the carpet.

He speaks about his wife, Maya, in fragments. "She's the one who got me here," he says. "She said I'm not the same. She's right." He married her just after his nineteenth birthday, and for the first year, they built a small life together in a rented apartment above a bakery. He worked as a line cook at a busy restaurant downtown-a job he loved for its chaos and rhythm. "I was good at it," he says. "I could move fast, I could handle the heat."

The trauma happened on a Thursday night in November, just over eight months ago. Liam had just finished a double shift when his phone buzzed with a call from his mother-in-law. Maya had been in a car accident on the highway. A driver ran a red light. The paramedics called it a "major trauma activation."

Liam remembers the drive to the hospital as a blur of streetlights and humming tires. He remembers the smell of the emergency room-antiseptic and fear-and the sound of a machine breathing for his wife. For eleven days, Maya lay in the ICU with a traumatic brain injury, a collapsed lung, and multiple fractures. Liam stayed in a vinyl chair beside her bed, eating vending machine crackers and drinking bad coffee. He didn't sleep. He couldn't.

"I made deals with God," he says, his fingers interlacing and unclasping. "I said, 'Please, just let her wake up. I don't care what happens after that.'"

Maya woke up. She is home now, walking with a slight limp and a scar that runs along her left temple. She has some memory gaps, but her doctors say she is expected to recover fully. That should be the happy ending.

But Liam cannot find his way back.

He lost his job three weeks after the accident. He went back to the kitchen, but the noise of the fryers and the clatter of plates sent a jolt through his chest every time. One night, he dropped a tray of hot oil because a customer laughed too loudly behind him. The manager sent him home. He never went back.

Now he spends his days at the apartment, often sitting on the floor of the bathroom because it is the smallest room, the only place without windows. "I feel like I'm waiting for something bad to happen again," he explains. "It's not a thought. It's like a low hum in my bones."

He has nightmares almost every night, but he doesn't call them nightmares. "My brain replays the phone call. The ringing. The way my stomach dropped. I see her face when she was in the bed, like a photograph stuck in my eyelids." He wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat, and cannot go back to sleep. Maya lies beside him, breathing softly, and he watches her chest rise and fall for hours. He touches her wrist to feel her pulse.

"Sometimes I get angry," he says, his voice barely audible. "I get angry at the ambulance for being slow. At the driver who hit her. At the doctor who took too long. And then I get angry at myself for being angry, because she's alive. I don't have the right to feel anything except grateful."

But gratitude does not come. Instead, there is a hollow feeling, like someone has scooped out everything inside him. He stopped calling his friends. He doesn't answer his phone. Maya asked him to go grocery shopping last week, and he stood in the aisle for twenty minutes, unable to decide which brand of cereal to buy, his heart hammering against his ribs. He left the cart and walked home.

"I feel like I'm disappearing," Liam says. He looks up for the first time during our session, his eyes red-rimmed but dry. "I'm still here. I don't know how to be."

He remembers the dust first. Not the sand of the desert, but the fine, pale grit that hung in the air after the mortar round hit the supply truck. He was twenty-two, a loader, barely a year in-country. The sound came a split second before the pressure wave-a crack that turned the world white and then silent, except for a high, thin ringing that stayed in his left ear for weeks. He remembers the smell of diesel fuel and burnt rubber, and the way the heat from the wreckage made his skin feel tight. He doesn't remember pulling the driver from the cab. He only knows his hands did it, because afterward they were red and raw from the metal. That afternoon is the one he keeps going back to, even now, almost forty years later.

On the warehouse floor, he moves between the racks of pallets with a practiced economy. His hands are always busy-stacking boxes, shrink-wrapping loads, checking inventory sheets. The forklift beeps in reverse, a high, repeated chirp that makes his shoulders climb toward his ears. He tells himself it's just a machine. But every time, his chest tightens, and he finds himself scanning the loading dock for cover that isn't there. The other workers have learned not to startle him. Once, a younger man clapped him on the back to ask a question, and he spun around with his fists up, heart hammering, ready to fight. He laughed it off afterward, said he was just jumpy. But he went home that evening and sat in the dark of his garage for an hour before going inside.

His partner, Rachel, knows the routine. She keeps the TV volume low. She doesn't walk up behind him. She learned not to touch his shoulder when he's asleep, because twice, he woke swinging, and once he gripped her wrist hard enough to leave bruises. He felt awful for weeks after that, and she didn't complain, which somehow made it worse. He tries to keep his nights quiet, but his brain won't cooperate. Around three in the morning, he jolts awake, gasping, convinced the ceiling is collapsing. The dream is always the same: he's back at the truck, and the driver is still inside, but he can't move his legs. He lies there in the dark, listening to his own breathing, until the streetlight through the blinds reassures him that he is in a bedroom, not a combat zone.

At work, he is reliable, never late, never sick. But he has a hard time with the loading dock supervisor, who barks orders over the intercom. The brusque tone-any tone that insists-floods him with an old anger. He has walked off the line twice, told to take a break, because he felt his jaw clench and his vision narrow. He doesn't understand why a raised voice still makes him want to hide or to strike. He just knows that his body remembers what his mind has tried to bury.

There are good days, too. Rachel makes a pot roast, and they watch old black-and-white movies. He laughs sometimes, genuinely. But even then, there is a vigilance he cannot drop. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He checks the rearview mirror more than the road ahead. He keeps a tire iron under the passenger seat, though he can't say why. The world, he has learned, can turn violent in a second. The mortar round taught him that. What it didn't teach him was how to feel safe again.

He is sixty now. His back aches from the warehouse. His hands are calloused. And every single day, he carries that afternoon like a stone in his chest. He doesn't talk about it. He doesn't think about it on purpose. But the stone is there, heavy and familiar, and the dust never quite settles.

Marta is seventy-nine years old and still works three mornings a week in the small tailoring shop she opened forty years ago. She keeps the door locked during business hours-only letting customers in one at a time-and she always positions herself so she can see the street through the front window. The work is precise: hems, zippers, the careful mending of silk linings. Her hands know the rhythm of the needle and the weight of good wool. But lately she has begun making small mistakes-forgetting a dart, misaligning a seam-and she blames the noise. The hum of the sewing machine sounds too much like the distant drone of engines.

She was twenty-three when she served as a field hospital nurse in a European conflict she rarely names. The war had been over for seventeen years by then, but the peacekeeping mission was brutal. Marta remembers the arrival of the wounded: men torn open, the smell of earth and metal and blood mixing with antiseptic. One night the hospital came under fire. She was holding a soldier's hand, trying to keep him still while a surgeon worked, when the shell hit the next tent. The soldier screamed and then went quiet. She still feels the sudden slack weight of his hand in hers.

After the war she returned home, married a quiet electrician named Henrik, and never spoke about those months. She raised two daughters and sewed their wedding dresses. Henrik knew not to ask. When he died five years ago, Marta found that the silence of the apartment was worse than any noise. She began sleeping with the radio on-talk shows, anything to fill the quiet. And the memories, which had been distant for decades, came back sharp and insistent.

Now, in her shop, she avoids certain fabrics. Olive green makes her stomach tighten. The sound of a zipper being pulled, fast, can make her drop her scissors. She has stopped taking orders for military uniforms, even though they pay well. She tells customers she is too old for that kind of work.

At night she checks the front door three times before bed. She stacks shoes in a specific order in the hallway. Her daughter once moved them and Marta did not sleep for two days. She cannot watch news reports about armed conflict-she changes the channel quickly, but sometimes the images catch her anyway, and then she feels the soldier's hand again, limp and warm.

During their therapy sessions, Marta sits on the edge of the chair, her back straight, her hands folded in her lap like she is holding an invisible spool of thread. She says she does not know why she is coming. "I am just old," she tells the therapist. "Old people have trouble sleeping. That is normal." But she mentions that last week, while sewing a wedding dress, she saw the hem of her own apron from 1963-the white apron she wore in the hospital-and she had to stop working. She sat in the back room for twenty minutes, staring at the wall, until her hands stopped trembling.

She has not told her daughters about these episodes. She does not want to worry them. She says Henrik would have known what to do, but Henrik is gone, and now there is only the hum of the machine and the weight of the fabric and the way certain smells-antiseptic, damp wool-still find her, even in a quiet shop on a safe street.

She was making her last delivery of the night, a routine drop-off at an apartment complex on the edge of town. The address was a second-floor unit, and she parked her sedan under a flickering streetlight, leaving the engine running and the hazard lights on. It had been a long shift-twelve hours of navigating traffic, carrying takeout bags, and forcing a smile for customers who often didn't look at her face. She was tired. The kind of tired that makes your bones ache and your thoughts go slow.

That was six months ago.

Now, she tells herself it was just a few seconds. A man came out from between two buildings, his face obscured by a hood. He grabbed her arm when she stepped out of the car with the food bag. He had a knife-small, dull-looking, but she saw the blade catch the light. "Give me your phone. Your wallet. Now." She didn't scream. She just handed over everything. Her phone, her wallet, the bag of food. He shoved her back against the car door and ran. She stood there for what felt like ten minutes, heart hammering, before she got back in the car and drove straight home. She didn't call the police until the next morning.

She still delivers food, because she needs the money. But everything is different now. She only works day shifts, though even daylight feels unsafe. Her mother, a widow who she lives with, tells her she is being dramatic. "You were not hurt. You still have your life. Move on." So she does not talk about it at home. She tries to smile when her mother asks why she's jumpy.

In the car, she checks every street corner three times before she pulls over. She locks the doors as soon as she sits down. She keeps a small can of pepper spray in the cup holder, even though it's not legal for her to carry it. When she has a delivery to a building with an alley near the entrance, she circles the block twice, then parks a block away and walks with her keys between her fingers. She has not told her manager about the mugging. She is afraid they will fire her for being a liability.

At night, she cannot sleep. She lies awake listening for footsteps outside her bedroom window. Every car door slamming makes her chest tighten. She has lost eight pounds because eating feels like a chore-her stomach clenches every time she sits down to a meal. Her mother complains that she is "wasting away," but she doesn't know how to explain that she can still taste her own saliva from that night, the metallic sour, the way her throat closed up.

She gave a statement to the police, but they never found the man. Sometimes she sees him in other people-a guy at the gas station with the same slouched shoulders, a customer who reaches too quickly for the bag. Her heart races, her palms sweat, and she has to sit on the curb until the world stops spinning. She stopped seeing her few friends because she cannot sit still in a cafe for more than twenty minutes without scanning every face, every exit.

The PCL-5 she filled out at a free clinic lasted two weeks ago just to "check in." She scored 49. She did not know what that meant, but the therapist who gave it to her seemed concerned. The therapist asked if she wanted to come back. She said yes, but she hasn't called. She isn't sure she deserves to take up time when others have it worse.

She was seven years old the first time she saw her father's hand close around her mother's throat. It happened in the kitchen of their home in Mumbai, the smell of cumin and coriander still hanging in the air from dinner. Her mother had said something-she never knew what-and then the sound of a slap, the thud of a body against the wall, and the sight of her mother's feet lifting off the floor as if she were being hanged. The little girl stood in the doorway, frozen. She did not scream. She did not run. She learned to be still.

For the next eleven years, she was a witness. Not every night, but often enough that her body learned a rhythm: the raised voice, the crash, the silence that followed. She became expert at reading the air-the tilt of her father's shoulders, the pitch of his breath. At school, she was quiet, precise, a girl who folded her clothes into perfect squares and never left a pencil out of place. Control became her religion. She could not stop the violence, but she could keep her own world orderly.

At twenty-three, she left India for a flight training program in Canada. It was an impossible dream for a South Asian woman of her generation, but she had saved every rupee from her secret tutoring jobs. Flying became the only place she felt safe. In the cockpit, she was the one with the yoke, the one who decided whether the plane climbed or descended. No one could hurt her there. She married a gentle man she met in Toronto, an engineer who never raised his voice. She chose him carefully-the opposite of her father-and she never told him about the kitchen, about the feet lifting off the floor. They had two children. She flew commercial routes for forty years. On the outside, she was a model of competence: captain, mother, wife.

Now she is seventy-nine, retired for over a decade. Her husband is still alive. Her children live in other cities. She spends her days in a tidy apartment in Mississauga, stacking the teacups just so. But the stillness she mastered as a child has curdled. She does not sleep. At night, she hears sounds that are not there-a thud in the hall, a creak in the wall-and she lies rigid, her breath shallow, waiting for the violence that never comes. She avoids television shows that have even a hint of conflict. When her son argues with his wife on the phone, she hangs up without saying goodbye. She cannot stand the raised voices, not even in a movie. Her husband once touched her arm suddenly in the kitchen, and she swung her fist before she knew what she was doing.

She tells me, in our sessions, that she feels like a fraud. "I was a captain," she says. "I flew through storms. But now I'm afraid to leave the house after dark." She has nightmares, but they are not about her father. They are about the cockpit: the instruments failing, the sky turning to water, the yoke going dead in her hands. In the dream, she has no control. She wakes up gasping.

She does not talk to her children about what she saw. She does not talk to her husband. She has carried this story inside her for seventy-two years, and now it has started to leak. She cries in the grocery store when a child screams. She cannot remember the last time she felt safe without an engine humming beneath her.

Reverend Amara sits in the armchair across from me, her Bible open on her lap, a small notebook beside her. She is eighty years old, her silver hair wrapped neatly in a purple scarf that matches her Sunday dress. She speaks with a measured, deliberate calm that I have come to recognize as a carefully constructed fortress.

She came to this country forty-seven years ago, but she does not begin there. She begins with the mango tree in her father's compound in rural Liberia. She was a girl of nine, she tells me, when the first soldiers came through the village. The mango tree was where she would hide, high among the leaves, her hands sticky with sap, her heart a trapped bird. She remembers the sound of boots on red dirt, the crack of gunfire that was always too close, the smell of smoke from houses that were not hers yet could have been.

She fled with her mother and two younger brothers. Her father stayed behind to protect the church. She never saw him again. There were weeks of walking, then months in a refugee camp in Sierra Leone. She describes the hunger-not as a memory but as a living thing that still sits in her stomach.
