He avoids the underground floor entirely, taking the stairs three flights up to avoid the elevator that stops there. He has stopped attending the monthly managers' dinner because it ends late, and the walk to the car feels too exposed.

At home, his wife says he is not himself. He wakes at 3:00 a.m. most nights, certain he heard a door open. He lies still, listening, his heart pounding so hard he can feel it in his throat. He has stopped watching crime dramas, stopped going to the grocery store after dark. He no longer jokes with the front desk staff the way he used to. He feels hollow, as if something inside him was taken that night and never returned.

He told me, with a tight smile, "I used to be the guy who handled emergencies. Now I'm the guy who can't handle a parking lot." He avoids talking about the event. When his wife brings it up, he changes the subject. When I ask him to describe the feeling of lying on the concrete, he pauses for twenty seconds and then says, "I don't remember much." But his hands are shaking.

He scored 62 on the PCL-5, endorsing every hyperarousal item and nearly all the avoidance and intrusion items. He does not see himself as traumatized. He sees himself as weak. He wants to go back to the man he was before-the one who walked through that garage without thinking twice. But every night, when the parking lot lights flicker, he is still on the ground, staring up at the fluorescence, waiting for someone to find him.

He stands at the edge of the dock before dawn, the same dock he has stood on for forty years. The air smells of salt and diesel, and the water slaps against the hull of his boat, the Lakshmi. He checks the ropes, the nets, the engine-once with the ease of a man who knew every knot by heart, now with a trembling that takes him by surprise. He does not want to be here. But he has no choice. Fishing is all he knows. His wife, Meena, died five years ago, and the sea became his only companion. Now the sea is his enemy.

The accident happened ten months ago. It was late monsoon, the season when even the old fishermen stay ashore. But he had a debt-a loan for the engine repair-and the forecast had been wrong. The sky turned black in an hour. The waves rose like grey walls, and his boat pitched and rolled as if it were made of paper. A wave caught him from behind, threw him over the rail. He remembers the cold-a cold that seized his chest and would not let go. He remembers the darkness of the water, the rope that tangled around his leg, pulling him down. He fought, but the water filled his lungs. He thought of Meena. He thought, This is how it ends.

The rescue came after two hours. A passing trawler heard his shouts, or perhaps it was luck. He does not call it luck. He calls it a curse.

Since that night, he has not slept more than two hours at a time. He lies in his narrow bed, the ceiling fan ticking like a propeller, and he feels the pressure of water on his skin. He wakes gasping, his hands clawing at the sheets. Sometimes he smells diesel and salt, and his stomach turns. Sometimes a child's cry on the street makes him jump, his heart hammering as if the wave were coming again.

He goes to sea because he must. But every time the boat rocks, even in calm water, his breath catches. He watches the horizon constantly, scanning for clouds, for the dark line that means trouble. His hands shake when he mends the nets. The other fishermen have noticed. They ask if he is ill. He says it is old age. They do not believe him.

He avoids the parts of the beach where the waves crash hardest. He avoids weather reports. He avoids thinking about the day he nearly died. But the images come anyway: the black water, the rope, the silence. He feels the guilt pressing on him like a weight. He should have seen the signs. He should have stayed home. Meena would have told him to stay home. He failed her again, in a different way.

He has stopped visiting the temple. The priest asked after him, and he made an excuse. The incense smoke makes him think of smoke on the water. The chanting reminds him of the sound of his own breath gurgling. He cannot pray. He cannot feel safe.

Now, as the sun rises over the bay, he steps into the Lakshmi. He starts the engine. The vibration travels up his legs. His palms are slick with sweat. He tells himself it is just another day, another haul. But behind his eyes, the wave is already rising. The water is already dark. And he is already drowning.

The mugging happened on a Tuesday evening in early autumn, just after she left the office. She is an accountant for a mid-sized firm, and that night she had stayed late to reconcile a client's quarterly report. The numbers had been stubborn, and she remembers feeling satisfied as she finally locked her office door. The walk to the train station was a route she had taken hundreds of times-past the coffee shop, under the old railway bridge, through the narrow alley that cut between two parking garages. She never thought twice about it.

He came from behind. She didn't see his face, only felt the shove that sent her shoulder into the brick wall, then the hard tug on her bag strap. She tried to hold on-her laptop, her notes, her wallet-but the strap snapped and he was gone, boots slapping the wet pavement. She stood there for a long moment, breathing in the smell of damp stone and diesel, her hands shaking. A passerby asked if she was okay, and she said yes, because what else was there to say? She walked the rest of the way to the station with her arms crossed over her chest, her empty hands cold.

That was seven months ago. She still works at the same firm, still balances spreadsheets and files tax returns, but something inside her has shifted, like a piece of furniture she can't push back into place. She no longer stays late. At four thirty, her stomach tightens and she starts packing her bag, even if the numbers aren't finished. She tells herself it's just efficiency, but her supervisor has noticed. Three times she has left a meeting early, claiming a headache, because the conference room has only one door and she couldn't stop thinking about someone coming through it.

Her desk is in a cubicle near the elevator bank. Every time the elevator chimes, her shoulders jump. She has learned to keep her back to the wall in the break room, even if it means standing instead of sitting with her coffee. The smallest noises-a dropped pen, a slammed drawer-make her heart punch against her ribs. She checks the lock on her office door four or five times before she can settle into work, and she has started carrying a small can of pepper spray in her purse, even though she never leaves the building except to go home.

Home is no longer the safe place it used to be. She and her husband, a high school teacher, used to take evening walks around their neighborhood. Now she refuses. If he suggests a walk, she says she's tired. If he pushes, her voice goes sharp and she walks away. She knows he is trying to help, but the thought of being outside in the dark, of hearing footsteps behind them, makes her feel like she is drowning. At night she wakes up gasping, her hands clutching the sheets, her body drenched in sweat. In the dream, the strap never breaks. He pulls her down, and she cannot get up.

She has stopped meeting friends for dinner. The noise of a restaurant-the clatter of plates, the loud laughter-feels too big, too unpredictable. She finds herself scanning faces instead of listening to conversations. Last month, at her sister's birthday party, she spent half the night standing in the kitchen, watching the back door. When her husband asked what was wrong, she said nothing. But she knows it's not nothing.

At work, her concentration has frayed. Numbers that once lined up neatly now blur. She rechecks each row three times, then still doubts herself. She has missed two deadlines, something that never happened before. She feels distant from her colleagues, as though a glass wall has slid down between her and the chatter around the coffee machine. She hears them talk about weekend plans, and she can't remember when she last had one.

She doesn't think about the mugging during the day-not deliberately. But the memory surfaces in flashes: the scrape of the brick on her shoulder, the grunt of the man's breath, the taste of fear, metallic and sharp. She pushes it away. She tells herself she is fine, that it was just a bag, that she should be grateful she wasn't hurt worse. But the guilt sits in her chest like a stone. She should have fought harder. She should have screamed. She should have been smarter, stayed in the office longer, taken a different route.

She has stopped taking the train. She drives to work now, even though parking costs half her lunch budget. The drive takes longer, but she controls the doors, the windows, the radio. She hasn't been back to that alley. She takes the long way around, even if it means adding ten minutes to her commute. She doesn't tell anyone why.

Her husband asked her last week if she wanted to talk to someone. She said no. But she is here, in my office, because she finally couldn't stand the weight of it anymore-the constant checking, the waking up afraid, the feeling that the world has become a place where anything can happen, at any moment, when she least expects it.

She wakes before dawn in her small apartment, the silence still heavy from another night of restless sleep. At nineteen, she is the youngest conductor on the line, and the first in her family to hold a steady job. Her uniform feels like armor. Each morning she checks the train's schedule with the precision of someone who learned early that order can keep the world from falling apart.

She was seven the first time she truly understood fear. It was a Thursday. Her father had come home late, and the shouting started before he reached the kitchen. She remembers the sound of her mother's body hitting the wall, the crack of a chair breaking, and then the muffled sobbing that followed. She hid under her bed, counting the floorboards, telling herself that if she didn't move, it would stop. It always stopped. But the counting never really ended.

Now she counts the seconds between stations, the number of passengers boarding, the exact distance between her hand and the emergency brake. On the train, she is in control. The rails are predictable. She can see everything ahead.

But the past finds her in small ways. A passenger raises his voice to his partner, and her chest tightens. She feels her jaw lock, her palms go cold. She turns away, busies herself with a door check, breathes through the memory of her mother's bruised arm. She avoids the sections of the city where she grew up. She tells herself it's just a shorter route, but she knows the truth: she cannot walk past that house.

She has never told anyone what she saw. Not her mother, who left when she was fourteen and never looked back. Not the few friends she made in high school, who stopped inviting her because she always said no. She keeps people at a distance. Relationships feel like a trap. She has never been on a date-the idea of letting someone close enough to see her flinch at loud noises, to ask why she wakes up screaming, feels impossible.

At work, she is excellent. Her supervisors praise her focus, her calm under pressure. They don't know that this focus is a cage. She scans every platform for potential threats. She rehearses emergency drills in her mind. She cannot stop. When a man slams his fist on a ticket machine, she nearly pulls the brake, heart pounding, before she realizes he is just frustrated.

Last week, a passenger argued with another about a seat. The voices rose-accusations, threats-and for a moment she was seven again, frozen under the bed. The world went gray. She heard herself say, "Stop," in a voice that didn't sound like hers. The passengers looked at her, surprised. She made the woman move cars. She handled it. But afterward she sat in her break room, hands shaking, unable to eat.

She has nightmares. Different variations-sometimes she is the one bruised, sometimes she is screaming, sometimes the train is the house. She wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, and lies still until the alarm forces her to move. She has learned not to expect peaceful sleep.

Her body remembers things her mind tries to forget. The smell of beer makes her nauseous. Arguments on TV make her leave the room. She watches people carefully, looking for the first hint of a raised voice or clenched fist. She has never had a panic attack on the job, but in private she feels the ground tilt without warning.

She wishes she could explain why she doesn't go home for holidays, why she works double shifts, why she can't sit with her back to a door. But no one asks. Everyone thinks she is strong. She wears that label like another uniform, heavy and isolating.

This morning, as the train pulls away from the station, she sees a child in a window seat, pressing her face to the glass. The child's mother sits beside her, reading. For a moment, the scene is so ordinary it aches. She looks away. She focuses on the track ahead. There is a schedule to keep, a world she can hold together if she just keeps moving.

Mei Ling sits at the small desk in her home office, a stack of algebra worksheets spread before her. The clock on her laptop reads 3:48-fifteen more minutes until her next student logs on. She rubs her left wrist, a habit she cannot shake, even though the ache there has long since healed. She tells herself it is just an old sprain, but she knows the real reason she touches it: her mind is already somewhere else, slipping back to a time she would rather forget.

She met him eleven years ago, when she was thirty-seven. He was charming at first-a colleague from the community college where she taught part-time. He called her "smart" and "elegant," words her quiet, obedient upbringing had rarely given her. She felt seen. Within months, they moved in together. The first slap came after a minor disagreement about dinner. He wept afterward, begged forgiveness, promised it would never happen again. She believed him. She had been raised to believe in second chances.

But the slaps became shoves. The shoves became punches. Over two years, the pattern calcified: a trigger-her voice too loud, a meal too cold, a look he called "defiant"-then the explosion of his fist against her ribs, her jaw, the back of her head. She learned to make herself small, to walk on the quietest feet, to memorize the shape of his moods. She stopped tutoring in the evenings because she could not predict when he would come home. Her students noticed she flinched at sudden noises, but she laughed it off as too much coffee.

She left after a cracked rib. It was not courage that moved her-it was the sight of her own blood on the bathroom tiles, and the sudden, cold understanding that if she stayed, her parents would have to bury her. She packed a single bag while he was at work and never returned. No restraining order, no goodbye. Just silence.

Now, six years later, she is married to a gentle accountant named Thomas, who asks before touching her shoulder. She loves him, but love does not erase the past. The PTSD is a tenant that refuses to leave.

This morning, for instance, she is tutoring Amir, a high school senior struggling with quadratic equations. As she explains the discriminant, Amir shifts in his chair, and the leg of his desk scrapes the floor. The sound-a harsh, metallic screech-sends a jolt through her chest. Her heart slams against her ribs. Her vision narrows, and for a fraction of a second, she is back in that apartment, hearing the screech of a chair being shoved back just before he lunged. She blinks, swallows. "Sorry," she says, her voice too bright. "Just a draft." She forces her eyes back to the worksheet, but her hand trembles as she writes the formula.

She avoids grading papers in public places now. The wrong tone of a stranger's laughter, the sight of a tall man in a leather jacket, the faint smell of cigarette smoke-any of these can trigger a flashback. She has stopped going to her favorite café because a barista once raised his voice calling an order, and she fled to the restroom, shaking.

Her nightmares are vivid: she is pinned to a bed, unable to scream, while a faceless weight crushes her chest. She wakes gasping, and Thomas stirs, reaches for her, but she cannot let herself be held. Not until the fear recedes. She lies rigid, counting her breaths, until morning.

During tutoring sessions, her concentration fractures. She catches herself staring at the wallpaper while a student reads a problem aloud. She forgets simple formulas, misplaces digital files, apologizes too much. Her students sense something, though they never ask. One mother once remarked that Mei Ling seemed "distracted lately." Mei Ling smiled. "Just a little tired."

She is tired. The hypervigilance is exhausting-scanning every room for exits, every new acquaintance for potential threat. She has become an expert at reading subtext, at detecting the first trace of anger in a person's tone. It makes her a perceptive tutor, able to sense a student's frustration before they voice it. But it also means she lives in a state of low-grade alarm, even in her own home.

Right now, she looks down at her wrist again. She wonders if the scar tissue under her skin will ever stop aching, or if it, like the memory, will simply become a part of her that she carries, day after day, worksheet after worksheet. The clock ticks to 4:00. Amir's face appears on the screen. She smiles, and the performance begins.

Daniel is a forty-five-year-old journalist who has been reporting from conflict zones for nearly two decades. He is married to Elena, a graphic designer, and they have two teenage children. He presents for therapy six months after his release from a nine-week captivity in a war-torn region.

The story begins in late spring, when Daniel was embedded with a local militia on the outskirts of a disputed city. His assignment was to document the daily life of fighters and civilians caught in the crossfire. One afternoon, a sudden ambush separated him from his unit. He was dragged from a dusty pickup truck by armed men, blindfolded, and driven to an unknown location. For the next sixty-three days, he was held in a windowless concrete room, his hands bound, his nights punctuated by interrogations and the sounds of other prisoners being beaten. Food was irregular-usually a bowl of stale rice and watered-down tea. He lost track of time, marking notches on the wall with a stolen nail. The only human contact came from his captors, who would taunt him in broken English, sometimes forcing him to read prepared statements on camera under threat of violence. He believed he would die there.

Since his release, Daniel's life has unraveled in ways he never anticipated. He returned home to a hero's welcome from his colleagues, but inside he feels hollow. In the present moment, he sits in my office with a tightness in his jaw, his eyes scanning the room as if cataloging exits. He tells me he cannot sleep through the night-the slightest creak of the house wakes him, his heart pounding, his mind instantly transported back to that dark room. He has begun sleeping in the guest bedroom because his wife's movements beside him trigger a surge of adrenaline. "I feel like I'm still there," he says, his voice flat. "Except now I have a lawn and a mortgage."

His work as a journalist has become impossible. He used to thrive on deadlines and chaos, but now the newsroom is a minefield. Any mention of the region, any sound of a helicopter overhead in the city, sends him into a cold sweat. He has been avoiding assignments that require travel, even to relatively safe places. His editor is sympathetic but growing impatient. Last week, he tried to write a short piece about local infrastructure and found himself staring at a blank screen for three hours, unable to form a coherent sentence. The words are there, but they feel like foreign objects. He has stopped answering calls from colleagues who want to debrief him about the captivity. "They think I should be grateful I'm alive," he mutters. "I know I should be. But I'm not."

At home, Elena has become a caretaker, a role she never wanted. Daniel has withdrawn from his children, unable to tolerate their laughter, which feels alien to him. He spends hours in the basement, going over his old field notes, trying to reconstruct the chronology of his captivity. He is haunted by the faces of other prisoners he never saw again. He replays moments of his own humiliation-the time he begged for water, the time he wet himself from fear. These memories arrive without warning, often triggered by a taste, a smell, or the sensation of a tight collar against his neck. He has started drinking more, two or three whiskeys a night, just to quiet the replay.

He describes a pervasive sense of numbness. He cannot bring himself to care about the news cycle, about world events, about his children's school plays. "I used to think I was making a difference," he says. "Now I think I was just chasing a story that didn't need me." He feels disconnected from his own life, as if watching himself go through the motions-shower, coffee, drive to the office, sit, drive home, whiskey, bed. The future looks like a gray wall. He has stopped making plans, even for the weekend.

In session, his hands tremble slightly when he recalls the sound of a heavy door slamming. He jumps at the muffled sound of a car backfiring outside. He tells me he feels like a fraud, that he should be stronger, that other journalists have endured worse. But the weight of those nine weeks sits on his chest, unshakable. He says he came to therapy because Elena threatened to leave if he didn't, but he doesn't expect it to help. He sits forward in his chair, ready to leave the moment the hour is up.

He can still feel the weight of his father's hand. Not the slap itself-that part is a blur of sound and heat-but the pause before it, the way the whole kitchen would go silent, the refrigerator humming as if it were listening. He was six, maybe seven, standing at the table with a glass of milk he'd spilled. His father's shadow fell across the linoleum first, then the hand. After that, he learned to watch shadows.

Now, at sixty-six, he spends his days watching code. He is a software engineer for a mid-sized firm, and his colleagues describe him as "meticulous," "unflappable," "the guy who catches the edge cases no one else sees." He does catch them-but not because he's gifted. Because he learned early that missing a detail meant pain. A misplaced semicolon in a deployment script once cost him a sleepless weekend, not because the bug was hard to fix, but because the knot in his stomach wouldn't let him rest until every line was clean. He runs the test suite three times before he can push to production. He checks his work, then checks it again, then checks the logs for errors he already knows aren't there.

His wife, Nora, knows parts of the story. She knows he flinches when she comes up behind him too quickly, and that he never lets anyone stand between him and the door in a restaurant. She knows he sleeps with his back to the wall. But she does not know that every time he hears a loud noise-a car backfiring, a dropped pan in the kitchen-his body remembers the crack of a belt buckle against a wooden chair. He does not tell her because telling would mean reliving, and he has spent fifty years not reliving.

The memories come anyway. Not as clear scenes, but as sensations: the smell of coffee and sweat, the cold sting of a leather belt left coiled on the bathroom sink. He will be writing a function, his mind perfectly focused on a loop of integers, and then suddenly his jaw is tight and his palms are damp. He doesn't know why. He looks at the clock and realizes he has been staring at the same line of code for ten minutes. The feeling passes, but the afternoon is ruined. He blames it on aging, on too much caffeine.

He avoids his father's side of the family entirely. He did not attend the funeral four years ago-he had a "conflict," a project launch, though the launch was two weeks later. His sister still sends Christmas cards, but he does not open them. He keeps a flat, professional tone with everyone, including his own children. They love him, he knows, but he cannot quite feel the warmth of it. There is a pane of glass between him and most of the world. When his grandson was born, he felt a flicker of something-maybe joy-but it was so brief and so thin that by the time he tried to hold onto it, it was gone.

At night, he lies awake beside Nora, listening. The house settles, the furnace clicks on. He catalogues every sound: a creak that could be footsteps, a rattle that could be a hand on a doorknob. He knows it is irrational. The man who hurt him has been dead for years. But the body does not believe in timelines. It waits. It listens. And when sleep finally comes, it is shallow and filled with rooms he does not want to enter.

He has never asked for help. He tells himself he is fine-he is functional, successful, married. He keeps his life small and orderly, and that works. Most days, the shadow is just a shadow. But sometimes, in the quiet of late afternoon, when the code compiles clean on the first try and there is nothing left to double-check, he sits very still, and he wonders why he still feels like he is holding his breath.

He remembers the morning clearly-the way the light fell across the steel beams, the low rumble of the crane, the scent of wet concrete. He was standing at the edge of the site, reviewing a structural detail on his tablet, when the world shifted. A cable snapped with a sound like a gunshot, and the boom of the crane swung wildly. He watched a worker-a young man he'd spoken to maybe three times-get caught in the arc. There was no scream, just a thud and then silence. He was the first to reach him, but there was nothing to do. The man's eyes were open, and the architect still sees them every night.

At work now, he avoids the job site. He tells his partners he prefers the office, that he's too busy with drawings. But the truth is, the smell of diesel and the sound of heavy equipment make his chest tighten. He finds himself checking the load ratings on plans three, four times, even for projects he's done for years. His junior architect asked him to review a simple column connection last week, and he spent an hour calculating and recalculating the same number, his mind drifting back to that cable snapping. He knows it's irrational-the accident was a mechanical failure, nothing to do with his design-but he can't stop the loop.

At home, his wife says he's not the same. She's right. He used to come home and talk about a building's proportions, the way light moved through a lobby. Now he sits in the dark after dinner, scrolling through news articles about construction accidents. He's edgy. Last week, when their son dropped a glass in the kitchen, he shouted before he could stop himself. The look on the boy's face-he saw that worker's eyes again. He apologized, but the distance is growing.

Sleep is a problem. He lies awake replaying the seconds before the snap, wondering if he could have noticed something, shouted a warning. He knows logically he couldn't have, but the thought claws at him. When he does sleep, he dreams of cranes falling, of buildings turning to dust. He wakes up sweating, heart hammering, and then he can't fall back. So he gets up and goes to his home office, where he draws by the dim light of a desk lamp. He finds himself sketching the same beam detail over and over, as if he can fix it on paper.

He stopped going to lunch with colleagues. The noise of the cafeteria, the conversations about deadlines and budgets-it all feels meaningless. He started drinking more, just a couple of beers at night, but it's become three or four. His wife hasn't said anything, but he sees her watching him.

He feels hollow. Not sad, exactly, but like something essential has been taken out of him. He used to love the precision of his work, the satisfaction of a building rising from plans. Now when he looks at a structure, he only sees what could go wrong. He drives a different route home to avoid the construction site. He avoids heights. He avoids the news. But he can't avoid the moment-it's always there, beneath the surface, waiting for a crane's silhouette or the sound of metal on metal to pull him back.

He's here because his wife made an appointment. He doesn't think talking will help, but he's tired of being this way. He sits in the chair, hands on his knees, and starts to tell the story again, hoping this time it might mean something different.

She is seventy-four years old, though her back tells her she is older. Every morning before the sun breaches the horizon, she rises from the thin mattress she shares with Joseph, her partner of forty years. Her body moves by memory: pulling on a faded cotton dress, tying a scarf over her gray hair, stepping into rubber boots caked with dry red soil. She has worked this land since she was a girl-first alongside her mother, then for white farmers, and now tending her own small plot of maize and beans behind the compound. The work is the one thing that has never betrayed her.

But the memories have found her even here.

It happened when she was twenty-three, walking home from the market along the path that cut through the tall grass. The man was someone she knew by sight, a farmer from the next village. He stepped out from behind the acacia tree and grabbed her arm. She remembers the smell of his sweat, the feel of his calloused hand over her mouth, the sound of her own voice trapped in her throat. Afterward, she lay in the dust until the moon rose. She never told anyone-not her mother, not the village elder, not Joseph when he courted her a year later. She washed herself in the river and buried the story deep.

But the story has claws.

Now, when she bends over the maize stalks, the scent of damp earth and sweat can pull her back. Her hands freeze. Her heart beats against her ribs like a trapped bird. She has to crouch there, gripping a hoe, until the world returns. Joseph thinks she is just tired. He touches her shoulder at night, and sometimes she flinches before she can stop herself. She sees the hurt flicker across his face, but she cannot explain. The words have never come.

She has learned to avoid certain things without knowing why she avoids them. She will not walk the old path to the market, even though it is shorter. She makes a wide detour through the church compound instead. She does not attend the annual harvest festival where men drink palm wine and laugh loudly. She avoids the neighbor who smells like the man-a sharp, sour scent she cannot name. Joseph grumbles that she has become "difficult," that she stays too close to home. She says nothing.

At night, the dreams come. She is twenty-three again, walking through grass that reaches her waist. The man's hand covers her mouth, and she cannot scream. She wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, Joseph's arm draped over her hip. She lies still, staring at the crack in the ceiling, counting the breaths until dawn.

She still goes to the fields. The soil is the only thing she can trust. She plants, she weeds, she harvests. But the world feels thinner now, as if a veil separates her from everyone else. She watches other women laugh and gossip at the watering hole, and she feels nothing. Joseph tells her she is distant, but she cannot reach across the distance. She is seventy-four years old, and the girl on the path has never left her.

He is a nanny for a young couple in a coastal town, caring for their two children-a boy of four and a girl of six. The work suits him, he says, because he likes the rhythm of it: school drop-off, lunch, park, homework, bath. He moves through the house quietly, knows where every toy lives, which cups don't spill. The children call him Uncle. He never corrects them.

Fifteen years ago, on a Sunday morning in early December, he took his own daughter to the beach. She was five. The tide was low, and the sand stretched wide and flat. He sat on a towel and watched her build a castle with a blue plastic shovel. He looked down at his phone-a message from his wife about groceries-and when he looked up, the water had swallowed the castle and the shovel and the spot where she had been crouching. He ran. He screamed. A lifeguard found her body forty minutes later, tangled in a fishing net half a kilometer down the coast.

He does not talk about this, not ever, but he lives inside it. In the mornings, when he pours cereal into bowls for the children, he hears his daughter's voice asking for the same brand with the honey and the bear on the box. He sees her small hands gripping the table edge. He blinks and the vision passes, but his heart pounds and his mouth goes dry. At the park, if the boy climbs too high on the monkey bars, he feels a sudden cold sweat, a tightness in his chest. He calls him down, his voice too sharp, then softens it with a joke. The boy doesn't understand. He is patient with them, but there is a tremor beneath the patience-a constant scanning, a counting of small limbs.

His marriage broke two years after the drowning. His wife said he had become someone she didn't recognize. He didn't argue. He moved into a small apartment and took a job cleaning houses, then found the nanny position through a friend. He thought it would be healing. Instead, it has become a kind of penance. He watches these children the way he should have watched his own-every second, every breath. He checks the gates three times. He never takes them near the water. When the family suggests a trip to the aquarium, he feels his chest seize and says he has a stomach ache.

At night, he dreams of her. In the dreams she is always the same age, always wearing a pink dress with a white flower. She is standing in shallow water, and he cannot reach her no matter how fast he runs. He wakes gasping. He lies in the dark, listening to the neighbors' dog bark, and thinks he hears her call out. He knows she is not there. He knows she is gone. But his body doesn't know.

He avoids photographs. He avoids the beach. He avoids the grocery aisle where they sell the cereal with the honey and the bear. He has no friends from before the accident-they tried, but he stopped returning calls. The only people he speaks to now are the children's parents and the cashier at the corner store. He feels a constant low hum of dread, as if something is about to be taken from him again. He does not trust himself. He does not trust the world.

He came to therapy because the boy's mother said he looked tired. She didn't know the rest. He sits in the chair now, hands folded, eyes on the floor. He says he is fine. He says it was long ago. But his knuckles are white, and he cannot look at the clock without feeling that the time is running out, that he has missed something, that someone has slipped away while he was not watching.

He is a seventy-nine-year-old man, broad-shouldered and slow-moving, who has worked in the same warehouse for forty-two years. The other men call him "Old Man," but they step aside when he lifts a pallet. He speaks little, and when he does, it is about the work-where the boxes go, which machine needs oil. He keeps his head down, his hands busy, and his back to the wall. In the break room, he sits alone by the door, facing the room, watching. No one notices that he never lets anyone stand behind him.

It was his father's hand that he still sees. Not the fist, but the open palm coming down on his mother's face, again and again, in the cramped kitchen of their flat in a West African city. He was five, maybe six. He remembers the smell of palm oil and the sound of her teeth hitting the floor. He remembers his own body frozen behind the doorframe, his throat closed, his bladder letting go. He remembers the silence afterward, his mother washing the blood from her mouth, his father sitting at the table as if nothing had happened. No one spoke of it. Not that night, not ever.

He learned early that the world was not safe-that the people who were supposed to protect you could hurt you, and that there was nothing you could do. So he learned to be small, to be still, to watch his father's moods like a weatherman watches a storm. He never cried. He never told. At school, he was called "the ghost" because he was so quiet. At night, he lay awake listening for the sound of footsteps, for the crash of a chair.

He left home at sixteen, worked in mines, then moved to this country, got a job in the warehouse, and married a woman who was patient and kind. But he could not let her close. He could not sleep beside her without jerking awake. He could not hear a sudden loud noise-a dropped pan, a slammed door-without his heart slamming inside his ribs. He would check every lock three times before bed. He would pace the house when she was gone, certain that something terrible had happened to her. She tried to hold him; he went rigid. She cried; he felt nothing but a hollow ache. After fifteen years, she left. He understood. He knew he was "hard to love." He did not fight it.

In the warehouse, he found his rhythm. The repetition of the work-stacking, wrapping, loading-keeps the past from rising. But it always rises. The clatter of a dropped crate sends him into the past; he sees his father's hand, his mother's blood. He freezes for a second, then moves again, hiding the tremor in his hands. He never talks about the old country. When a younger worker asks about his scarred hands, he shrugs. He does not say that the scars came from a moment he does not remember-a broken bottle, a fight he walked into blind.

Now, at seventy-nine, his body is slowing down, but his mind is still fast with fear. He drives home the same route every day, avoiding the street with the bar where men sometimes argue. He eats alone and watches television, but he does not watch movies with violence. He flinches at the sound of a door slamming in the apartment next door. He has dreams, bad ones, of the kitchen, of being trapped, of not being able to scream. He wakes at three in the morning, every night, and waits for dawn.

He came to therapy because his doctor told him his blood pressure was dangerous. The doctor asked about stress. He said nothing for a long time. Then he said, "I saw things. When I was small." That was all. But he came back the next week, and the week after. He sits in the chair with his hands on his knees, ready to stand, watching the door. He is still watching. He is still waiting.

Linh arrives for her appointment exactly on time, as she always does. She sits in the chair with her back to the wall, her purse clutched tight in her lap. Before the session began, she asked if the door could remain slightly open - a request she makes weekly and apologizes for each time. She is a dentist, fifty-one years old, married for twenty-three years, and the mother of two grown children. She speaks in a measured, careful voice, as though she is still deciding how much to reveal.

Two and a half years ago, a male patient - mid-thirties, soft-spoken, always polite - began requesting Linh specifically for his cleanings. At first she thought nothing of it. Many patients preferred her gentle technique. But soon he started asking personal questions: where she grew up, what her husband did, whether she had children. She gave vague answers, changed the subject. Then the gifts appeared: a small box of chocolates left at the reception desk, a hand-written card thanking her for "the light she brought into his life." The office manager thought it was sweet. Linh felt something cold settle in her stomach.

She told the patient gently that gifts were not appropriate. He agreed, apologized, and seemed to understand. But the next week, he was waiting in the parking lot after her shift. He waved, smiled, and said he happened to be in the area. She told herself it was a coincidence. A week later, he was there again. And again. She stopped parking in the lot and began using a garage two blocks away. He found her there too. That was when she started to feel truly watched - a heavy, invisible pressure at the back of her neck, even inside her own home.

The patient left notes under her windshield wiper, then under the door of her house. He called the dental office repeatedly, asking for her personal schedule. Linh filed a police report. They spoke to him. He denied everything. Without concrete threats, they said, there was little they could do. She transferred to a different clinic across town. She and her husband moved to a new apartment. She changed her phone number, her route to work, her daily routines. But the feeling never left.

Now Linh is always scanning. In the grocery store, she notices every man who walks past the same aisle twice. In her dental chair, with a patient reclined and her hands in their mouth, she sometimes freezes mid-procedure, her heart pounding as she tries to remember if she locked the exam room door. She has started asking her hygienist to stay in the room when she treats any male patient who is roughly the same height and build as the stalker. She cannot explain why, only that her throat closes and her hands shake.

She sleeps poorly - wakes at 3 a.m. thinking she hears footsteps in the hallway. She checks the locks three times before bed, then checks again. Her husband tries to comfort her, but she finds herself pulling away from his touch, feeling unsafe even in their bed. She is irritable with him, snaps at small things, then feels guilty and withdraws further.

At work, she is still competent, but she avoids certain procedures that require prolonged, uninterrupted focus. She has begun delegating more complex cases to a colleague, telling herself it is because she is tired. She is tired. The hypervigilance consumes energy she once had for her family, her hobbies, her patients. She no longer goes to the park for her morning walks. She stopped attending her daughter's soccer games because the open field felt too exposed.

She tells me all of this without tears, her face composed, but her fingers twist the strap of her purse. She wants to understand why she still feels the stalker's presence even though she has not seen him in over a year. She is angry at herself - for not being stronger, for not catching him sooner, for letting a stranger steal her peace of mind. She says, "I used to love my work. Now I count the minutes until I can go home and lock the door."

He doesn't remember her name. She told it to him twice that evening, first at the parish soup kitchen where she was serving, then again when he followed her out to the parking lot. He called her mamacita and güerita and she corrected him both times. Marina, she said. My name is Marina.

That night, after the shift ended, he was waiting by her car. She thought he wanted to thank her for the meal. Instead, he pushed her into the back seat and held a knife against her rib cage. She kept her eyes open the whole time-on the cracked vinyl ceiling, on the streetlight through the fogged glass, on the crucifix dangling from the rearview mirror that swung and swung and never stopped moving.

That was seven years ago last November.

Marina still closes her eyes when she sees a crucifix. It's not a conscious thing. Her husband, Tomás, notices when they sit in the third pew at Sunday Mass-she shifts her gaze, drops her chin, fumbles with the hem of her sleeve. He thinks she's praying. She lets him think that.

She works at the diocese now, coordinating emergency aid for migrant families. It's the same building where the soup kitchen used to run, though they moved the pantry to a different wing after the incident. Marina requested the transfer herself. She told the director it was for efficiency, but really it was because she couldn't walk past that stretch of parking lot without her palms sweating and her heart slamming against her sternum like a trapped bird. She still can't. She enters through the side door now, always during daylight, always with a colleague. If she has to leave after dark, she asks someone to walk her. She says it's because of the neighborhood.

She doesn't tell them why she really can't stand the dark anymore, or why she flinches when a car door slams two blocks away, or why she stopped driving a sedan and bought a truck with an automatic lock that beeps three times. The beep is loud, and she presses the button three or four times before she's sure.

Tomás knows something happened. She told him it was a mugging. That was easier-a faceless stranger, a stolen purse, a quick shove. No mention of the knife. No mention of the weight of his chest against her back. No mention of how she kept whispering Hail Marys into the upholstery, but God didn't answer, and she hasn't finished a full rosary since.

In their bedroom, she sleeps on the far edge of the mattress, turned away from the door. She used to love his arm draped over her waist; now she tenses at any touch from behind. He thinks she's just getting older, getting colder. She lets him think that.

At work, she is efficient. She organizes food boxes, fills out forms, listens to mothers tell stories of crossing the border. Their stories are full of violence, but she listens without flinching. She is good at that. It's the only place she feels anything close to control. But when a young man with dark eyes and a heavy accent thanks her with a hand on her forearm, she pulls away so fast the coffee sloshes onto her sleeve. She apologizes. She says she's clumsy.

She dreams about the rearview mirror. She dreams about the crucifix. In the dreams, she is still in the back seat, but now she is older, and the man is younger, and the knife is gone, but she cannot open the door. She wakes with her teeth clenched and her hands balled into fists under the pillow.

Last week, she found herself standing in the parking lot at dusk, staring at the exact spot. She didn't remember walking there. She stood for maybe a minute, then turned around and went back inside. She told the secretary she forgot her keys. The secretary said, You're shaking, Marina. Marina said she was just cold.

She doesn't cry about it. She hasn't cried about it since the first month, when she sat in the shower with her clothes on and let the water run cold. Now she just feels tired. Heavy. Like someone filled her bones with lead.

She goes to Mass on Sundays. She crosses herself at the holy water. She kneels. She stares at the altar, but she does not look at the crucifix.

She does not know how to tell Tomás that God didn't hear her that night, and that maybe that's the part she can't forgive.

He doesn't remember the shouting the way you'd expect. The sounds he carries are small: the crack of a ceramic mug against a linoleum floor, the wet gasp his mother made when she fell, the scrape of a chair being shoved backward. He was six years old, sitting at the bottom of the stairs in the house in Lagos, his knees pulled to his chest. His father was a man who could fill a room with silence just as easily as he could fill it with fury. That night, the silence came last, after the shouts had died and the front door slammed. His mother got up, wiped blood from her lip with the back of her hand, and told him to go back to bed. He went. He never told anyone. Not her. Not the neighbors. Not the teachers. He just learned to watch.

Now he is eighteen, an officer with the Lagos State Police Command. He is the youngest in his unit by nearly a decade, and the others still call him "Small Boy" even though he stands six feet tall. He wears his uniform like armor-every button polished, every crease sharp. He volunteered for day shifts in the busiest precinct because night patrols are worse. At night, the city gets quiet, and in the quiet he hears things that aren't there. The voice of his father. The sound of his mother apologizing. The soft, terrible click of a lock turning.

Today, he responded to a domestic disturbance call in a low-income flat. A woman screaming, a man shouting, neighbors gathered in the hallway. He knocked. He identified himself. When the door opened, he saw a toddler sitting on the floor, watching. The child did not cry. He just stared, the way children stare when they have learned that crying does nothing. The man was yelling at the officer now, but he doesn't hear the words. He hears the crack of the mug. He hears the wet gasp. His hands start to shake. He grips his belt until his knuckles turn white. His partner touches his arm, asks if he's okay. He says yes. He is not okay.

At night, he cannot sleep. He lies on his cot in the police barracks and counts breaths. When he closes his eyes, the toddler's face becomes his own face, and he is six again, and the fear wraps around his throat like a collar. He wakes sweating, heart hammering, convinced someone is in the room. He checks the corners. He checks the window. There is no one. He stays awake until sunrise.

He stopped calling his mother six months ago. Not because he is angry-he has never been angry with her. He doesn't know why he stopped. The calls feel like stepping into a room he has locked for a reason. She asks how work is. He says fine. She asks if he is eating. He says yes. He does not eat. Food tastes like paper. His uniform is loose on him, but he tightens the belt and tells no one.

At roll call, Sgt. Adebayo jokes that he looks like a ghost. He laughs. The sound is hollow. He volunteers for extra shifts because being busy means not thinking. But the thinking follows him. He replays scenes from calls he went on yesterday, and scenes from the hallway when he was six, and the two become the same memory: a woman crying, a child frozen, a man who is supposed to protect but does not protect. He wonders if he is like his father. He wonders if every man is.

He does not drink. He does not smoke. He just holds the shaking in his hands, and keeps the uniform polished, and waits for the next call that will take him back to that flat, that child, that door. He is eighteen years old. He has been an officer for eleven months. He has not told anyone what he saw when he was six, and he does not plan to.

Charles is a sixty-two-year-old man who sits in my office each week with the careful posture of someone who has learned to hold himself together. He wears pressed shirts, even on Saturdays, and his hands rest flat on his thighs as if he is waiting for a bell to ring. He is a stock broker, or was-now he works from a small home office, managing a few long-standing clients by phone, because the thought of stepping onto a trading floor makes his chest seize. He tells me this matter-of-factly, the way he might quote a closing price.

The event happened three years ago, on a Tuesday in late October. His twenty-eight-year-old son, David, was driving home from a sales meeting when a driver ran a red light and hit him broadside. Charles got the call while he was in the middle of a volatile close. He remembers the exact second he heard the words-Dow was down two hundred points-and he remembers hanging up and finishing the trade. He says he doesn't know why he did that. "I thought, I can't leave now. The market won't wait." He got to the hospital forty minutes later. David was already gone.

For the first six months, Charles did not cry. He organized the funeral, handled the insurance, returned to his desk after three days. His colleagues called him stoic. He called it "functioning." But at night, alone in his apartment, he would replay the phone call, the drive, the fluorescent lights of the hospital waiting room. He began to avoid driving past the intersection where it happened, then any major intersection, then any road with traffic lights. He took back streets, sometimes adding forty minutes to a trip. He stopped visiting his son's grave because the sight of the headstone made his throat close. He stopped going to his son's favorite restaurant, stopped listening to the radio station David always played.

His sleep collapsed. He wakes at 3:17 a.m. almost every night-the time the hospital called his phone-and cannot fall back asleep. He lies in the dark and hears the market noise in his head, numbers and names, but also the sound of the doctor's voice. He has not touched a bottle of whiskey since David died, because one night he drank half of one and woke up on the bathroom floor with no memory of getting there. He told me that story without emotion, then looked at the clock on my wall.

At work, he finds he cannot concentrate on long-term trends. He scans the news for headlines about fatal crashes, car recalls, red-light cameras. He has a client who lost a son in a car accident two decades ago, and Charles avoids taking his calls. "I don't know what to say," he said. "I don't want to talk about it. I don't want to think about it." But he thinks about it constantly. He replays the last conversation he had with David-a brief call about a dinner reservation. He thought there would be more time. That sentence comes up in almost every session.

He feels watchful now, hyperaware. In a grocery store he scans every aisle for sudden movements. He flinches at car horns. He has not driven himself to a single session; he takes a rideshare, sitting in the back seat with his eyes on the driver's speedometer. Two months ago, a woman rear-ended him at a stoplight-a gentle tap, no damage-and he screamed at her in the parking lot, shaking, until a security guard came. He was ashamed for days. "That's not who I am," he said. "I don't raise my voice. I don't lose control. I'm the one people come to when they need steady."

Now he is less steady. He has no desire for relationships; his ex-wife calls sometimes, and he lets it ring. He has deleted all photos of David from his phone because seeing them makes him feel like he cannot breathe. He knows he is avoiding the grief, but he does not know how else to survive. He told me last week, "If I let it in, I think it will drown me." And then, quietly, "But it's already drowning me."

She first came to my office on a humid Tuesday afternoon, still wearing her olive-green ranger uniform under a lightweight jacket. She sat at the edge of the chair, hands clasped tight in her lap, scanning the room once, twice, before letting her eyes settle on the floor. Her name is Amara, and she is thirty-three years old, an African woman who works as a park ranger in a large national reserve. She has been married for six years. Her PCL-5 score was 46.

The trauma happened eighteen months ago. Amara and her younger brother, Kofi, were both rangers. They had grown up in the shadow of the park, their father a retired ranger, their mother a schoolteacher. Kofi was twenty-nine, quiet, good with animals, always the one who could read the wind. He and Amara often patrolled together. On that day, they responded to a report of poachers near the eastern boundary. It was late afternoon, the light going amber through the acacias. They found the carcass of a rhino, horns roughly hacked off. Then the gunfire came from the thicket. Amara remembers diving behind a termite mound, shouting for Kofi to take cover. He didn't. A single bullet caught him in the throat. She crawled to him, held him as the blood soaked through her shirt, tried to stop it with her hands. The poachers fled. By the time backup arrived, he was gone.

She did not cry at the funeral. She remembers standing in the cemetery, the red earth fresh and heavy, her mother weeping. She felt nothing except a pressure behind her eyes and a numb, electric hum in her skull. That night, she did not sleep. She lay awake, replaying the sound of the shot, the way his body went slack. Over the following weeks, the images became more vivid. She started seeing Kofi in crowds, in the reflection of windows, in the shadow of a tree at dusk. Once, while driving a park vehicle, she slammed on the brakes because she thought she saw him standing on the road. It was a goat.

She stopped going on patrol. She told her supervisor she needed desk duty for a while, citing fatigue. That "while" has stretched into over a year. She now works in the administrative office, processing permits and filing reports. Every time a helicopter flies overhead-the park uses them for anti-poaching surveillance-her heart hammers so hard she feels it in her throat. She avoids the eastern sector entirely, taking a longer route even when it costs her an hour. Loud noises make her flinch. The crack of a branch during a nature walk with her husband, Daniel, sends her into a cold sweat. Daniel has learned not to surprise her from behind. He treads carefully around her, and she hates that.

Her sleep is broken. She has nightmares two or three times a week-Kofi's face, the blood, the silence after the gunshot. Sometimes she wakes up hitting the mattress, her fists tight, screaming his name. Most nights she lies awake, hyper-aware of every creak in the house, every rustle outside. She has started drinking gin before bed, just enough to dull the edges, but it doesn't stop the dreams.

At work, she is irritable with colleagues who joke too loudly. She cannot stand the sound of laughter in the break room; it feels like a betrayal. She has withdrawn from her closest friends at the park, people she once camped and hiked with. She tells herself they don't understand, that they would look at her differently if they knew she froze instead of saving him. She believes, in some wordless part of herself, that she should have died instead of Kofi. That her mother lost the wrong child.

She does not talk about Kofi. When her husband brings up his name, she changes the subject or leaves the room. She has not visited his grave since the burial. She avoids looking at photos on her phone. The only thing she keeps is his old ranger hat, which she hung behind the door of her study, out of sight, but she knows it is there.

She told me all this slowly, over several sessions, her voice flat, her hands seldom still. She is a woman holding a trembling engine inside a calm exterior. She does not yet believe that talking can help, but she came because Daniel asked her to, and she came because she is tired of feeling like a stranger to herself.

She sits in the chair across from me with the careful posture of someone used to managing crises-back straight, hands still, eyes scanning the room before they settle. She is a network engineer for a regional telecom company, a job that demands she anticipate failures, reroute traffic, keep systems running even when circuits overload. She tells me she is good at this, at staying calm when something breaks. But there is one thing she cannot reroute.

The story starts two years ago, in the summer. Her daughter, then four years old, began to bruise easily, to wake up with fevers that came and went. A general practitioner sent them to the children's hospital. Within seventy-two hours they had a name for it: acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She remembers the word "acute" hitting her chest before the rest of it registered. She remembers how the air in the consultation room seemed to thin, how the doctor's mouth kept moving but the sounds were underwater. She remembers her ex-husband-already distant, already halfway out the door-saying, "We'll get through this," as if he were reading a script.

The treatment protocol stretched across months: chemotherapy, spinal taps, isolation days when a common cold could mean an ICU stay. She took a leave of absence from work initially, but the bills piled up, and her divorce was finalized during week six of her daughter's first round of treatment. She went back to her job part-time, then full-time, scheduling her daughter's appointments around system upgrades and overnight maintenance windows. She learned to compartmentalize. At the hospital she was the mother who never cried in front of the nurses. At work she was the engineer who could trace a packet drop across three time zones.

But the trauma does not stay compartmentalized.

Now, her daughter is in maintenance phase. The doctors say the prognosis is excellent. She should feel relief. Instead, she feels like she is holding her breath underwater, waiting for the next surge. She does not sleep through the night. If her daughter coughs in the next room, she is up, pulse thudding in her temples, already halfway to the bedroom before she realizes it is only a cough. She has become attuned to the sound of her daughter's breathing-she can tell from the rhythm alone if it is obstructed, if it is too shallow. When it is quiet she finds herself listening for it, which means it is never really quiet.

At work, she has started to avoid certain tasks. She used to run the quarterly disaster-recovery simulation; now she volunteers to update documentation instead. When the fire alarm goes off during a routine drill, her hands shake for the rest of the shift, and she walks out to the parking lot three times to check her phone, even though she knows her daughter is at school. She has told no one about this. She deletes the call history to the pediatric oncology hotline even though she does not call it anymore.

The divorce, she says, was not about the illness. It was already unraveling. But she wonders now if she pushed him away on purpose, because she could not bear to have one more person she might lose. She lives alone with her daughter in a small apartment near the hospital. She has not dated. She has not gone to a single playdate or birthday party for other children since the diagnosis. She tells herself she is just busy. But the truth is she cannot sit in a room full of healthy children without feeling a kind of dread she cannot name, a sense that the next routine symptom will be the one that changes everything.

When I ask her what she thinks about most, she says: "The first night in the hospital. The beeping. The way the IV pump sounded when it was about to alarm. I can still hear it." She hears it sometimes when she tries to fall asleep, so she stays up late configuring network switches, running diagnostic scripts, anything to drown out the sound. She is tired. But staying busy is the only way she knows to keep the story from replaying-the story she has told herself a hundred times, always waiting for a different ending that never comes.

Mira is thirty-five years old and has been a physical therapist at a suburban rehabilitation clinic for six years. She is married to David, a gentle, soft-spoken accountant, and they live in a small house with a garden. Her patients trust her-she is patient, precise, and kind. But what they do not see is the clock ticking inside her chest, counting the minutes until she can retreat to a room with no windows.

The story of what haunts her began seven years ago, before David, before the clinic. She was living with a man named Evan, a marketing executive whose praise felt like sunlight and whose rage felt like a door slamming shut. The first time he struck her, he apologized with tears in his eyes. She believed him. Over the next eighteen months, the apologies grew shorter, the bruises deeper, and the intervals of calm shrank until she could no longer recognize the shape of a safe day.

She remembers the weight of his hand on her throat, the way he would whisper "you made me do this" into her hair. She remembers the smell of his cologne and the sound of the front door lock clicking after he left for work. She remembers looking at her own reflection and seeing a stranger's hollow eyes.

She left after a broken rib-hollowed out, quiet, and afraid of her own shadow. She met David a year later. He is kind. He has never raised his voice. She married him because she thought love could erase memory. It cannot.

Now, at the clinic, she works with a patient who reminds her of Evan-the same broad shoulders, the same way of laughing. Mira's hands shake when she guides him through hamstring stretches. She shortens the session, invents a scheduling conflict. She avoids him on the treatment floor. At night, she lies rigid beside David, listening for footsteps that are not there. She has not slept through the night in four years.

Her PCL-5 score of 79 reflects what she feels every day: intrusive images of Evan's face contorted with anger, a cold sweat when a door closes too loudly, a compulsion to check the locks even when David is home. She startles when David touches her from behind. She has stopped going to the grocery store alone because the aisles feel like corridors. She avoids the left side of the bed, the side where Evan used to sleep.

Her work is a double-edged sword. Physical contact is her profession, but every hand she holds, every shoulder she palpates, demands that she override a survival instinct screaming danger. She has become deft at dissociation: she can count repetitions, measure range of motion, and speak in a calm voice while her mind is somewhere else-watching herself from the ceiling, nodding, performing the role of a therapist.

She has never told David about Evan's hands on her neck. She tells herself it would hurt him to know, but the truth is that saying it aloud would make it real again. So she carries the story inside her like a locked box.

Today, after her last patient, Mira sits in her car in the parking lot. She stares at the dashboard. The sun is setting, and she feels an old familiar pressure in her chest-the sense that something terrible is about to happen, that she must be ready. She grips the steering wheel until her knuckles turn white. She waits. The thing does not come. It never comes. But she is always waiting.

Mr. R is a 79-year-old South Asian man who lives alone in a small apartment near the city's industrial district. He works three mornings a week at a wholesale warehouse, stacking boxes and checking inventory. He is wiry, quiet, moves with a careful economy-no wasted motion, no sudden turns. When he speaks, his English is precise but halting, as if he is translating from a language he has not used in years. He divorced his wife in the early 1990s and has not remarried. He has two adult children who live in another province; they call once a month, and he keeps the conversations short.

He came to see me after his primary care doctor suggested he "talk to someone" about his sleep problems and his "short temper" with other workers. He agreed reluctantly, but he does not think talking helps.

The story he tells begins in 1971. He was 21, a lance corporal in the infantry. His unit was ambushed in a mangrove swamp near the border. He remembers the heat, the mosquitoes, the way the water came up to his thighs. He remembers the sound of mortars-not the explosions themselves, but the high, thin scream before each impact. During the ambush, he saw his section commander shot in the throat. The man did not fall at once. He tried to speak, but only a red froth came out of the hole. Mr. R carried him for half a mile. The commander died in his arms. Mr. R still feels the weight of that body across his shoulders, the wet warmth, the smell of mud and blood.

After the war, he tried to act normal. He married, had children, worked in a garment factory, then in a warehouse. He never spoke about the ambush or the commander. When his wife asked why he sometimes woke up screaming, he said it was a stomach ache. He avoided loud noises, crowded places, the color red. Eventually his wife stopped asking. She left him, he says, because he was "not there."

Now, at 79, the war is still in the room with him. He avoids the news, especially anything about the military. He will not attend religious ceremonies where drums are played. At the warehouse, he always puts his back to a wall when he takes a break. He scans every door for exits, every face for potential threats. His co-workers think he is just grumpy and particular. They do not know that the sound of a pallet jack dropping makes him drop to the floor, heart pounding, hands squeezing his old knees.

At night, he lies awake and replays the ambush. Sometimes the commander's face is replaced by his own son's. He tells me he is tired-tired of the flashbacks, tired of the constant alertness, tired of feeling like a coward for having survived. He says he has no one to talk to about these things, and even if he did, they would not understand. He recently scored 65 on the PCL-5, which measures severe PTSD symptoms.

He finishes his shifts at the warehouse, goes home, eats a simple dinner of rice and dal, and sits in the dark. He does not watch television. He listens to the hum of the refrigerator and the distant traffic. Sometimes he catches himself crying, but he is not sure why. The feeling that follows is a thick emptiness, as if someone has scraped out the inside of his chest. He does not believe he will ever feel different. He is not even sure he wants to.

He remembers the day clearly, though he wishes he didn't. It was a Tuesday, five years ago now, and the sky had been a dirty gray over the Gulf of Thailand. He and his youngest son, Chai, had been out on their boat since before dawn, hauling nets heavy with mackerel. The wind picked up fast, turning the sea from flat glass to rolling hills of dark water. Chai was twenty-one then, strong and sure-footed, but when the wave hit-a rogue wall that came without warning-he lost his footing on the wet deck and went over the side. The boat pitched, the engine sputtered, and by the time his father cut the throttle and dove in, the water was already closing over Chai's head. He swam until his arms burned, but the current was too strong, the visibility too poor. He never found him. The Coast Guard recovered the body two days later.

Mr. Nguyen still goes out on the water. He has to-fishing is all he knows, and there is no pension, no other work. But he no longer takes the same route. He avoids the stretch of coast where Chai went under, even if it means longer hours and smaller catches. His wife, Somsak, has started packing his lunch the night before, but he often forgets to eat. He sits in the stern, staring at the horizon, his hands gripping the wheel so hard that his knuckles blanch. The sound of a sudden splash-a dolphin, a piece of debris-sends his heart slamming against his ribs. He will scan the water for minutes afterward, his mouth dry, his breath shallow, until he convinces himself there is nothing there.

At night, he dreams. The dreams are not always the same, but they always feature Chai. In one, he sees his son standing on the dock, waving, but when Mr. Nguyen reaches him, Chai's face dissolves into seawater. In another, he is drowning himself, unable to scream, and the weight of the ocean presses down until he wakes gasping, tangled in sweat-soaked sheets. Somsak reaches for him sometimes, but he cannot bear to be touched. He lies rigid, staring at the ceiling, watching the fan blades trace their endless circles.

His memory has become unreliable. He will forget where he left his gear, or why he walked into the kitchen. But the details of that day are etched in perfect clarity: the color of Chai's shirt (a faded blue), the sound of his last shout, the salt on Mr. Nguyen's lips as he gulped air between dives. He replays it like a film he cannot stop, and each time he asks himself the same useless question: Why didn't I tie him to a line? Why didn't we stay in port? He knows the answer-the storm came too fast, Chai was an experienced fisherman-but the guilt sits in his chest like a stone, heavy and permanent.

His temper has shortened. Last month, a deckhand accidentally dropped a crate of squid on the deck, and Mr. Nguyen screamed at him for ten minutes-loud, raw, the kind of shouting he used to associate with other men, not himself. Later, he apologized, but the shame lingered. He does not laugh as much as he used to. He does not tell stories at the dock. He keeps to himself, even when other fishermen call out greetings. The sea, which once felt like a partner, now feels like an enemy he must endure.

Somsak has noticed. She tells him gently that he is not the same man she married. He knows she is right, but he does not know how to become that man again. He comes to therapy reluctantly, because she insisted, because he cannot keep living this way: half-present, half-drowning on dry land. He sits in the chair across from me, his hands folded, his eyes fixed on a spot just past my shoulder. He speaks in a voice that is soft and careful, as if the words themselves might break something inside him. And when he finishes telling me about that Tuesday, he falls silent, and the room fills with the sound of a man breathing around a grief that will not let go.

Mr. R is a 64-year-old man who has worked in the same warehouse for nearly twenty years. He loads boxes onto pallets, checks inventory sheets, and keeps his head down. He has been married to his wife for thirty-five years, and they live in a quiet suburban home. He does not speak about what happened to him before he came to this country.

He remembers the morning it began. It was 1983. He was a university student in his hometown, walking to a bus stop when armed men pulled him into a van. For the next nine months, he was held in a concrete room with no windows. The men were from a faction fighting the government, and they accused him of being a spy. They kept his hands bound, his eyes covered, and they questioned him for hours at a time. He learned to listen for footsteps, for the creak of the door, for the sound of a key turning. He learned that begging only made them hit harder. He learned to make his mind very small, to focus on the pattern of water dripping in the corner, to count the seconds between each drop.

When he was finally released-in a trade, he was told, though he never understood the details-he weighed less than a hundred pounds. His family found him walking along a dirt road. He did not cry. He did not explain. He went back to school, finished his degree, and married the woman his mother had chosen for him. He told his wife a shortened version of the story: "Some bad men held me for a while, but it's over." She never pressed him for more.

They moved to the United States in the early 1990s, and Mr. R found work at the warehouse. He is reliable. He never calls in sick. But his coworkers have noticed that he startles easily. One day a forklift backfired in the shipping bay, and Mr. R dropped to the ground, covering his head with his arms. He stayed there for five minutes, unable to speak. The supervisor helped him to the break room, and Mr. R said it was just a headache. He has never told anyone at work the truth.

At home, he sleeps in a separate room from his wife. The bedroom door must be open, but the closet door must be closed. He checks the locks on every window three times before bed. He cannot stand the sound of keys jingling-it makes his chest tighten and his palms sweat. He avoids television shows about war or prisons. When his wife asks him to go to a family gathering, he often agrees, then finds an excuse at the last minute. He says he is tired. He says his back hurts from lifting boxes. He says he doesn't feel well. What he feels is a pressure behind his ribs, as if the room is collapsing inward. He has not told her about the nightmares: the same concrete wall, the same gag in his mouth, the same voice asking questions he cannot answer. He wakes gasping, and he lies still until the feeling passes.

His daughter, who lives in another state, calls every Sunday. He listens to her voice, but he forgets what she says moments after hanging up. He remembers the texture of the blindfold against his eyelids more clearly than the color of her eyes. Sometimes he wonders if he ever really left that room.

Last month, his wife found him standing in the bathroom at 3 A.M., staring at his reflection. When she asked what was wrong, he said, "Nothing." She has started to cry in the kitchen when she thinks he cannot hear. He knows she is worried, but he does not know how to give her the words. He has never said out loud that he still hears the footsteps. He has never said that the counting has never stopped.

She still remembers the smell of diesel and dust, the way it clung to her clothes for days. That was twenty-two years ago, when she was thirty, a lawyer on leave with a humanitarian organization in a disputed border region. Now she is fifty-two, a judge in a county courthouse, and the scent of a passing truck can stop her mid-sentence.

She came to my office three months ago at the urging of her clerk, who noticed her flinch at the bang of a closing door. At first, she insisted she was fine-busy, tired, nothing more. She spoke in the measured tone she uses on the bench, each word chosen for weight and neutrality. But over the weeks, the story has emerged in fragments, like testimony that contradicts itself while telling the same truth.

The incident happened on a Tuesday afternoon. She was part of a small team distributing blankets and medicine at a makeshift clinic on the outskirts of a town that no longer appears on some maps. An artillery shell struck a nearby market. She remembers the way the ground moved, a sideways lurch that threw her against a wall. Then the sounds: a high-pitched ringing, then screams, then a terrible silence. She helped carry the wounded, a young girl with a leg wound that would later require amputation. The girl's mother kept repeating a name-Leila, Leila-as if calling her back from somewhere. The mother's face is the image that intrudes most often, superimposed now on the faces of litigants, on the faces of her own children, now grown.

She returned home six weeks later and tried to resume her life. She married a year after, threw herself into law career, had two daughters. She did not talk about the relief work, not even to her husband. He called her cold, distant. She called him demanding. The divorce was finalized seven years ago. She told herself it was for the best, that she was not built for intimacy.

Today, her life is carefully structured. She rises at 5:30, runs exactly five miles, eats the same oatmeal, reviews case files in chambers before anyone arrives. The courtroom is her sanctuary-a place of rules and predictable procedures. She needs the ritual. When a lawyer raises his voice, she feels a tightness in her chest, a surge of irritability she barely suppresses. She rarely loses her temper, but she often feels as if she is holding herself very still, like a rabbit in tall grass.

At night, sleep is elusive. She avoids news coverage of war zones, but sometimes the footage breaks through anyway-a grainy image of a relief convoy, a reporter's voice describing shelling. Her heart hammers. She gets up, makes tea, reads case law until her eyes burn. She does not date. She does not call friends. She tells herself she prefers solitude, but the truth is she feels constantly on alert, even in her own home.

Last week, a young female attorney argued a motion with zeal, her voice rising with emotion. The judge felt a sudden, unbidden rush of anger-not at the woman, but at the memory of that mother calling for Leila-the same desperate pitch. She had to call a recess. In her chambers, she pressed her palms flat on the desk until the tremor passed.

She tells me these things with a flat, clinical tone, as if describing someone else. When I ask how she feels, she pauses. "I feel... tired," she says. "Like I'm holding something heavy, and I've been holding it for a very long time." She does not know how to put it down.
