He checks his rearview mirror obsessively, expecting to see the mountain rushing toward him. Loud, unexpected sounds-a car backfiring, a door slamming-make him drop to a crouch, his hands covering his head. He once yelled at a bagpiper at a funeral because the drone reminded him of the engine spooling down.

Tane has difficulty trusting his own body. He still walks with a slight limp from a knee injury sustained on ejection, but he refuses physical therapy because the examination table reminds him of the hospital bed where he first learned the co-pilot did not survive. He avoids going to the doctor altogether. He no longer drinks alcohol, which he used to enjoy, because even one beer "loosens the walls" and the memories flood in. He has not had a truly restful night's sleep since the accident.

He tells me he feels like the person who ejected from that aircraft is someone else-a younger man who believed in his own invincibility. The man sitting across from me now is cautious, isolated, and always scanning the horizon for something that might fall out of the sky. He says he has never spoken about these things before, not even to Maria.

Margaret is seventy-three years old, but her body still remembers the precise weight of a hand on her shoulder. It is a cool Tuesday morning and she sits in the therapy office with her hands folded neatly in her lap, her wedding ring catching the light. Her husband, Edward, waits in the car-she insisted. The drive here took forty minutes of scanning every rearview mirror, counting license plates, checking for any car that followed too long.

She grew up in a small town in the Midwest, the only child of a schoolteacher and a carpenter. Her father was the caregiver who abused her. The abuse started when she was six, and it was never the dramatic beatings you see in movies. It was the quiet, systematic kind: a pinch that left a bruise on her upper arm that she learned to cover with long sleeves even in summer; a slap across the face if she spilled milk; being locked in the basement closet for hours because she asked a question he thought was disrespectful. Once, when she was nine, he grabbed her by the hair and dragged her across the kitchen floor because she had left a cabinet door open. She learned to open cabinets silently, to never let a dish clink against another, to walk on the balls of her feet so no floorboard squeaked. Her mother never intervened-she was afraid, too.

Margaret escaped to a state college on a scholarship, became a QA engineer in her twenties-a job that suited her perfectly. Finding errors in code, logging every anomaly, tracing bugs to their source: this was what she was already trained to do. She could spend hours bent over a test case, repeating the same sequence until the failure happened, because failure was always hiding somewhere. She married Edward at twenty-eight, a gentle man who never raised his voice. She never told him about her father, not the whole truth. When he asked about her family, she said, "We weren't close," and he accepted it.

Now she is retired, but she still lives like a QA engineer. Her day follows a strict protocol: wake at six, check the locks on all doors twice, make the bed with hospital corners, eat the same breakfast (oatmeal, black coffee, half a grapefruit). She keeps a written checklist on the kitchen counter: stove off, windows closed, front door deadbolt engaged. If she cannot complete the checklist, or if she is interrupted mid-sequence, she must restart from the beginning. Edward once came home early and found her in the kitchen, retracing her steps to the front door three times. He asked if she was okay. She said she thought she smelled gas.

The flashbacks do not announce themselves. Sometimes a sharp sound-the clatter of a pot lid hitting the tile floor-and she is nine years old again, frozen in the kitchen, waiting for the blow. Her heart drums, her breathing goes shallow, and she grips the edge of the counter until her knuckles are white. The world tilts, and for a full thirty seconds she is not a retired woman in her own home; she is a child paralyzed by the creak of a floorboard. Edward has learned to say her name quietly, to wait until her eyes come back into focus. He does not touch her from behind.

She avoids certain things without thinking: basements, unlocked closets, the sound of a belt being unbuckled. She cannot watch movies where a father hurts a child. She left a dinner party once when a friend mentioned a "firm hand" in parenting-Margaret excused herself to the restroom and stood with her hands on the sink, breathing in a pattern she taught herself as a girl. Inhale for four, hold for four, exhale for four. She is an expert at keeping her face neutral.

At night, she sleeps on the side of the bed closest to the door. She always has. If Edward moves in his sleep, she wakes instantly-fully awake, no grogginess, eyes scanning the dark for the shape of a man. She tells herself she is just a light sleeper. But her body knows.

The PCL-5 score of 74, which the clinician calculated during the initial intake, is a number Margaret will never see. She does not need a number to know that the past is never past. Each morning she checks the locks, traces the same safe pattern, and tries to convince herself that the door is closed-that no one can open it anymore.

She is seventy-eight years old, though she does not feel it-except when she wakes at three in the morning, heart hammering, convinced someone is in the bedroom. Her husband sleeps beside her, his breathing slow, but she cannot shake the feeling that the lock on the front door is not enough. She has changed the locks three times since the assault. Her husband says nothing when he sees the new keys on the counter; he just clips them onto his ring and nods.

The assault happened three years ago, in the parking lot of the courthouse where she had worked for four decades as a public defender. She was leaving late, past ten o'clock, after a resentencing hearing. Her client had been convicted of a violent crime, but she believed he deserved a second chance-had argued it fiercely, felt the judge's skepticism, the prosecutor's contempt. She won. He would be out in eighteen months. She remembers feeling buoyant as she walked to her car. Then a man came out of the shadows. She does not remember his face, only the weight of his hand over her mouth, the cold metal of a knife pressed against her throat. He took her purse, her briefcase, and her wedding ring. He did not hit her. He did not say a word. He pushed her to the ground and ran.

She did not scream. She got up, walked into the courthouse, and told the security guard what happened. She gave her statement. She went home. She showered. She did not cry for three days.

Now, three years later, she still works one day a week at the public defender's office-not in court, not in the field, just reviewing files from a small desk in the back. She tells herself it keeps her mind sharp, but really she cannot let go of the work that defined her. She avoids the courthouse. She takes the long way to the office, past the hospital instead. She never parks in the same spot twice. Her husband offered to drive her, but she refuses. She needs to feel in control of the car.

At night, she checks the locks twice before bed. She keeps a small pepper spray in her bedside drawer, though she knows she would never reach it in time. She has stopped wearing her wedding ring. Her husband does not ask why, but she sees the hurt in his eyes when he touches her bare hand. She cannot explain it: the ring feels like a target now, a sign of vulnerability. She knows this is irrational. She knows her husband is not the man in the parking lot. But the fear does not reason.

She has nightmares about being chased. Not always in a parking lot-sometimes in a courtroom, sometimes in her own kitchen. She wakes gasping, covers her mouth so she does not wake her husband. During the day, she replays the attack in fragments: the pressure of the hand, the glint of the knife, the thud of her knees on asphalt. She tries to push the images away, but they surface when she is quiet-while washing dishes, waiting in line at the grocery store, sitting on the couch watching the news. The news makes her jumpy. She turns it off.

She has stopped going to the local diner where she used to meet former colleagues. She claims she is tired, but really she cannot bear the open space near the windows, the way anyone could walk in from the street. She eats meals at the kitchen table, back to the wall. Her husband sits across from her, and she watches his face soften with worry. He asks if she wants to talk to someone. She says no. She says she is fine.

She is not fine. She is seventy-eight years old, a woman who spent her life fighting for others, and now she fights to feel safe in her own home. She keeps her keys in her hand when she walks to the mailbox. She scans every stranger's face for the one she cannot remember. She lives in a world that feels smaller and darker than it used to, and she does not know how to find her way out.

Captain Maya Chen is twenty-nine years old, a combat pilot who flies F-35s out of a joint base in the Pacific. She has been flying since she was twenty-three, logging over a thousand hours in theater. She came to talk because she can't sleep, because her hands shake when she holds a coffee cup, because she has stopped talking to her mother on the phone.

It started eighteen months ago. Maya was scrambled on a night mission over hostile terrain, a routine CAS run. Her wingman, Captain Jake Morrison-ten years older, quiet, a man who always let her lead on the radio and bought her pad thai on R&R-was flying low cover. She saw the surface-to-air flash on her left peripheral, heard the garbled call over comms, then silence. She orbited for twenty minutes waiting for his beacon. It never came. The recovery team found nothing but sheet metal.

In the weeks after, Maya threw herself into sorties. She told herself the best way to honor him was to keep flying. She flew harder, lower, faster. Then the dreams started. In them, Jake is still alive, sitting in the ready room, and he turns to look at her, but his face is made of chrome and she can't hear what he says. She wakes up with her sheets soaked, her heart pounding. She stopped drinking coffee because it made her jump at the smell of jet fuel.

She avoids the hangar now. She drives the long way to the flight line so she doesn't pass the maintenance bay where Jake's locker used to be. When she straps into the cockpit, her hands freeze on the throttle. She has to repeat the preflight checklist three times because her mind drifts to the radio silence, to the way the afterburner flame looked orange against the smoke. Her squadron commander noticed a drop in her simulator scores. He suggested she see someone.

Maya lives alone in a one-bedroom near base. She hasn't dated since the incident. She says she doesn't have the energy. She spends her nights cleaning her pistol, over and over, or watching old movies on mute. She rarely eats. She lost twelve pounds. She stopped replying to her mother's texts-her mother lives in a city half a world away, and the last time they video-called, Maya started shaking and said the connection was bad. She feels a constant, low-grade guilt. She should have seen the SAM. She should have called a break turn sooner. If she had, maybe Jake would still be alive.

At work, she is functional but hollow. She can still fly-her muscle memory is intact-but the joy is gone. She feels like she is operating a machine that used to be her body. When the briefing officer says "hostile territory," she sees Jake's canopy shattering. When she hears a siren on base, she flinches. She has started checking the memorial page for the squadron every morning, even though she knows no one else has died. She doesn't know why she does it.

The therapist notes that Maya's narrative is precise, almost clinical. She uses aviation jargon to describe her feelings: "My affect is flat, like a dead-stick landing." She doesn't cry when she talks about Jake. She says she has already cried all she can. But at night, she lies awake, and she sees his wedding ring on his flight glove, and she hears the last transmission, just static.

She is a combat pilot. She was trained to never leave a wingman behind. But he is gone, and she is still flying, and that feels like the worst kind of betrayal.

Anna is nineteen. She is a dancer. She has been dancing since she was four, and it has always been the one place she felt safe and in control-the studio, the mirror, the way her body knows exactly what to do when the music starts. But now, when she walks into the rehearsal space, she feels like she is standing in a room full of smoke.

It happened eight months ago, on a Friday night in late winter. She was performing in a small club downtown, a contemporary piece with two other dancers. The place was packed. Halfway through the second set, someone smelled gas. Then someone yelled. Then the back wall lit up like a curtain of fire. She remembers the sound-not the explosion, but the screaming. She remembers the heat pressing against her back as she ran. She remembers a man in a red jacket pushing her toward the emergency exit, and then the crush of bodies, the way the air turned thick and black, and the taste of ash in her mouth for days afterward. She got out. Sixteen people did not.

Now she wakes up three or four times a night, drenched in sweat, her heart pounding so hard she can feel it in her teeth. Sometimes she sees the fire. Sometimes she sees the man in the red jacket, but his face is melting. She does not tell anyone this. She lives alone in a small apartment above a laundromat, and she has not been back to a club or a crowded bar since that night.

Her therapist-she started seeing someone two months ago, after her boss said she was missing too many rehearsals-wrote down a score of 76 on some form. Anna does not know what that means. She only knows that she cannot breathe when the house lights dim. She only knows that she stopped taking the subway because the tunnels feel too much like that hallway. She walks everywhere now, even in the rain, even if it takes an hour. Her feet hurt all the time.

At the studio, she gets through the warm-up by staring at a single spot on the floor. She does not look at the other dancers. She does not look at the fire alarm on the wall. When the music swells too loud, her hands start to shake, and she has to stop and pretend she is checking her shoelaces. Her choreographer, a patient man named Lars, keeps asking if she wants to talk. She says she is fine. She says she just needs more sleep. But she cannot sleep. When she closes her eyes, she smells the gas again.

She has not told anyone the full story. She told the police once, and then she told her mother, but her mother cried so much that Anna decided it was easier to say nothing. Now she tells herself that the fire was not that bad. She tells herself that she is lucky, that she got out, that sixteen people did not. But the guilt sits in her chest like a stone. She replays the exit door in her head a hundred times a day: she was the third person out. She could have turned back. She did not.

Last week, she tried to go to a small café with a friend from the company. The friend ordered coffee. The gas burners on the stovetop were blue. Anna stared at them, and then she started to cry. She could not explain why. She left before the coffee came.

She still dances. It is the only thing she knows how to do. But the joy is gone. When she moves, it feels mechanical, like a body going through steps that used to mean something. She cannot feel the music anymore. Sometimes she wonders if the fire burned something out of her that will never come back. She is nineteen years old, and she is so tired.

Charles is a fifty-seven-year-old tutor at a small community learning center. He works with adults preparing for their high school equivalency exams, sitting across a cluttered desk from each student, helping them wrestle with algebra or essay structure. He keeps the door propped open with a doorstop-he always does, even in winter. The cold air feels better than the alternative.

Twenty-three years ago, Charles was a young high school teacher. He lived alone, too much in his head, and had never been good at reading people. After a department gathering, a senior colleague offered him a ride home. Charles accepted, grateful to avoid the bus. The colleague did not drive him home. He pulled into a quiet park, locked the doors, and, without warning, forced himself onto Charles. Charles did not fight. He went still, the way he imagines a rabbit does when a dog pins it. He said nothing. He did not scream. When it was over, the colleague drove him home as if nothing had happened. Charles never told anyone-not the principal, not the police, not even his own mother. He stopped teaching two years later. He could not stomach the hallways, the staff meetings, the way the colleague remained on faculty, greeting him with a confident smile.

Now, Charles tutors. The work feels safer-shorter sessions, no formal authority, no faculty rooms. But safety is a fragile word. When a student leans too far across the desk, reaching for a pencil or to point at a page, Charles flinches. He tries to cover it by shifting in his chair or pretending to cough. He has learned to stand during tutoring, keeping the desk between himself and the student. He never touches anyone. A student once reached out to thank him, her hand brushing his shoulder, and he pulled back so quickly that she stared. He said he was sorry-he was a "jumpy guy." He feels the shame hours later, replaying the moment in his head.

At night, Charles does not sleep well. He lies in bed with the light on, his back to the wall, facing the door. He wakes from dreams he cannot fully recall-just a heaviness, the sense of a hand on his mouth. He walks to the kitchen, pours a glass of whiskey, and sips it until his pulse slows. He never finishes the bottle, but he comes close. The next day, he tutors with a dull headache, snapping at students who ask for help a second time. He apologizes quickly, explaining that he did not sleep well. He has used that excuse for so many years that it no longer sounds like an excuse, just a fact.

He has stopped going to the grocery store late at night. Sometimes a man walking too close behind him in line triggers a racing heart, a wave of heat, the urge to bolt. He scans parking lots before exiting his car. He scans every room he enters. He does not call it scanning-he calls it "being aware." He does not date. He tried once, five years ago, but the first kiss sent him into a full-blown panic, tears streaming, the woman confused and then angry. He stopped trying.

This morning, a student asked him to close the door so they could concentrate. Charles felt his chest tighten. He said no-the door stays open, that is the policy. The truth is, there is no policy. The student shrugged, but Charles could not shake the feeling of being trapped. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood in a stall, breathing through his mouth, waiting for the nausea to pass. He stared at the tiled floor and thought, I am fifty-seven years old. I am still afraid of a door.

He is thirty years old, African, single, and works as a curriculum designer for a nonprofit educational organization. His apartment is neat, almost sterile-a space he keeps ordered so nothing can surprise him. He comes to therapy because his supervisor suggested it after noticing that he flinches whenever a coworker walks up behind his desk. He does not think he needs therapy, but he also knows he has not slept through the night in over a year.

The trauma began two years ago, when he was living with a woman he had been with for almost three years. She was charismatic, successful, and intensely jealous. At first her jealousy felt flattering, a sign of devotion. But the first slap came six months in, after a party where he spoke to a female colleague for too long. She apologized immediately, crying, promising it would never happen again. He believed her. He loved her.

The physical abuse escalated slowly-shoves, pinches, a thrown phone, a punch to his ribs that left a bruise he covered with gym excuses. He started walking on eggshells. He changed how he dressed, whom he texted, how long he stayed at work. He stopped seeing his friends. At the time he told himself he was being a good partner. He told himself she was under a lot of stress. He rationalized every incident until the night she hit him in the face with a glass bottle, splitting his eyebrow open. He sat in the emergency room and told the doctor he had tripped. That was the last time he saw her. But she did not leave him-he left her, in the middle of the night, with only a backpack and his laptop.

Now, he designs curricula for middle-school social studies. He is good at it-he writes lesson plans that guide students through complex historical topics with clear, predictable steps. He likes the structure. He avoids units on conflict, power dynamics, or personal relationships. When he has to include content about domestic violence for a health class module, he delegates that section to a colleague without explaining why. His desk is arranged so that his back is to the wall and he can see the door. He does not tolerate loud noises. A door slamming in the hallway makes his heart pound and his hands go cold.

He has not dated since the breakup. He deleted all his dating apps. When a friendly barista smiles at him, he feels a cold dread instead of warmth. He tells himself he is protecting others from his baggage, but deep down he knows he is protecting himself from being hurt again. He avoids crowded places, especially at night. He changed his commute to a longer route that passes fewer bars and restaurants where couples might be laughing. At home he keeps the television on low volume, checking the locks three times before bed.

His sleep is fractured. He wakes up at least twice a night, often from a dream in which he is pinned down, unable to move or shout. In the dream her face is not her face-it is an abstract, monstrous shadow. He lies awake afterward, listening to the silence, waiting for something to break. On workdays he functions on four or five hours of sleep, surviving on caffeine and willpower.

He is irritable with colleagues over small things-a misplaced file, a last-minute meeting request-and then he apologizes excessively, fearing he has made someone angry. He has trouble concentrating on reading, needing to re-read paragraphs multiple times. His PCL-5 score of 33 reflects the weight he carries: the hypervigilance, the avoidance, the numbing, the negative beliefs about himself. He believes he should have been stronger, should have left earlier, should have seen the signs. He believes that loving someone means being vulnerable, and vulnerability is now synonymous with danger.

He comes to therapy because his supervisor said it was a good idea. He sits on the edge of the chair, not fully relaxed. He speaks quietly, measuring his words. He does not know if talking will help. But he is tired of checking every corner, tired of flinching at kindness, tired of living in a world where the safest place is alone.

He hasn't slept more than three hours in a night since the Fourth of July, though the fireworks aren't really the problem. It's the quiet that gets him-the way the house falls still around two in the morning, the way the streetlight through the blinds throws a pale grid across the bedroom wall. His wife, Sarah, lies beside him, her breathing even, and he envies that. He lies perfectly still, listening for something he can't name, his jaw tight enough that his molars ache by dawn.

Tom is thirty-six, a tax consultant at a mid-size firm in a Midwest city. He keeps a framed CPA license on his desk and a coffee mug that says "Audit? I'd rather fight a war." He bought it himself, years ago, when he still thought that kind of humor was okay. He doesn't think so now.

The war was Iraq, 2007. He was a specialist in a logistics unit, tasked with convoy security. The event that broke the seam in his mind happened on a road south of Baghdad. An IED ripped through the lead vehicle. He remembers the smoke, the screaming, the smell of diesel and burnt rubber. He pulled a man from the wreckage-a private named Kowalski, nineteen years old, legs gone below the knee. Tom held a tourniquet on what was left while the medic worked. Kowalski lived, but Tom still sees his face in the instant the sound hit, the open mouth, the eyes that said this is real.

Back home, he told himself he was fine. He married Sarah six months after redeploying. They bought a house, adopted a dog. He went to work, filed extensions, calculated deductions, answered client calls about capital gains. He was good at it. Numbers don't lie; they don't scream.

But the numbers started to blur. He finds himself staring at a Schedule C for twenty minutes, the lines swimming, because somewhere in the back of his head he's replaying that road, checking for tripwires in the median, scanning rooftops. In client meetings, he flinches when someone drops a binder on the floor. He apologizes, says the coffee is too strong. He's stopped taking the highway to work-the overpasses make him feel trapped, and once, last winter, he pulled over on the shoulder because his heart was pounding so hard he couldn't see straight. He told Sarah he had a migraine.

At night, the dreams come. Not every night, but enough. In the dream, he's back in the Humvee, and the radio is static, and Kowalski is in the seat beside him, whole and grinning, and then the ground opens up and Tom is falling, falling, and he wakes with his fists clenched and the sheet soaked. Sarah has learned not to touch him when he wakes up. She waits until he says her name.

He's irritable in ways that frighten him. Last week, a telemarketer called during dinner and he slammed the phone on the counter so hard the screen cracked. Sarah looked at him, not afraid, but tired. He saw her face and felt a shame that burned all the way down. He doesn't talk about Iraq. When coworkers ask about his time in the service, he says "supply chain stuff" and changes the subject. He avoids the veterans' group at the library. He avoids the news. He avoids anything that might trigger-but the triggers are everywhere. A car backfires and he's on the floor of the garage before he knows what happened. A certain smell-grilled meat, or diesel-makes his stomach clench.

He hasn't told Sarah about the PCL-5 he filled out in the waiting room. Score of seventy. He knows what that means-he's seen the scoring guide on the psychologist's clipboard. He's here because his doctor insisted, because his blood pressure is through the roof, because Sarah said she couldn't live with the man he'd become. So he sits in the chair, across from the therapist, and tells her about the sleepless nights and the client who complained that he seemed "distracted." He doesn't tell her about the moment last month when he found himself checking a restaurant's exits six times before he could sit down. He doesn't tell her that sometimes, when he looks at his wife, he feels so far away from her that he wonders if he's already gone.

He glances at the clock on the wall. It's eleven in the morning. He has three hours before his next appointment, a couple with a small business and a messy partnership return. He needs to focus. But the therapist is asking him about the Fourth of July, about the fireworks, about the quiet. And Tom realizes that somewhere inside, he's still on that road, and the road hasn't ended.

She first noticed him because he was always there. Not in a way she could prove at first-just a shape at the edge of her peripheral vision, a figure who seemed to be walking the same route home from the train station, browsing the same grocery aisles, sitting two tables away at the café she liked. She told herself it was coincidence. She was a graphic designer, trained to notice patterns, and she knew that the mind often creates meaning where none exists. So she dismissed it.

But then the notes began. Small, folded pieces of paper tucked under her windshield wiper: You look prettiest when you're focused. She had been hunched over her laptop at a coffee shop the day before, working on a branding project for a local bakery. When she saw the note, her stomach dropped. She looked around the parking lot. No one. The next day, another note: Your hair smells like rain. She had been caught in the rain on Tuesday. That afternoon she told her husband, Mark, and they went to the police. There was nothing they could do yet, the officer explained-no direct threat, no physical harm. She should document everything, keep a log.

Over the next few weeks, she stopped going to the coffee shop. She took different routes home, sometimes driving an extra fifteen minutes just to lose him. She changed her routine at work, leaving at odd hours, her eyes scanning the sidewalk before she stepped out. Mark started picking her up when he could, but he couldn't be there all the time. The notes kept coming. Once, she found one taped to her studio door: I know when you're alone. That was the night she couldn't stop shaking. She barely slept.

Now, months later, he has been arrested and charged. The trial is pending. She knows she is safe-she moved offices, changed her phone number, installed cameras at home-but her body doesn't believe it. She still checks her rearview mirror compulsively, her hands sweating on the wheel. She walks through the grocery store with her head on a swivel, heart hammering every time a man of average height with brown hair turns down an aisle. She no longer works in coffee shops; she works from home, curtains drawn, jumping at every sound. Her design work suffers. She stares at the screen for hours, unable to choose a font, unable to commit to a color palette because her mind is stuck in a loop: He knew I was working there. He knew what I smelled like. What else does he know?

She avoids crowds. She avoids the train station. She avoids the email notifications she used to ignore, now checking each one twice before opening. Her husband tries to comfort her, but she feels distant from him, hollowed out. She snaps at him for little things-leaving the back door unlocked, telling a neighbor about their new security system. She doesn't trust anyone anymore, not even her closest friends. She canceled a coffee date last week because she saw a man in a blue jacket that looked like the one he always wore.

At night, she dreams of notes. Hundreds of them, piling up on her desk, her bed, her keyboard. She wakes up gasping, her skin crawling. She tells herself it's over. But her body remembers.

He is a 54-year-old Latin American man, married, and the owner of a mid-sized construction company. He came to see me at his wife's insistence, after months of tension and silence in their home. During our first sessions, he speaks in short, clipped sentences, his hands resting flat on his knees, eyes fixed somewhere past my shoulder. He tells me he volunteered as a relief worker in a war zone eighteen years ago.

He remembers the day clearly. It was late afternoon, and he was part of a convoy distributing food and medical supplies near a village that had been shelled the night before. He stood in the back of a pickup truck, handing bags of rice to a line of women and children. The sound was not loud-it was more like a punch of air. The mortar hit fifty feet away. He was thrown from the truck. When he stood up, his ears ringing, he saw the body of a colleague he had been talking to moments before. The man's name was Carlos. They had shared coffee that morning. He tried to lift Carlos, but there was no point. The next few hours were a blur of dust, screaming, and the metallic smell of blood. He kept working for another three weeks, then returned home.

Now, in the present, he cannot watch news reports of any conflict. He changes the channel immediately, but sometimes the sound of helicopters on television sends a jolt through his chest, and his palms sweat. He avoids driving past the local veterans' hall. At his construction sites, he is known as a demanding boss-he walks the perimeter several times a day, checks every invoice twice, and cannot tolerate a worker standing still without an explanation. He tells me he feels a constant need to be prepared, though he cannot say for what. His wife has stopped asking him to go to family gatherings because he always finds an excuse, or, if he goes, he spends the evening scanning doorways and exits.

At night, he dreams of dust and shouting. He wakes up with his heart pounding, reaches for his phone to check the time, and then lies still until morning. He has not told his wife about Carlos. When she asks what is wrong, he says he is tired. He drinks three beers most evenings to quiet the restlessness, but it only makes him more irritable. Last month, he yelled at a subcontractor over a minor delay, then felt a wave of shame that lasted for days. He describes himself as "on a short fuse" and says he does not understand why small things make him so angry.

During our sessions, his posture rarely changes. He speaks of the war zone as if it were a story about someone else. But when I ask about the moment Carlos died, he stops. His hand goes to his jaw. He stares at the floor and says nothing for nearly a minute. Then he says, "I should have done more." He does not elaborate. In his business, he has started taking on fewer new projects, afraid he cannot handle the pressure. His wife tells him he is not the man she married. He agrees with her, but he does not know how to go back.

Mr. Pham is a small, quiet man of sixty-nine, with silver hair and fine hands that never seem to stop moving-picking at a loose thread on his sleeve, smoothing the knee of his trousers, folding and refolding a handkerchief. He speaks in a soft, careful voice, and his eyes water easily.

When he was thirty-nine, his son Minh, then five, was diagnosed with leukemia. The year that followed-the year of needles and fevers, of the smell of disinfectant and the sound of machines beeping in the dark-never left him. Minh survived. He is now a healthy thirty-five-year-old living in another city. But Mr. Pham did not survive it in the same way.

Every day now, he works as a nanny for a two-year-old boy named Leo. The job is meant to fill his days since his wife died of cancer ten years ago. He loves Leo. He is gentle, patient, tireless. But he is also afraid. Leo sneezes once in the morning, and Mr. Pham spends the rest of the day checking his temperature with a digital thermometer he carries in his pocket. He keeps a careful log-on a notepad, not on his phone, because he doesn't trust technology-of how many ounces Leo drinks, how many times he pees, the exact color of his stool. The parents tell him, kindly, that he is overdoing it. He nods in agreement and does not stop.

At night, Mr. Pham does not sleep. He lies in bed and hears the beeping of Minh's old hospital monitors, even though he has not set foot in a hospital in twenty years. He sees his wife's face as she held Minh through the chemo, her eyes hollow and fixed. He sees the doctor's mouth moving, words he cannot remember but whose shape he still feels-a pull inside his chest, like an anchor scraping the seabed.

He does not go to the park anymore. The sight of other children running near the slide-especially children who look about five-makes his hands go cold and his heart thump so hard he thinks he might faint. He once told his daughter-in-law that he was "not a park person." That was four months ago. Leo's mother noticed and asked if he was okay. He said he was just tired.

He is irritable in ways he was not before. A loud noise-the clatter of a pan in the kitchen, the sudden cry of a bird outside-makes him flinch and snap at Leo, whom he never snaps at. Then he apologizes, over and over, holding the boy's hand too tightly. He has stopped calling his son Minh. He texts him instead, short messages: "Eat vegetables." "Take vitamin." He cannot bear to hear his voice on the phone-it sounds too much like the little boy in the hospital bed.

His memory is strange now. He forgets where he put Leo's sippy cup, but he remembers, in perfect detail, the pattern of the hospital curtain in room 312: little blue triangles, like a child's drawing of mountains. He remembers the nurse's name-Tina-and the way she hummed while changing the IV bag. He remembers the exact date Minh's fever broke: March 14, 1995. He does not know what day it is today.

He feels, most of the time, as if he is still in that year. The years after-his wife's illness, her funeral, the quiet apartment-all feel like a blur, like a long corridor he walked through without seeing the walls. Only the hospital room is real. Only the fear is real. And now, when Leo coughs in his sleep, Mr. Pham sits beside the crib, hand over his own mouth, trying not to shake.

He walks into the office at 7:03 each morning, always three minutes late, always with a travel mug of black coffee that he never finishes. The security guard nods; he doesn't nod back. By 9 a.m. he has logged into his work queue, forty-seven unresolved tickets blinking on his screen, and his shoulders are already tight. He works from a cubicle near the emergency exit - he picked it himself, first day on the job, told his manager he liked the natural light. The truth is he needs to know the way out.

He was twenty-two when he joined the army of his home country, a small Southeast Asian nation still fingering the scars of a decades-long civil war. His unit was sent to clear a village north of the capital, something about insurgent activity. He remembers the heat, the way the rice paddies shimmered like broken glass, and the smell - wet earth and something metallic. He was the radio operator, crouched behind a low wall, calling in coordinates when the mortars came. The first round hit fifty meters left. The second landed directly on the command post where his sergeant, a man named Chandara, had been standing. He saw Chandara's torso separate from his legs, and he remembers thinking that isn't real, even as the blood soaked into his own uniform.

He was the one who called the medevac. He still hears the radio static, his own voice cracking. For two weeks afterward he stayed on base, slept with his boots on, could not close his eyes without seeing the red mist. He was sent home with a commendation and a diagnosis no one used the words for. He never spoke about it. His family said he seemed "quiet." His fiancée, now his wife, said he had changed. He said nothing.

Now he is forty-six. He works from a beige cubicle in a tech park outside Austin, writing code for a logistics platform. The work is good - repetitive, logical, predictable. He likes that. But he cannot sit with his back to a door. He has rearranged his desk so he can see the hallway. When a coworker claps him on the shoulder unexpectedly, his hand jerks and his heart hammers for thirty seconds. He has learned to say "Sorry, I'm just jumpy today." He says it at least twice a week.

At home he is quieter still. His wife of twenty-three years has learned not to ask about the nightmares. She hears him thrash in the dark, sometimes shouting numbers - coordinates, she thinks - and she waits. In the morning he says nothing. He takes his coffee and drives to work with the windows up, scanning every intersection for something he cannot name. He avoids crowds. He avoids the news. He avoids the Vietnamese grocery store because the smell of fish sauce brings the rice paddies back. He has not visited his mother in ten years. She lives in Phnom Penh. He sends money, but he cannot explain why he will not come.

Last month his manager asked him to lead a team meeting in the glass-walled conference room. He said he had a dentist appointment. He went to the parking lot and sat in his car for an hour, sweating. He does not think of himself as broken. He thinks of himself as someone who learned to hold very still. The world has a high ceiling and he is always listening for a sound he cannot identify - a whistle, a hiss, the first whisper of an inbound round that never comes.

He is twenty-eight years old, and he spends most of his day staring at a screen that doesn't feel like a screen. It feels like a window he can't close, a feed that won't stop feeding him images he never asked for. He works as a social media manager for a mid-sized outdoor gear company, which means his job is to curate optimism-sunlit trails, smiling hikers, clean tents pitched beside calm lakes. He is good at it. He knows the algorithms, the right hashtags, the cadence of a caption that makes people stop scrolling. But the scrolling itself is the problem. Every time he opens Instagram or Twitter, he is waiting for the wrong image to appear. A dust cloud. A twisted piece of metal. A face he used to know.

The trauma happened three years ago, during his second deployment to Afghanistan. He was a vehicle operator in a logistics convoy, driving supply trucks between forward operating bases. That day, the route had been quiet, which made everyone nervous. He remembers the heat pressing through the armored cab, the taste of dust and diesel, the way the radio crackled with static. Then the blast. An IED buried in the road, detonated under the lead vehicle. He didn't see the explosion-he was two trucks back-but he heard it, felt it in his chest, and then he saw the smoke and the fire and the pieces of things that used to be whole. They pulled the driver out, or what was left of him. The man's name was Corporal Reyes. He had a wife back home and a baby girl he'd only seen in photos. He had been twenty-two.

That night, and every night since, the images repeat themselves. He does not have full-blown flashbacks with visual hallucinations, but the memory is so vivid it might as well be happening. He feels the heat. He smells the burning fuel and something else, something organic. He hears the shouting and the crying. And then he feels nothing, which is worse-a numbing emptiness that slides over him like a shroud. He tells himself he should have been in the lead truck. He tells himself he could have done something. He knows, rationally, that is not true, but the thought sits inside him like a stone he cannot swallow.

When he came home, he tried to go back to his old life. He finished his degree in communications, found the social media job, moved in with his girlfriend, Olivia. She is patient. She is kind. But he cannot tell her what he sees when he closes his eyes. He cannot tell her why he flinches when a car backfires on the street, or why he sometimes cancels plans because the thought of a crowded bar makes his skin crawl. He avoids loud noises, crowds, even the news-anything that might trigger the memory. He has unfollowed every veteran's page on social media. He has blocked all military-related hashtags. Still, the algorithm finds him. A video of a convoy in Ukraine. A photo of a soldier hugging his daughter. The image of a boot. He freezes, his heart pounds, his palms sweat, and then he closes the tab and opens a spreadsheet of hiking trail photos, and he tries to breathe.

At work, his boss praises his engagement metrics. He is always online. He is always responsive. But inside, he is hollow. He does not feel pride in his work. He feels like a machine performing a script. His relationship with Olivia is strained-he loves her, but he cannot be present. He lies awake next to her at night, scanning the dark for threats that are not there. He has not cried since the deployment. He has not felt joy in months. He simply exists, scrolling forward, waiting for the next blast.

She is nineteen years old, though she carries herself like someone much older. The first time she came into the clinic, her hands were still raw from hauling nets the night before-salt-crusted, calloused, trembling slightly as she tucked them under her thighs. She is a fisherman, like her father and his father before him, and she works the morning tide out of a small village on the Atoll's leeward side. Her boyfriend, also a fisherman, rides in the same skiff. They have been together since she was sixteen, and he is the only person who knows the full weight of what she carries.

The thing that broke her happened eighteen months ago, in the shallow lagoon just beyond the reef. She had been out with her uncle and two cousins, hauling in a night's catch under a half-moon. The weather was calm, the water clear enough to see the coral below. They were laughing about something-she cannot remember what-when her cousin, a boy of fourteen, stood up too quickly to reach for a line. The skiff tipped. Not badly, not dangerously, but enough that he lost his footing and slid over the gunwale. She saw it happen. He hit the water, came up sputtering, laughing, waving a hand. And then the current took him. It was not a dramatic wave or a shark-just the undertow that runs along the outer drop-off. He was gone before she could even call his name. They found his body two days later, tangled in the mangrove roots on the far side of the island.

She does not talk about that night. She cannot. Whenever she tries, her chest tightens, and the words catch in her throat like fish bones. But the images come anyway-without warning, without mercy. She will be standing at the cleaning table, knife in hand, gutting a tuna, and suddenly she sees her cousin's face, his open mouth, the dark water closing over his head. The smell of the ocean, which she once loved, now makes her nauseous. She has stopped eating fish. She avoids the village wharf. Her boyfriend has started taking the boat out alone, because when she steps onto the deck, her legs go weak and she has to sit down. She used to be the strongest of her crew. Now she cannot even stand the sound of water lapping against the hull at night. She sleeps with the windows shut, a fan running, to drown it out.

Her relationship is strained. Her boyfriend is patient, but she knows he is tired. She snaps at him for no reason-when he comes home smelling of salt, when he laughs too loud, when he looks at her with that worried, searching expression. She knows he loves her. She also knows she is pushing him away, and she cannot stop. At night she has dreams where she is underwater, lungs burning, and she wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat. Sometimes she does not wake up at all-she just lies there, frozen, listening to her own heartbeat, convinced that if she closes her eyes again she will see the boy's hand disappearing beneath the surface.

She stopped going to church. The pastor's voice reminds her of the prayers they said at the funeral. She cannot look at the ocean without feeling that pull, that cold certainty that it is only a matter of time before it takes someone else. She grips the armrest of the chair in my office as she tells me this, knuckles white. She is here because her grandmother insisted. But she does not believe talking will fix anything. She just wants the images to stop. She wants to be able to stand on her own boat again. She wants to sleep without seeing that hand, still reaching, still reaching, as the water swallowed him whole.

He lives alone in a small house at the edge of town, the kind with a corrugated iron roof and a wooden porch that looks out toward the ocean. He has lived here for almost forty years, ever since he moved to this island as a young man. The house is cluttered with half-finished canvases, tubes of oil paint, and brushes that he cleans every evening with a patient, almost ritualistic care. He paints every day, usually from early morning until the light fades, but he no longer paints what he used to.

Before, he painted the market. He loved the market. He would set up his easel near the fish stalls or the fruit vendors, mixing bright yellows and reds and greens, trying to catch the way sunlight hit a pile of mangoes or the glint of a knife as a fishmonger scaled a catch. People knew him there. They would stop and look at his work, sometimes buy a small canvas to hang in their homes. He was known as the painter who captured the life of the village.

That morning, he was at the market. It was a Tuesday, he remembers, because Tuesdays were less crowded. He was working on a painting of a woman selling woven baskets. The explosion came from somewhere near the bus stop. He does not remember the sound, only the pressure, the way the air seemed to turn solid and then push him sideways into a pile of burlap sacks. When he opened his eyes, there was dust everywhere and a ringing in his ears, and someone was screaming. He tried to stand but his legs would not hold him. He saw a man he knew-a baker, a quiet man who always gave him free bread-lying on the ground, not moving.

He was helped to a clinic. His eardrum was ruptured in one ear, and he had cuts from flying debris, but nothing broken. The physical wounds healed. The hearing in that ear never fully returned.

Now, he stays home. He cannot go to the market. Even the thought of it makes his chest tighten and his hands begin to tremble. He tried once, about a year after the bombing, but he made it only as far as the edge of the square before his vision started to blur and he had to turn back. He has not tried again. He buys his food from a small store a few blocks from his house, one that never has more than two or three customers at a time. He goes early, before the crowds.

He still paints, but the colors have changed. He uses more grey now, more brown. He paints the sea at dusk, the shape of rocks, the empty spaces between things. He paints the view from his porch, over and over, because it is safe. He does not paint people anymore. Once, he tried to paint a figure, just a silhouette in the distance, but his hand shook so badly he could not control the brush. He set the canvas aside and has not touched it since.

At night, he has trouble sleeping. He lies awake and listens to the wind or the creak of the house, and sometimes he hears the sound that is not a sound, the impossible pressure of an explosion that happened eight years ago. He gets up and walks through the dark rooms, checking the locks, even though he knows they are secure. There is no danger here, he tells himself. But his body does not believe it.

He has a daughter who lives on the mainland. She calls every Sunday. He tells her he is fine, that he is painting, that the weather is good. He does not tell her about the dreams, or the way he startles when a truck backfires, or how he sometimes stops mid-stroke and stares at the canvas without remembering what he was doing. He does not tell her that he feels as though part of him is still lying on that ground, in the dust, waiting for someone to help him stand.

The PCL-5 score of 48 means little to him. He only knows that his life has narrowed to this small house, to these quiet mornings, to the steady work of filling a white surface with color. He is still a painter. He is just painting a different world now.

He remembers the exact sound of the beep. Not the monitor's normal rhythm-the one that stayed steady for three weeks in the PICU-but the sudden flatline tone that ripped through the 3 a.m. silence. That was six years ago. His daughter, Mira, was four. She had been a healthy, giggling child until a sudden fever turned into sepsis, then multiple organ failure. He can still feel the cold vinyl of the hospital chair pressing into his back, the way his wife's nails dug into his palm, the way his own voice sounded foreign when he screamed for a nurse. They coded her twice that night. She survived. He didn't.

These days, Ravi works from the small studio he built in the garage. He is a character animator for a streaming network, known for his fluid, whimsical movements-cartoon animals that bounce and dance. But since Mira's illness, his hand has tightened. He draws scenes of hospitals, waiting rooms, IV poles, but always erases them before anyone sees. When a director sends a storyboard with a sick child, even a minor background element, Ravi's chest tightens. He finds a reason to reject the assignment: the deadline is too short, the rig is too complex. He doesn't say why. He cannot say why.

At home, he checks on Mira's breathing every night. She is ten now, healthy and strong, running through the backyard with her friends. But Ravi still stands in her doorway at 2 a.m., watching the rise and fall of her chest. He times each breath. If she shifts in her sleep, his stomach drops. He once drove her to the emergency room because she coughed twice in a row. The doctor said it was allergies. Ravi didn't sleep for two days.

His wife, Priya, has stopped asking why he sleeps on the couch. She knows about the nightmares-Mira's face turning blue, the beep, the doctors saying "we're losing her"-but she doesn't understand why he won't talk about it. When she tries to bring up that night, Ravi's jaw locks. He stares at a fixed point on the wall. His mind goes blank, or full, he can't tell. He just knows the pressure in his chest is unbearable, and the only way to stop it is to leave the room. He goes to his studio and animates a single looping sequence: a butterfly landing on a flower, again and again, for hours.

At work meetings, he is sharp. He notices every detail-a dropped coffee lid, a flickering light, a colleague's hand tremor. These details lodge in his mind like splinters. He cannot stop tracking them. He has constructed elaborate mental escape routes for every room he enters. He keeps his back to the wall in restaurants. He avoids hospitals entirely, even for his own checkups. Once, when his mother-in-law was admitted for a minor surgery, he drove her to the entrance and said he had a deadline. He waited in the parking lot for four hours, shaking, gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened.

Last week, his supervisor asked him to lead a short film about a child's first day at school. Ravi said no. He gave no reason. He feels the old tightness climbing up his throat now, just thinking about it. He hasn't cried since the night Mira coded. He doesn't trust himself to start.

He sits in his studio, cursor blinking on an empty canvas. He wants to draw a laughing child. He cannot. The beep is still in his ears.

She still wakes before dawn, the same way she did for fifty years, though now there is no field site to drive to, no data to log. At seventy-seven, Margaret lives alone in a small house at the edge of a town that was once a logging camp. The walls are covered with topographic maps and photographs of rivers, but she cannot look at the one taken in the Klamath Basin-not without her chest tightening. She does not need to see it; she remembers every detail.

The event happened in 1972, when she was a twenty-five-year-old environmental scientist fresh out of graduate school. She had been sent to a remote part of the Pacific Northwest to conduct a vegetation survey for a proposed dam. The work was solitary, and she loved it. On the third night, the camp host-a man in his forties, someone she had exchanged pleasantries with-came to her tent. He did not ask. He did not stop when she said no. She remembers the smell of pine resin and the sound of her own breath. She remembers the weight of him, and the way the tent canvas pressed against her face.

Afterward, she told no one. She finished the survey in four days instead of seven, barely sleeping. She filed her report, which was thorough and correct, and then she requested a transfer to a desk job analyzing water quality samples. She told herself it was a logical career move-more stability, less fieldwork. But she never again spent a night in a tent. She never again camped under the sky.

Margaret's professional reputation grew. She became known for her meticulous data and her refusal to collaborate with male colleagues after office hours. She never married, never had children. When asked, she would say she was married to her work. And she was. The lab was a fortress: four walls with a lock, predictable instruments, no one who could reach her without permission.

But the fortress had cracks. For decades, she has had nightmares-vivid, recurring scenes of being pinned in a small space. She avoids forests entirely, even now. She lives in a house with no trees close to the windows. She drives only on main roads. When a stranger knocks at her door, she freezes, heart hammering, and waits until they are gone. She has not been to a doctor's appointment alone in twenty years-a female neighbor drives her.

At work, she became obsessive about safety protocols, especially for young women. She once told a junior scientist, "Never trust a man who offers to help you set up camp." She did not explain why. She could not.

Now, in retirement, Margaret has more time, and the silence is worse. She cannot ignore the thoughts anymore. She replays that night in loops, trying to find a detail she might have missed-something she could have done differently. She feels guilty for not reporting him, guilty for surviving, guilty for being too afraid to tell her mother. She has not spoken the word "rape" aloud in fifty years. When the news reports a sexual assault, she turns off the television. She has stopped going to the grocery store at night because the parking lot lights make her feel watched.

She did not come to therapy willingly. Her neighbor noticed she had stopped eating properly and made the call. Margaret sat on the edge of the couch, hands clasped, and said, "I don't know why I'm here. It happened a long time ago." But her foot was tapping, and her eyes scanned the room for exits. The PCL-5 score of 73 tells a different story than her words. The forest of her own mind is still the place she cannot enter.

He was twenty-two when the men came. They took him off the boat, just outside the territorial waters where the fishing was best-a spot his father had shown him years ago. He remembers the cold metal of the deck railing against his back, the smell of diesel and salt, and then the blindfold. For three weeks, he was held in a concrete room with no windows. The questions were always the same: who did he work for, what did he know, where were the patrols. He had no answers, but they kept asking. They used electricity. They used water. They used his own hands to show him what they could do to his fingers if he didn't talk.

Now he is twenty-six. Married for two years. The wedding was small, on the dock where his boat still moors-the same dock where he used to tie the lines without thinking. Now he cannot step onto it without his chest tightening. He leaves the house an hour early every morning so he can walk a longer route, avoiding the harbor until the last possible moment. He tells his wife it's for the exercise. She knows better, but she has stopped asking.

On the boat, he works with his cousin, Mikka. They head out before dawn, past the buoys, into the gray water. The engine hum is a sound he once loved-a kind of heartbeat under the deck. Now it makes him flinch. Every time the radio crackles, he freezes. Mikka has learned not to talk to him during those seconds. He just waits until the color returns to his face.

The worst part is the nights. He cannot sleep in the bedroom anymore. The walls are too close. He sleeps on the couch, with the television on, volume low, so he can hear the door. His wife wakes sometimes to find him standing at the window, staring at the driveway. He tells her he couldn't sleep. He does not tell her about the dream where the concrete room floods and the water tastes like copper.

He has stopped going to the pub. He used to drink with the other fishermen, telling stories about the one that got away. Now the noise of laughter makes his skin crawl. He tells himself they wouldn't understand anyway. How can you explain that the smell of diesel brings back the taste of the rag they stuffed in his mouth? How can you say that the feel of a fish line tightening on his palm reminds him of the rope around his wrists?

At work, he is competent but hollow. He baits the traps, pulls the nets, bleeds the catch. But he no longer looks out at the horizon. He looks only at what is immediately in front of him-the next knot, the next hook, the next minute. His hands do the work, but his mind is somewhere else, tracing the edges of a room he cannot leave.

His wife told him last week that she found him under the bed, curled up, not moving. He doesn't remember it. He only remembers a sound-a car backfiring-and then the darkness under the frame, the dust smell, the way it felt almost safe because nothing could see him there.

He has not told anyone about the scar on his lower back. He hides it from his wife in the shower, turning away. It is a small, clean circle, like a cigarette burn. But it was not a cigarette. He never talks about the fingers. He cannot bend his left thumb all the way. Every morning when he ties his boots, he feels the stiffness, and he remembers how they bent it back until he heard something pop. He does not tell the doctor. He does not tell anyone.

The sea is the same as it always was. Flat. Infinite. Indifferent. He goes out on it every day because it is all he knows how to do. But he no longer trusts the horizon. He no longer trusts the silence. And when Mikka claps him on the shoulder to say the nets are full, he does not smile. He flinches.

Fatima sits at her desk, the fluorescent light humming overhead. She is running her finger down a column of numbers for the fourth time. The digits blur and then sharpen, blur and sharpen, but she forces her eyes to stay on the page. She knows the column balances-she checked it yesterday, and again this morning-but the thought of missing a single error tightens her chest. Her supervisor once told her she is the most meticulous auditor on the team, and Fatima smiled stiffly, because she cannot explain that her thoroughness is not patience. It is fear.

Three years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon, Fatima received a phone call from her cousin in the old city where she grew up. She was at her desk then too, in the same gray cubicle, and she remembers the way her hand shook as she pressed the phone to her ear. The line crackled, and her cousin's voice was hollow, reciting words that seemed to belong to someone else's story. Her younger brother, Khalid-the one who stayed behind when she emigrated fifteen years earlier-had been shopping in the market when a bomb hidden inside a vegetable cart detonated. He was not killed instantly, the cousin said. He died in a clinic an hour later. Fatima did not cry. She hung up, opened her spreadsheet, and continued typing until her shift ended.

She flew back for the funeral, and she insisted on seeing his body before the burial. The morgue was cold and smelled of bleach. The attendant pulled back the white sheet, and Fatima saw Khalid's face-pale, peaceful, a small cut above his eyebrow that she had never noticed when he was alive. That image embedded itself behind her eyelids. She still sees it every night when she closes her eyes, usually at three in the morning, when she wakes gasping from a dream where the bomb is still ticking and she is running, running, always too late.

After the funeral, Fatima returned to her apartment in the Midwest and tried to resume her life. She cancelled her subscription to the Arabic news channel because every report from the region triggered a hot, tightening sensation in her throat. She stopped calling her cousin, not out of anger but because hearing his voice brought back the crackling phone line. She told herself she was moving on.

But moving on, for an auditor, is not possible when every number feels like a clue to a catastrophe she failed to prevent. At work, she triple-checks the smallest line items. If a $3.50 discrepancy appears in a quarterly report, she cannot rest until she traces it to its source. Her colleagues joke that she is obsessive, but Fatima does not laugh. The stakes feel absolute. One mistake, she thinks, and the whole system collapses. This is not professional pride-it is a vigilance she cannot turn off. She once stayed until midnight to verify a single decimal point, and when she finally drove home, she found herself scanning every shadow between streetlights, her foot hovering over the brake.

She has not dated in years. She tells herself she is too old, too set in her ways. But the truth is simpler. She does not trust herself to protect anyone. If she could not save Khalid from a market street two continents away, how could she keep anyone safe in the same city? That guilt sits in her chest like a stone, and some days she presses her palm there while waiting for the elevator, feeling the slow thud of her heart.

Last week, the senior manager asked her to mentor a new junior auditor. The young woman reminded Fatima of herself thirty years ago-eager, precise, unaware that the world could split open on a Tuesday afternoon. Fatima agreed, but she gave the new hire only terse instructions and avoided eye contact. She did not want to attach herself to someone she might fail.

Tonight, as she locks her desk drawer and walks to the parking lot, she notices a sedan idling a few spaces away. The driver is talking on the phone, his face half-lit. Her pulse jumps, and she stops breathing for a moment. It is nothing-just a man waiting for a passenger. But she does not relax until she is inside her locked car, doors locked, engine running, already planning the safest route home.

She has been a paramedic for eight years, and for most of that time the job felt like a calling. But now, pulling on her uniform in the dark hours of a 6 a.m. shift, she pauses with her fingers on the zipper. The fabric is stiff, and for a moment she is not in her own apartment-she is back on that street last February, the cold air sharp in her lungs, the weight of the trauma kit digging into her shoulder.

That night started like any other call: a man down, possible overdose, dispatched with a police priority. She arrived with her partner, and the scene was already loud-officers shouting, one of them kicking a plastic bottle out of the way. She knelt beside the patient, a young man not much older than her own brother, his lips already blue. She started compressions, counting in her head, trying to shut out the noise. Then the shouting got closer, and one of the officers grabbed her arm. You need to back off, we need to secure the scene first. She explained-two minutes, just give her two minutes-but he yanked her backward so hard she fell onto the asphalt, her knee scraping through the pants, the radio skittering away. By the time she was allowed back, the patient had no pulse. She remembers the officer's face, the way he looked at her like she was nothing.

That image has not left her. It comes back when she is trying to fall asleep, or when a car backfires on the highway. It comes back when she sees a police cruiser in her rearview mirror, and her hands tighten on the steering wheel until her knuckles go white. She has started requesting only non-emergency transfers, avoiding the 911 response calls she used to love. Her supervisor has noticed, asked if she is okay. She said she is fine, just tired.

Divorced two years before the incident, she lives alone now, and she prefers it that way. The quiet is easier to control. She checks the locks on her apartment door three times before bed-has done that since childhood, but now it is worse. She avoids the news. If a story about police violence comes on the radio during her drive, she turns it off mid-sentence. Her mother called last week and asked why she sounds so distant. She said she was busy.

On shift today, her partner hands her a coffee and tells her about his weekend. She nods, but she is scanning the parking lot, looking for any patrol cars. An hour later, they get a call for a chest pain, and the address is near the same intersection from February. She tells her partner she has to pull over. She opens the door and vomits onto the curb, just clear bile and coffee. She wipes her mouth, says she thinks she ate something bad.

She knows this is not just bad food. At night, she lies awake with the memory of the officer's hand on her arm, the sting of the asphalt, the sound of her own voice begging him to let her save a life. She dreams about the patient's face, and sometimes she dreams the face is her own. She wakes up gasping, sure she is being dragged again.

She has stopped going out with friends. She cancelled her gym membership. The only time she feels partially safe is when she is driving alone on a back road, no sirens, no radios, no uniform. But even then, she watches every mirror, waiting for the lights to appear behind her.

Mr. A. is a 78-year-old man who has been married to his wife, Fatima, for 53 years. He sits in the chair across from me with his hands resting on his knees, his back straight, his eyes fixed on a spot on the floor. He speaks slowly, with a slight accent, choosing each word carefully. He is a roofer by trade, or rather he was-he retired at 72, but the work has never really left him.

The story he tells begins in the summer of 1978. He was 32, working on a new high-rise in downtown Los Angeles. It was a job he had done a hundred times before: sweeping the tar, heating the asphalt, laying the felt. That afternoon, the foreman told him to seal a patch near the ventilation shafts. The chemical was a solvent-based primer, strong enough to make his eyes water. He didn't have a mask-none of the men did. The fumes were thick, clinging to the air like fog. He remembers the taste of it, metallic and sweet, coating his tongue. Within ten minutes, his head was pounding, his vision blurring. He vomited on the roof. The foreman told him to go home. He drove himself, white-knuckled, unable to stop shaking.

That was the first time. But it wasn't the last. Over the next decade, he worked on dozens of roofs where the same chemicals were used. He learned to ignore the nausea, the dizziness, the burning in his lungs. He told himself it was part of the job. He was a roofer-men didn't complain. He had a wife and three children to support. So he kept working, his hands black with tar, his skin rough from the wind.

The nightmares started in his late fifties. He wakes up gasping, his throat tight, smelling the sweet chemical even though the room is clean. Fatima has learned not to reach for him in the dark-he flinches, sometimes swats her arm away without meaning to. He avoids the garage where he keeps his old tools. He can't stand the smell of paint thinner, and he refuses to let anyone use a gas stove if the flame is even a little blue. At family dinners, his grandchildren sit at the other end of the table. He knows they think he is grumpy. He doesn't correct them.

He retired because his hands started trembling. But the symptoms only got worse. He is hypervigilant-he checks the thermostat three times a day to make sure the gas isn't leaking. He cannot drive past a construction site without his heart racing. Once, two months ago, he saw a poster for a new housing development and had to pull over. He sat in the car, gripping the steering wheel, waiting for the world to stop spinning. He told Fatima it was a dizzy spell. He does not want to worry her.

His memory has become patchy. He forgets appointments, loses his keys, leaves the kettle on until it boils dry. Fatima writes notes for him on the kitchen counter. He feels stupid. He was a good roofer-he could read a blueprint, estimate a slope, balance on a ridge like it was flat ground. Now he cannot remember the names of his old crewmates. The shame sits in his chest like a second heartbeat.

He has not slept through the night in years. The intrusive images come during the day too: a flash of blue tarpaulin, the hiss of a pressure washer, the taste of metal in his mouth. He thinks he is going crazy. He is here because his son, a nurse practitioner, made the appointment. Mr. A. does not believe talking will help. But he came anyway, because he does not know what else to do. He sits in the chair, and he tells me about the roof.

He remembers the sound first-not the explosion itself, but the way the air seemed to tear apart, a ripping noise that followed a flash of white. It was a Tuesday afternoon, and he had stepped out of the courthouse to grab coffee, walking through the plaza where a memorial ceremony was being held for a fallen officer. He never saw the bomber, only the aftermath: bodies on the ground, a woman screaming, a child's shoe lying beside a broken flower arrangement. Marcus helped carry a wounded man to an ambulance, his hands slippery with blood he couldn't wipe away for hours. That was three years ago.

Now, at thirty-three, Marcus is a prosecutor in the same office. His wife, Elena, says he hasn't been the same since that afternoon. At first she was patient, understanding. But now she watches him from across the dinner table, her fork halfway to her mouth, waiting for him to finish a thought that never comes. He knows she's tired of his silences. He's tired of them too.

At work, Marcus still wins cases-he has to. The courtroom is the only place he feels any sense of control. But lately, during pretrial conferences, he finds himself scanning the gallery for suspicious bags, counting exits, measuring the distance to the nearest door. One afternoon a junior associate brought a birthday cake into the conference room. The sharp pop of a champagne cork sent Marcus under the table before he could stop himself. He laughed it off, said he was just clumsy, but his hands shook for the rest of the day.

The nightmares started about six months after the bombing. They're not always the same, but the pattern is consistent: a bright light, the tearing sound, then he's running through the plaza, except now the people are made of stone, frozen in terror while he stumbles toward an exit that keeps moving farther away. He wakes gasping, heart hammering, drenched in sweat. Elena used to reach for him. Now she turns over, pretending not to notice.

He avoids crowds. No more farmers' markets on Saturdays, no more subway commutes-he drives an extra forty minutes to work each way to avoid the underground station where he used to transfer. He canceled their annual trip to the state fair, claiming it was a budget thing. Elena didn't push. She knows what he's doing, but she also knows he won't talk about it.

Marcus is a good prosecutor because he can compartmentalize. He can read the autopsy report of a murder victim without flinching, argue motions about a defendant's prior violent acts, stand before a jury and describe the details of a beating. But the moment he leaves the courtroom, the composure crumbles. On the drive home, he replays the bombing in fragments: the shoe, the woman's scream, the weight of the wounded man on his shoulder. He wonders if he could have done more, if he should have stayed longer, if the man he carried survived. He never checked.

His therapist-Elena made him go-says he avoids emotions the way he avoids crowds. He nods, agrees, then spends the rest of the session talking about the finer points of criminal procedure. He knows he's deflecting. He also knows he can't keep going like this, but the idea of letting the memory in fully feels like another bomb going off.

Last week he prosecuted a case involving a threat to a government building. The defendant's lawyer argued diminished capacity; Marcus pushed for a maximum sentence. After winning, he sat in his office for an hour, staring at the blank wall, not sure if he felt relief or rage or nothing at all. When Elena asked how his day was, he said fine. She looked at him, her eyes soft and sad, and said, "You always say fine."

He is fine. He has to be. There's no room for a traumatized prosecutor in a courtroom built on certainty-and he has built his life on the idea that the world is rational, that justice follows logic. But the bombing taught him otherwise. So he works harder, avoids more, and waits for the moment when the sound comes back. It always does.

He still drives his delivery route, but the familiar streets have become a maze of invisible threats. At seventy-seven, Raymond has spent forty years behind the wheel of his small delivery truck, navigating the same suburban neighborhoods, handing packages to the same friendly faces. He knows every shortcut, every house with a dog, every cul-de-sac where he can turn around without backing up. That knowledge used to make him feel competent, even proud. Now it makes him feel like a target.

The assault happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. He was making his usual stop at a strip mall, delivering a heavy box to a pharmacy in the back corner. He remembers the way the afternoon sun slanted through the glass storefront, how it cast long shadows on the linoleum floor. He remembers the man-young, maybe twenty-five, with a faded hoodie and restless eyes-who stepped out from behind a display of greeting cards and asked for the time. Raymond remembers reaching for his wristwatch, and then the explosion of pain as the man's fist connected with the side of his head, the world turning sideways, the floor rushing up to meet him. He never saw the punch coming. He never saw the man's face again, only the blur of sneakers running toward the exit. The security footage was useless-the man's hood had been pulled low.

Raymond spent two nights in the hospital with a mild concussion and three broken ribs from where he'd landed on the edge of a display shelf. The doctors said he was lucky. His wife, Edith, said the same thing, her hand trembling as she held his in the emergency room. But Raymond does not feel lucky. He feels hollowed out, as though the punch knocked something loose inside him that cannot be put back.

Now, every time he approaches a delivery, his heart begins to pound before he even opens the truck door. He parks as close as possible to the entrance, scanning the area for anyone who might be hiding behind a pillar or a parked car. He hates that he does this. He knows it's irrational-the same strip mall, the same afternoon light, the same ordinary customers. But his body does not listen to reason. His hands shake when he hands over a package. His voice comes out thinner than it used to. Customers have started to ask if he's feeling okay.

At night, he lies awake in the bedroom he has shared with Edith for fifty-two years. The memory of the assault plays on a loop behind his closed eyes: the young man's shadow stretching toward him, the fist, the terrible crack in his skull, the taste of blood and dust. He jerks awake gasping, convinced he hears footsteps in the hallway. Edith sleeps beside him, her breathing even and slow. He does not wake her. He gets up and walks through the house, checking the locks on every door, the windows, the basement hatch. He knows the doors are locked. He checks them anyway.

His driving has changed. He takes longer routes now, avoiding streets where he might have to stop and get out, avoiding alleyways, avoiding any place where a stranger could approach without warning. His boss has noticed the delays and told him to "shake it off." Raymond nodded, said nothing.
